# PREFACE.

*...the book on the **Composition of Alchemy** was born. And*
*since your Latin world* <note>original: "latinitas"; referring to the Latin-speaking scholars of Western Europe.</note> *has not yet truly known*
*what Alchemy is, and what its composition*
*might be, I will clarify it in the present discourse.*
*I have set down this word, though it is unknown*
*and marvelous, so that it might become clear*
*through a definition. Indeed, Hermes the Philo-*
*sopher,* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> *and others who came after him, define*
*this term as it appears in the book **On the Change***
***of Substances**:* <note>original: "de Substantiarum mutatione"</note> *Alchemy is a bodily substance*
*composed of one and through one, joining together*
*things of greater value through their kinship and*
*effect, and naturally transforming them into*
*superior natures by a natural blending. In*

# THE DISCOURSE OF MORIENUS OF ROME,
## THE HERMIT OF JERU-
->*salem.*<- <note>original: "Hierosolymitani"; Morienus is traditionally depicted as a Roman who moved to the mountains near Jerusalem to live as a hermit and practice alchemy.</note>

The divine mind of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded by alchemists as the founder of their science.</note> fully grasped all branches of philosophy. When he had spent many years studying the discovery and publication of the higher mastery <term>mastery: Latin *magisterium*, the technical term for the successful completion of the alchemical process, or the "Great Work."</term>, he was the first to finally discover and publish it. He composed a book about it, which he kept as his own, and upon his death, he left it as an inheritance to his disciples. After his passing, his disciples studied this book and its instructions for a long time, so that they might achieve its intended effect. Once they had attained that result, they provided various and even countless instructions about it. They did this specifically so that those who came after them and attained this knowledge would not reveal it to the foolish <note>original: "insipientibus"; the uninitiated or those lacking spiritual preparation.</note>, as if it were something common and vulgar.

A long time after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there arose a certain divine man, endowed with spiritual gifts. After he had spent a great deal of time studying divinity, he discovered this book among the sacred texts. This man was a native of Alexandria; hence, he was called by his name, Adfar of Alexandria. After he found the aforementioned book, he never ceased to study it with a watchful mind and great industry. Once he had studied it for a long time, he achieved its full effect and knowledge. From this knowledge, this divine man gave many various and countless instructions. When these were spread under his name throughout all parts of our region, the fame of this man’s name and his science reached me while I was staying in the city of Rome, as if it had flown there. For at that time, I was living in Rome (where I had been born). I was then a young man,

<header>MORIENUS OF ROME.</header>

...whose chin the first down of a beard had not yet covered; he was indeed a dedicated student, and had been raised as a Christian in doctrine from his earliest years by both his parents. The entire breadth of Latin learning had already revealed itself to him. Having heard, therefore, of this man’s name and fame, I hastily left both my parents and my homeland at once, nor did I allow my limbs too much rest until I had arrived at Alexandria. Indeed, I entered the city, and as a new guest I walked through the streets and alleys for a long time until I found this man’s house. At last, I found his home and went inside. When I had entered, I found this man sitting in his oratory <note>original: *oratorio*; a private room or chapel dedicated to prayer and study.</note> and studying his books.

But after he fixed his eyes upon me, gazing at me, he said: "Friend, come here." I approached him and sat down beside him on the straw matting that had been placed there. He was a man already very advanced in years, yet still vigorous in expression, and handsome in both face and stature. Indeed, his countenance revealed everything that lay hidden in his mind to those who observed him carefully.

After we had conversed, he asked by what name I was called, where I was from, and what the reason for my journey had been. I replied and said to him: "I am called Morienus, a Roman by nation, whom the fame of your name and knowledge <note>original: *scientię*; here referring to the specific "science" of alchemy.</note> forced to leave my parents and my homeland."

But he added: "What is your faith, or which of the gods do you worship?" I replied: "I profess my faith to be Christian; for I am a worshiper of Christ, and I adore Him as God, three and one."

Then Adfar said: "It is well that you sought me out, and found me while I am still hedged in by this mortal life <note>original: *homine mundano septum*; literally "fenced in as a worldly man," implying he is still alive in the physical world before his impending death.</note>. For I will disclose to you the secrets of all divinity <note>The "divine science" or "divinity" in this context refers to the sacred art of alchemy, considered a gift from God.</note>, which until now I have refused to reveal to almost anyone. You, however, must attend to me with all the strength of your mind, for I shall make you a son of my entire discipline."

When these things had been said by both sides, I was filled with exceeding joy. What more can I say? It would be tedious for us to list and describe every detail of what we discussed together regarding the principles of this work. I remained with him at last, and showed myself so devoted to him that he told me the secrets of all divinity. Afterward Adfar died; and a few days after his passing, from...

### ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

I departed from Alexandria and traveled to Jerusalem, where I chose a hermitage within its borders. There, I could lead a life suited to my faith and my religious profession. However, not many years later, a certain King arose in Egypt named Maçoya <note>original: *Maçoya*; likely referring to Muawiya I, the founder of the Umayyad Caliphate</note>. He fathered a son named Gezid <note>original: *Gezid*; referring to Yazid I</note>, who reigned in Egypt after his father’s death and inherited his kingdom. Gezid, in turn, fathered a son named Calid <note>original: *Calid*; referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, a historical prince famously associated with the beginnings of Arabic alchemy</note>, who reigned for a long time in Egypt after his father died. That King was a wise and prudent man, insightful in every branch of knowledge; he held a great love for wise men and philosophers because of the knowledge contained in this book <note>The "book" refers to the secret art of alchemy or the specific teachings Morienus possesses</note>. Indeed, he did not cease to search throughout the provinces, asking both known and unknown people if he could find someone capable of revealing the teachings of this book to him. Driven by this passion, he kept many wise men and philosophers with him who claimed to know the mastery <term>magisterium: the completion of the "Great Work" of alchemy, the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</term> of this book, though they were entirely ignorant of it. He enriched these men with many great gifts, having trusted their words for a long time.

While I was living in a certain hermitage, the fame of this king was brought to me by a traveler. When I heard of it, I left the wilderness and traveled as quickly as I could to the borders of his kingdom. My intent was not to seek riches or gifts from him, but rather to diligently instruct him in spiritual gifts. After I entered his borders, I traveled through many places and finally found the King. Once I had met him and discussed certain matters with him, I found him to be a man of great wisdom, adorned with every virtue and most prudent. Therefore, I said to him: "O good King, may God turn you toward better things. I wish for you to order a house to be prepared for me, one suitable for my mastery." The King then ordered a house to be prepared for me and decorated according to my wishes. I entered this house and did not leave it until I had completed the entire mastery, and I left the finished work there in the house. But around the vessel in which it had been placed, I painted these words:

->THOSE WHO HAVE ALL THINGS WITHIN THEMSELVES,<-
->REQUIRE THE HELP OF ANOTHER IN NO WAY.<-
<note>original: *OMNES QVI SECVM OMNIA HABENT, ALIENO AVXILIO NVLLATENVS INDIGENT.*</note>

After I had written these words, I secretly departed from the city and the entire region, and I returned to my hermitage. Later, the King entered the house I had left behind—

<meta>This page continues Morienus's narrative, describing the immediate aftermath of his departure from King Khalid (Calid). ->### MORIENUS THE ROMAN<-

...and he found the completed mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical "Great Work," often implying the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</term> that I had left behind. When he looked at it more and more closely, he saw the words which I had written around the vessel. Once these were read and well understood, he immediately mourned my absence; and as for all those whom he had kept with him for many years for the sake of this mastery, he ordered their heads to be cut off. Afterward, the King said: "Call Galip, my faithful servant." Now, Galip was his captive <note>original: *captiuus*; likely a high-ranking prisoner of war serving as a trusted official</note>, whom his father Gezid <note>original: *Gezid*; referring to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid I</note> had given to him before his death because of his faithfulness. For the King trusted him greatly, and said to him: "O Galip, my servant, I do not know what I should do hereafter." But Galip said to the king: "My leader, God will provide what we are to do next." The king was greatly saddened, and he grieved day and night more than can be believed.

It then happened after several years, while the king was going out one day for the purpose of hunting to the place called Dirmaroni <note>likely referring to the monastery of Dayr al-Murran near Damascus</note>, that Galip the captive found a certain man praying in the wilderness. He questioned him and said to him: "Friend, who are you, or where do you come from, or where are you going?" And that man answered: "I am a Jerusalemite; for I was born in Jerusalem, and for many years I lived in the mountains of Jerusalem with a certain hermit. While I was staying there, I heard how King Calid <note>original: *Calid*; Khalid ibn Yazid</note> was incessantly searching for someone who could show him the mastery of Hermes <note>original: *magisterium Hermetis*; the secret alchemical art attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note>. After I heard this about the king, I soon departed from my homeland so that I might announce this to King Calid. For I know a man most learned in this mastery, whom I greatly desire to show to the King."

Then Galip said: "Be silent, brother, be silent; let it be enough that you have said this much to me. I would rather you live than die; for many have come to the King who professed that they knew this mastery, but when they could not reach the conclusion of their profession, they were killed by the King. I fear, therefore, that if you stand before the King with this kind of talk, you too may be killed." Then that man said: "Do not fear this, but do not delay in bringing me into the presence of the King." Galip then said: "This pleases me well enough, but take care that you do not die." Galip therefore brought this man and stood him before the King and said: "O good King, here is a man who does not fear to die." As the king [turned] his...

He fixed his eyes upon him, and looking at him, said: "Who are you?" But he, responding, said: "I am a Jerusalemite <note>original: *Hierofolymitanus*; a resident of Jerusalem</note>, who, having lived in the mountains with a certain hermit, heard from many the fame of your name and goodness—and how you unceasingly seek the wise and the teachers who might earnestly show you the Mastery of Hermes <term>magisterium Hermetis: the ultimate secret of alchemy, named after the legendary founder Hermes Trismegistus</term>. I have come to you, therefore, O good King, that you might follow my advice and become the master of your desire. For I know a man living in the mountains of Jerusalem to whom all wisdom has been revealed by the Lord God. Indeed, he is judged most firm in his faith by both God and men. For one day, when we were discussing many things in his hermitage, it happened by chance that he told me he could perform this mastery. Having heard this, and trusting in his truthfulness—which I had often experienced—and also because every year he sent many weights of gold and silver to the city of Jerusalem, as I had often seen, I concluded with certainty in my own mind: that if I were to stand in your presence, you would enrich me with many and great gifts, and you would never separate me from your favor." 

Then the King said: "What kind of speech is this that you utter? Or what ignorant mind persuaded you to come here? Do you not know, you most foolish man, do you not know how many and what kind of men have been killed by me because of such talk? But if those things you say were true (which I do not believe), you would indeed be enriched with many gifts and never again be separated from my favor. However, if they are not true, know that you shall undergo the greatest torment." 

Then the man said: "O good King, I am content with both of your promises; only follow my advice." 

The King said again: "O man, tell me a few things about the character of this man and his appearance. For in years past, a certain man came to me who, to confess the truth to you, performed this mastery for me. When he had finished, he left the completed work with me, but not the knowledge of it <note>The King possesses the alchemical gold, but not the "science" or recipe to recreate it</note>, and he secretly withdrew and departed." 

Then the man said: "This man is very aged, tall in stature, noble in look and face, and adorned with fine manners. His life and appearance are not displeasing to God; for he is a hermit in the mountains of Jerusalem. But if you greatly desire to know his name, he is Morienus the Roman, an old man..."

"May you be well, my King: The good which I now possess, and that which I expect in the future, is from God and placed in His hand. May He do what He wills. Nor do I doubt that among meetings and assemblies a greater rest might be found for me, and in the wilderness and mountains, labor; but no one reaps except he who sows: and what he has sown, that also shall he reap <note>A reference to the biblical principle found in Galatians 6:7, emphasizing that spiritual or alchemical success requires prior effort and "planting."</note>. The King then said: "Everything that you say is indeed undoubtedly true: but because it proceeds from a faithful soul, it seems false." The King said this because he was still a worshiper of idols <note>The text highlights the religious divide; King Calid is depicted here as a pagan/idolater who finds the hermit's monotheistic or ascetic framework alien, despite its logical truth.</note>.

Morienus replied: "If you concede that those things which I bring forth are true, it is necessary that you concede the soul from which they proceed is true and truth-telling. For from true things, true things proceed; and from false things, false; from eternal things, eternal; from transitory things, transitory; from good things, good; and from evil things, evil."

The King then said: "O Morienus, many things indeed have been reported to me concerning you, and your constancy, and your faith; wherefore I wonder greatly, since I now see and hear those things to be true. This, therefore, was the reason why I have long desired both to see you and to hear you at the same time. For I wish that among certain matters (which we shall be discussing), you might instruct me with certain other documents <note>The term "documentis" here refers to proofs, teachings, or written instructions.</note>, and teach me at the same time."

Then Morienus said to him: "O King, may almighty God turn you to better things: for I am not one at whom you ought to wonder much. I am one of the sons of Adam. Indeed, we all proceeded from one, and again to one we shall return, although by a different path. Truly, the long change of time confounds and changes a man who is established under time. Nor have I yet been changed so much that many others, who were before me, were not changed more. Moreover, a dire death follows the final change, by which, clearly, no penalty is judged worse. For before the joining of the body and the soul, and after their dissolution, a punishment more cruel than any death awaits the soul <note>Morienus is likely referring to the state of the soul after death and the importance of spiritual preparation.</note>. But may the almighty Creator, who creates and forms all things from Himself, always be in our aid."

### ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

If you examine it closely, you will clearly recognize that we all agree, and that everything we say is true. Therefore, receive what you have asked in this way. The first and principal substance and <term>materia: the raw material used in alchemy</term> of this thing is one; from it, one thing is made, and while it exists with it, nothing is added to it or taken away. Behold, you now have what you asked for. Now, however, I will bring before you the testimonies of the ancients, so that we may be judged to all agree as one.

Indeed, **Hercules** <note>In alchemical literature, Hercules is often portrayed not just as a hero, but as a "wise King and Philosopher" who understood the secrets of nature.</note>, a certain wise King and Philosopher, when he was questioned by some of his followers, said: "This <term>magisterium: the Great Work or the mastery of alchemical transformation</term> proceeds first from a single root, which afterwards is expanded into many things, and again returns to one." And he said it would be necessary to receive the air.

**Africanus** <note>Likely referring to Sextus Julius Africanus, to whom several alchemical works were attributed in the Middle Ages.</note>, the philosopher, also says: "The four elements—that is, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—proceed from one source, and some of them are made from others among these same things. Of these four, some are like roots, and some are like compounds made from these roots. The roots are **water** and **fire**; those composed from them are **earth** and **air**."

Likewise, **Africanus** said to **Maria** <note>Maria the Jewess, a famous early alchemist credited with inventing the 'bain-marie' or water bath.</note>: "Our water," he said, "holds a mastery over our earth, which is great, bright, and pure. For the earth is also created from the thickness of the water."

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> also says: "Earth is the mother of the elements: from the earth they proceed, and to the earth they return." Hermes says again: "Just as all things proceed from one, so my mastery is made from one substance and matter. And as the four elements are contained in the human body, so God created them situated and distinct, and joined, collected also and diffused through the whole body: since one body merges them and retains them as one, and yet each one of them performs a work unlike the work of the other. And although they are in one body, they nevertheless have different colors and different domains." In the same way, therefore, this mastery is to be understood.

The Philosophers have spoken many such testimonies about this mastery, some of which we shall speak of in what follows.

**King Calid:** "How, and by what reason, can it be that there is one root and one substance and one matter for this mastery, when many and manifold names for that root are found among the Philosophers?"

**Morienus:** "The names of that root are indeed manifold..."

**Morienus:** **Hercules** <note>original: "Hercules quidam"; Hercules was often cited in alchemical texts as a philosopher-king who understood the secrets of nature.</note> said to some of his disciples: "The little stone of the date is nourished by the palm tree, and the palm tree from its own little stone, and from its root many branches grow together, which multiply and increase their number because of it."

Similarly, the ear of corn proceeds from the grain, and many branches come out of one tree, even though the tree takes its beginning from its own seed. 

A certain wise man, who for God's sake had left the whole world <note>This likely refers to a monk or a hermit, similar to Morienus himself.</note>, brings a similar example to us. For he says: "The first creation of man is <term>sperma: the biological seed or essence</term>, and from one grain a hundred grains are procreated, and from a sprout a great tree grows, and from one man a woman similar to him is drawn out, from whom often many sons and daughters are born who are dissimilar in color, appearance, or outward look." 

Again the same wise man says: "Consider the tailor, who is accustomed to sew clothes; from cloth he composes a shirt, or any other garment, whose parts are assigned different names. If these are considered according to their nature, they will be found to be formed from the cloth itself; yet there is but one cloth and principal material from which the garment is made. For the coverlet, the sleeves, and the <term>gussets: the triangular inserts in a garment</term>, although they have different names as parts of the garment, yet their principal material is cloth. Even the threads by which the parts of the garment are joined into one are drawn from the cloth itself; it is not as if the cloth needs something else different from itself for this purpose." 

In a similar way, therefore, this <term>magisterium</term> is a single thing existing by itself, and it needs nothing else. Because among the **Philosophers**, this mastery is hidden and concealed, and wherever it may be, it is called by a thousand names. It is also sealed, nor...

# MORIENUS THE ROMAN

<meta>catchword: What (Quid)</meta>

God’s command cannot fail to happen. For certain people believe that the secret of this <term>mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterium*; the "Great Work" or the hidden art of alchemical transformation.</note> is earth, or stone, or wine, or blood, or even vinegar: and by themselves, they grind and cook all these things, and from their boiling they extract a substance, and they bury what they have extracted. They do this because they believe they are following their own theories, so that their error might be further encouraged and they do not lose hope in finding what they seek. But know that earth and stone, and all these things, are useless for the mastery and lead to a bad end. It is also proper for you to know that the greatest power of this work is judged in its **fire**: for with fire, the minerals are prepared, and the "bad souls" <note>This likely refers to volatile impurities or "spirits" that need to be stabilized or transformed within the base metal.</note> are held back in their bodies. Fire is also its entire nature, as well as the nature and the perfect proof of this matter. Whatever you may achieve in this mastery, if you do not find the "One" at the beginning, it is useless. For what good can be hoped for when the thing itself does not act, nor create within the World? That is to say, it must be reduced into **one body**. If, however, you handle these things according to what we have said, your intention will be fulfilled by the help of God. Therefore, understand well what we have said, and commit what you have understood to your memory; study that arrangement according to its order, and study their arrangement frequently. For frequent study of it will show you its path more clearly. Similarly, you should know that the greatest root of this work lies in the search for the "species" which are best for this mastery. For every mineral is of many kinds.

Regarding what you asked about the **white smoke**, it is proper for you to know that the <term>white smoke</term> <note>original: *fumus albus*; a symbolic term for the purified vapor or "spirit" released during the heating of the materials.</note> is the **tincture**, and it is also the **soul** of these dissolved and even "dead" bodies—those bodies, namely, whose souls we have already extracted and then joined back to their bodies once more. For every body, when it lacks its soul, will be dark and obscure; and the white smoke is that which flows into the body like a soul, so that it might entirely take away its <term>blackness</term> <note>original: *nigredo*; the initial stage of the work, representing rot, darkness, or the "death" of the base material.</note> and its impurity, and consolidate the bodies into one, and multiply their "water." For the impure thing is black and very light: and therefore, when its blackness is taken away, its <term>whiteness</term> <note>original: *albedo*; the second major stage of the work, representing purification and enlightenment.</note> is strengthened, and its water is multiplied, and its beauty will be more apparent, and the tincture will then work more effectively within it.

<summary>Morienus warns against using common substances like blood or vinegar, emphasizing that the true Work depends on fire and the "white smoke" (the soul) to purify the "black" body into a "white" and beautiful state.</summary>

### OF THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

<page-num>37</page-num>

What more is there to say? If all these things have been handled well, the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: *tinctura*; a substance capable of "staining" or transforming base metals into a higher state.</note> will work well within it, and its gold will emerge most pure and reddish—indeed, you will find none better or more pure. For this reason, this gold is usually called "Roman Gold" or "Roman Ethees" <note>original: *Ethees*; a specialized term in this manuscript, possibly a corruption of a Greek or Arabic technical name for the "hidden" or "purified" state of the metal.</note> by some. I also want you to know that if the <term>white smoke</term> <note>original: *fumus albus*; a symbolic term for the volatile spirits or vapors released during heating that must be captured or transformed.</note> were not present, the pure or useful Ethees gold of Alchemy could in no way be produced. This is the very heading of this <term>mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterium*; the complete alchemical process.</note> and, as it were, its entire direction. When the alchemy has been completed, let one part of it be placed among nine parts of silver, for the whole will be converted into the purest gold. Blessed be God, Amen, forever and ever.

->*Here ends the book of Alchemy, translated from Arabic into Latin, in the year one thousand one hundred and eighty-two, in the month of February, and on its eleventh day.*<-

## to Thomas of Bologna, physician
### of King Charles VIII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap letter O, inside of which is a circular diagram featuring a central point with radiating lines, similar to a compass rose or a stylized sun.</image-desc>Having offered you all the service I am able, venerable Doctor and honored lord. You should know that I have received from Lord Alderisus your immense and copious letter, together with the <term>stone of your most secret work</term> <note>original: *lapidem secretissimi operis*; likely referring to a sample of the Alchemical Elixir or "Philosopher's Stone" Thomas sent for Bernard to evaluate.</note>: which was certainly a distinguished proof of friendship. From this, the confidence you have placed in me is manifest and very weighty, as is the greatness and sharpness of the intellect with which you shine. Now, however, I shall gladly respond to your letter. For there are certain things learnedly and ingeniously written by you that I approve of, yet others I shall not arrogantly refute, but by touching upon them more strictly and philosophically, I will treat them differently out of respect and observance for your honor. For in this sacred and hidden art, as in others, practical experience ought to <term>corroborate</term> <note>original: *corroborare*; to strengthen or provide evidence for.</note> the truth of theory. Therefore, venerable Doctor, let us now visit one another through such replies and little books, since we are unable to be united in bodily presence.

Furthermore, it belongs to your wisdom (as you know best) to know and contemplate things through their causes, since experience is deceptive <note>This is a reference to the famous first aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experience deceptive, judgment difficult."</note> if understanding has not preceded it. For in those who practice philosophy, there is a firm meditation of discernment, so that the perfection of the work which must be done may be conveniently brought to its conclusion. Indeed, the chance of error happens to those wishing to approach the work who have omitted and neglected the judgment of <term>mental practice</term> <note>original: *mentalis practicæ*; the intellectual visualization or conceptual planning of an experiment before physical labor begins.</note>, which theory produces in the soul before the physical operations for completing the work begin. For the work follows nature, and not the reverse. Therefore, he who wishes to achieve anything should prepare his soul so that he understands the natures and outcomes of things; only then may he safely set his hands to the labor. In these matters, I clearly recognize your sublime mind, as shown by the experiment described in your letter. ->### BERNARD OF TREVISO ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS<-

[...your intellect to understand how a substance] assumes another quality, and in the <term>decoction</term> <note>original: *decoctione*; the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its nature, much like making a broth.</note> of the mixed thing, it takes on and puts on that quality. In this same way, <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note> in those things familiar and mixed with it, assumes other natures and qualities. For example, if it is joined to <term>Gold</term> <note>original: *Soli*; literally "the Sun," the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>, it takes the qualities of Gold; if to <term>Silver</term> <note>original: *Lunae*; literally "the Moon," the symbol for Silver.</note>, the qualities of Silver; if to <term>Copper</term> <note>original: *Veneri*; literally "Venus," the symbol for Copper</note>, the qualities of Copper; and so it is with other metallic species. 

For this reason, these species must be "boiled" in it, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> itself is their water, in which, through the process of alteration, it convertibly undergoes their changes. And this "water" contracts a nature from them similar to that of <term>vegetables</term> <note>original: *vegetabilium*; in medieval science, this referred to any plant life.</note> boiled in simple water. However, this species is not outwardly altered in color while in its fluid form, because of the density of the matter and the "earth" immersed and united proportionately to the water of the Mercury—though in other transparent liquids, it is found differently. 

For when this nature is altered, it is truly changed, and the color is hidden from the outside under the appearance of the Mercury, so that it does not appear to the sight. This, however, has been more widely discussed and shown by you: how the simple water of rivers is the <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: *prima materia*; the fundamental, formless base of all physical things.</note> and nourishment of plants, and therefore of all living and sentient beings. Therefore, if any of these things are boiled in it, the water receives and puts on the virtue and property of their nature. Thus, although water is naturally extremely cold, by reason of the things boiled in it, it works within us with the effect of "heat in the first degree," to use your own phrasing. 

Furthermore, there is nothing that provides more nourishment than a <term>broth</term> <note>original: *jusculum*; a medicinal or nutritious soup.</note> or decoction of good meats. If the water in which the meat and herbs were boiled—or the things themselves in which they were boiled—are taken while moist, or if that simple water is taken or drunk after the boiling, it does no harm; indeed, it profits and helps much, even though previously, in its simple nature, it might have been harmful. 

This happens because that water is no longer what it was before. Similarly, quicksilver is the "matter" of all metals, and is like water because of the <term>homogeneity</term> <note>original: *homogeneitatem*; having a uniform nature throughout.</note> it shares with plants and animals. It receives the virtue of those things which adhere to it and are mixed with it during the boiling. Thus, although it is naturally very cold, it can be made very hot in a short time; and in the same way, it can be made "temperate" with temperate things through the most subtle ingenuity of the art. However, no metal adheres to it better than gold (as you say), and for this reason, as some believe:

### BERNARD OF TREVISO

->**Gold is nothing other than quicksilver coagulated by the power of sulfur, etc.**<-

Therefore you wish to conclude, as I think—and rightly so—that if gold is <term>boiled</term> <note>original: *decoquatur*; the process of "decoction" or slow heating to extract or refine a substance.</note> or dissolved in quicksilver duly and by the natural path of the art, that quicksilver will acquire the natural properties of that gold. Nevertheless, the way of this boiling and dissolution of metals is known and open to very few: because the cause of that dissolution is the moisture of the quicksilver, constrained by the density of <term>homogeneous earth</term> <note>original: *homogeneæ terræ*; "earth" refers to the solid, dry principle in alchemy; "homogeneous" implies it is of the same nature as the metal itself.</note>, and conversely: the coldness of the earth by its homogeneous water, with the homogeneity of qualities remaining permanent. 

This exists as a simple dryness in it, a double coldness, and a simple moisture under the disproportion of immaturity compared to the <term>equal proportion</term> <note>original: *anaticam proportionem*; likely derived from the Greek "ana," used in pharmacy to mean "of each an equal part."</note> of the mature, digested <term>Sun</term> <note>original: *Solis*; the alchemical name for Gold.</note>. Therefore, the solvent differs from the thing to be dissolved in its proportion and its state of "digestion," but not in its essential matter. For without any external admixture, nature would form the latter from the former, just as nature wonderfully—and through simple means—procreates gold from quicksilver; as you learnedly discussed in your Letter. 

For in <term>vegetables</term> <note>original: *vegetabilibus*; meaning plants or organic matter.</note>, the moisture of simple water is taken for internal dissolution, so that things congealed by art may spread their effects into it. The dissolution of things happens alongside the "congealing" of the water, and the congealing of the water happens with the dissolution of things, and vice versa. It is the same and in the same manner with <term>mineral water</term> <note>original: *aqua minerali*; here referring to Mercury in its fluid state.</note> and its species. 

He who therefore knows the art and secret of dissolution has indeed reached the secret of the art, which is to mix the species and to extract natures from natures, which lie effectively hidden within them. How then can he find the truth who destroys the moist nature of quicksilver? I speak of the fools who distort its form away from its metallic disposition or dissolution, and who corrupt the natural moisture during the process of dissolving. They pull the quicksilver out of proportion, away from that primary mineral quality which requires nothing other than purity and simple boiling. 

For example: those who defile it, destroy it, and change it into something other than the nature of quicksilver by using <term>salts, vitriols, and aluminous things</term> <note>original: *salibus, vitriolis, & aluminosis*; common alchemical additives like sea salt, metallic sulfates (vitriol), and alums. Bernard considers these "corrosives" that ruin the "living" metal.</note>. The <term>Seed</term> <note>original: *Semen*; the essential "starting material" or "sperm" of the metal.</note> which nature has constructed with sagacity and mercy, they attempt to "perfect" by violating and destroying it; thus, they undoubtedly destroy the success of the work. For the seed in humans and sentient beings is formed by nature and not by art, but by art it is <insert>joined</insert>...

<meta>catchword: joined</meta>

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

Cc 5

...it is joined and mixed: however, by subtracting nothing from it, and adding nothing to it, if the same species must be procreated by a newness of kind: thus, while the same matter remains and stands firm, the same form follows, and not otherwise. Therefore, distinguished Doctor, false and vain is every doctrine that alters Mercury, which is the <term>seed</term> <note>original: *sperma*</note>, before the conjunction of metallic species with it. For if it has been dried out, it does not dissolve. What then will it do in dissolving species? For if it has been heated beyond natural <term>digestion</term> <note>original: *digestionem*; in alchemy, this refers to a slow, gentle heating process resembling biological digestion.</note>, it will not effect nor generate heat—as if a feverish heat—in mineral species, and inappropriately it will make the cold hot and the passive active; from which there will be an incorrigible error and a vain work. 

For example: fools make and extract <term>corrosive waters</term> <note>original: *aquas corrosiuas*; likely referring to early mineral acids like nitric or sulfuric acid.</note> from lesser minerals, into which they cast metallic species, and corrode them. They think for that reason that they have been dissolved by a natural solution, which solution indeed requires the simultaneous permanence of the solvent and the solute, so that from both—namely the male and female seed—a new species may result. I tell you truly that no water dissolves a metallic species by natural reduction except that which remains in them in matter and form, and which the dissolved metals themselves can recongeal. 

This does not happen in <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; historically, this term specifically referred to nitric acid, which "violently" attacked metals.</note>, but rather it is a defilement of the compound, specifically of the body to be dissolved. Nor does a water belong to bodies in solutions which does not remain in them during congelations; and finally, Mercury is of this kind, and not strong waters or what fools imagine—a clear and transparent "Mercurial water." For if they divide or obstruct the <term>homogeneity</term> <note>original: *homogeneitatem*; the state of being composed of parts all of the same kind.</note> of Mercury, how will the first proportion of the female seed stand and be preserved? Because in that case Mercury does not undergo <term>congelation</term> <note>original: *congelationem*; the process of becoming solid or "fixing" a liquid substance into a stable form.</note> with the dissolved body, nor will the species rise again in the administration of the art hereafter; instead, it becomes something else, filthy and useless. 

Thus they think they dissolve, wandering away from nature, but they do not dissolve. Because once the strong waters are removed, the body melts as before, nor will that water be permanent for it, nor does it stand under that body as its <term>radical moisture</term> <note>original: *humido radicali*; the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all things, which cannot be destroyed without destroying the thing itself.</note>. The bodies are indeed corroded, and all the more are they alienated from their metallic species. Therefore, solutions of this kind are not the foundation of the art.

<summary>Bernard argues that true alchemical solution requires Mercury to act as a "permanent" seed that merges with the metal, rather than corrosive mineral acids (aqua fortis) which merely destroy the metal's form without creating a new substance. He emphasizes that the solvent must share the same "radical moisture" as the metal to achieve a natural transmutation.</summary>

### BERNARD OF TREVISO

...brought to completion, [transmutation] is not achieved, but rather the impostures of sophisticated Alchemists, who think that in these [corrosive solutions] this sacred art lies hidden. They claim indeed that they perform solutions, but they do not produce perfect metallic species: because they do not naturally remain under that first proportion or species which Mercury allows in metallic species. For Mercury is <term>corrupted</term> <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the Aristotelian concept of a substance losing its current form to take on a new one, much like a seed "dies" to become a plant.</note> with them by alteration and not by dissipation. Because bodies dissolved in it will never be separated from it—as they are by <term>strong waters</term> <note>original: *aquis fortibus*; nitric acid or other mineral acids.</note> or other corrosives—and one species takes on and hides the other, holding it latently and perfectly: just as <term>Sol and Luna</term> <note>The "Sun and Moon," alchemical code for Gold and Silver.</note> are held secretly when dissolved in it. 

For their nature is hidden in Mercury until its <term>reinspissation</term> <note>original: *reinspissationem*; the process of a liquid thickening or re-congealing into a solid.</note>, the cause of which will be that very latency while they are hidden within it: and just as Mercury dissolves them and hides them in its **belly**: so also do they congeal it: and that which was hard, becomes soft: and that which was soft, becomes hard, yet the species remains: which species are metals and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum viuum*; literal translation "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note>. He therefore who dissolves in this way, rather congeals, and the corrupted species, once joined, receive their former shape through the <term>decoction</term> <note>original: *decoctione*; a process of heating or "cooking" the substance over a long period.</note> of the art. Although this dissolution causes various colors to appear—because the species remain as if they were dead—the internal proportion nevertheless remains whole and intact. Whence the Lord speaks in the Gospel in a similar way regarding Vegetables:

> Unless (He says) a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24, used here to explain that the metal must "die" (lose its form) to be "reborn" as the Elixir.</note>

Therefore, this alterative corruption hides forms, releases natures, preserves proportions, and alters colors from the beginning to the end. Because as the "water" begins to cover the "earth," the color **black** begins to be hidden under the **white**; then, as "air" covers the "water" and "earth," the **yellow** color appears, which finally turns into **redness**, specifically when "fire" covers the "air" or the remaining three elements. And these final colors remain hidden and intrinsic and appear under the appearance of a **white spirit** in liquid Mercury, until its re-thickening into the **powder** which is in the bodies: for the <term>animal</term> <note>In this context, the "animal" refers to the "soul" or the animating principle of the metal.</note> lies hidden in the spirit, just as in the thickening of the spirit, the spirit and soul lie hidden in the powder or in the body. For there is corruption in the alteration of things, but not a dissipation of the parts, unless there be superfluous parts to be cast out.

He uses the biblical metaphor of the grain of wheat to describe how the metal's form must "die" and pass through a sequence of color changes (black, white, yellow, red) to be perfected.</summary>

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

[to be] known, are useless for generation: wherefore the craftsman <term>purifies</term> the work, so that <term>digestion</term> <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to a slow, gentle heating process, similar to biological digestion, used to mature or "ripen" a substance.</note> might better occur. An example is clear in grains. For of two grains of wheat, if one is thrown into good earth, there it <term>putrefies</term> <note>original: *putrefit*; the stage of decay necessary for new growth.</note> and dies, and loses its outer form, and nothing from it is dissipated; rather, in its own time, it grows into a multitude of fruit: and thus it is said, and it happens, that there is only a <term>corruption of form</term> and not a <term>dissipation of matter</term> <note>The substance changes its appearance or state, but its essential material remains intact to provide the foundation for new life.</note>. But if another grain is thrown into the fire, then it is corrupted in both matter and form, and the whole is dissipated: and that corruption is useless for generation.

Wherefore water does not dissolve bodies, except those which are of its own species, and which can be <term>thickened</term> <note>original: *inspissari*; the process of a liquid thickening or re-congealing into a solid.</note> by the bodies: nor are bodies ever nourished for generation, except by something similar, to preserve the species lost from that transmutatory body through the art of the craftsman: although vegetables are nourished from different species, yet before they first provide nourishment, they are first assimilated to the proportion of those attracting them once a dissolution has been made.

It must be noted, therefore, that the <term>dissolutions</term> of metals happen in different ways. One is that which fools know: as was said above, using foreign things that do not remain with the dissolved metals themselves: which is called rather a corrosive destruction and a defiling of the compound. The second solution is that which occurs by the power and force of fire, which also is not a true solution, but rather a <term>liquefaction</term> <note>original: *liquefactio*; simple melting as opposed to a chemical or alchemical dissolution.</note> of the elemental parts bound to one another. 

For the heat of the fire externally finds the internal natural fire—or <term>native fire</term> <note>original: *ignis nativus*; the inherent "vital heat" believed by alchemists to exist within all matter.</note>—of its composition within it by dissolving; this internal and proportional fire also dwells in the air, and therefore it dissolves the air itself. Moreover, that dissolved air resides and dwells in water, and water in earth, and the water itself dissolves the earth, so that it liquefies both the <term>active and the passive</term> <note>The "active" and "passive" qualities (such as heat and moisture) that govern the behavior of the four elements.</note>; but that liquefaction is not a true dissolution, indeed it is dissipative: because the elements there are <term>homogeneous</term> to one another, of a fixed proportion from mixed digestion, and one is generally led out from the power of one by the other. And therefore this happens in clean bodies <note>In this context, "clean bodies" refers to pure metals like Gold or Silver.</note>, in which the elemental natures are fixed. Wherefore in them the flame of the fire liquefies them, and dissolves that whole same compound into a flow, and not toward a separation: because fire cannot flow unless it has flowed [toward]...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how elements interact within the alchemical process. Bernar. Trev.

air is substantial to itself: nor does air flow unless water is dissolved; nor does water flow unless the earth also flows, and vice versa: just as the earth is dissolved by water, so conversely, water retains and <term>congeals</term> <note>original: *congelat*; the process of a liquid becoming solid or thickening, often through cooling or chemical reaction.</note> the air, and in the same way, ascending upward, air retains fire in congelation: because the more <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *fixa*; refers to substances that are stable in heat and do not easily evaporate or change.</note> and "fixing" elements, acting together, produce <term>fixation</term>, namely earth and water; and conversely, fire and air act together toward <term>dissolution</term> <note>The process of breaking a solid down into a liquid or vaporous state.</note>. But this "solution" is called the <term>liquefaction</term> of the composite, and not properly its "solution" in the strict sense, because the parts are not dissolved so as to be separable from one another during the generation of the composite—as happens in the third and true Philosophical solution. In that case, when the composite is dissolved in the aforementioned way, the parts nonetheless remain inseparable, although they are "separable" in potential, so that the virtue of the most highly <term>digested</term> elements can be extracted from the things to be dissolved by the dissolving agent, namely by <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*; Mercury. Considered the "womb" or universal solvent in many alchemical traditions.</note>: and the coarse parts in such a dissolution take on the breadth of subtlety: because the body is turned into <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritum*; a substance in a volatile or gaseous state, capable of penetrating other materials.</note>: and conversely, the spirit is turned into body, and fixed things are converted into <term>volatile</term> things, and volatiles into fixed things.

For this solution is possible and natural, namely through the art of nature's minister, and it is the only necessary solution in the work of the Philosophers: which can be achieved by no other thing, except by quicksilver alone with a wise proportion: just as a good craftsman, knowing the inward natures and proportions, must balance them at the start of the work. For this work, my Lord, these two are capable of, and nothing else enters into it, nor generates and multiplies it, as was said before.

Furthermore, you say that gold, according to the opinion of many, is nothing other than quicksilver naturally congealed by the power of <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: *sulphuris*; in alchemy, Sulfur often represents the active, masculine, or combustible principle, while Mercury represents the passive or feminine principle.</note>: yet in such a way that in the substance of the gold, nothing remains of the sulfur which congealed that gold: just as in a human fetus when it is conceived in the womb, nothing remains of the father's seed, according to the opinion of **Aristotle**, but the male seed only congealed the woman's menstrual blood: in the same way, after the quicksilver has been so congealed, you say that the form of gold is perfected in it by the power of the celestial bodies, and especially the **Sun**: Truly, with your leave and respect, I would say that it should not be thought of in this way. For while it should be believed philosophically that gold is nothing other than <term>anatized Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurium anatizatum*; a specialized term likely meaning Mercury that has been "re-iterated," refined, or brought back to its essential state through repeated cycles.</note>:

<summary>Bernard explains the elemental mechanics of alchemy, distinguishing between simple melting and a "Philosophical solution" where bodies and spirits are exchanged via Mercury. He also begins to refute the common theory that gold is formed by sulfur congealing mercury, using a biological analogy from Aristotle.</summary>

->that is, equally <term>digested</term> <note>original: *digestum*; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to a process of slow, constant heating that matures a substance, similar to how food is broken down in the body.</note> in the bowels of the mineral earth, and in this way the Philosophers indicated that it is created from the contact of <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: *sulphuris*; here referring to the active, masculine principle of combustion and "fixation," rather than the common yellow mineral.</note> coagulating the Mercury itself, and from the cause of its work—that is, from Mercury—with a proportional heat digesting and thickening it. ...is found to be subtler and more simple, although not entirely pure. Then, descending further through the **sphere of fire**, they move that fire and reflect it into the denser air. And likewise, these rays, proceeding perpendicularly to the lower regions through the sphere of air, move into the water itself (which is denser than air), from which they are reflected back into the air. And so, in their own way, they are reflected back into the air by the water they have moved, which is seen even more greatly in the earth, given its different density compared to the other elements. 

From this **decoction** <note>original: *decoctione*; a process of heating or "cooking" that leads to refinement or ripening.</note> and reflection, the elements are moved invisibly, though not imperceptibly: for we feel heat from the motion of the heavens. This heat is always reflected from a higher or subtler element into its lower and denser neighbor, down to the surface of the earth, by means of the rays of the stars descending perpendicularly from above into the lowest depths. Thus, when they are moved and reflected in this way, and through the reflected rays of the **Sun**, **accidental heat** <note>original: *calor accidentalis*; heat that is not essential to the ray itself but produced as a secondary effect of its motion and reflection.</note> is produced in this middle realm. 

Sometimes, however, other qualities are produced here below through the rays of other stars, such as dryness or coldness, as is clear from **Astronomy**. This is not because the rays are hot in themselves, but they are merely the cause of heat for the reason already stated. That these things are true is clearly known from **Astronomy** and the art of **Perspective** <note>original: *Perspectiua*; the medieval science of optics and the behavior of light.</note>, from which we learn how generations or "influences" occur in plants and sentient beings. Therefore, let these remarks suffice. 

Vain **Astrologers**, however, feel differently: they think the influences of heaven exist by virtue of its active power <note>original: *virtute actiuitatis*.</note>, and not by virtue of its motion—which is false. For the rays of heaven produce or effect nothing in the upper orbits from which the heaven might actively "flow" into lower things. Indeed, such rays cannot be reflected into the aforementioned orbits, nor can they be mixed with them, in the same way they are reflected in and mixed with the elements...

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

...arranged as this or that metallic species requires. However, that which is considered to be a "second sulfur"—which ought to be cast aside—is a kind of dross <term>scoria; the waste material or "slag" left over after metal is smelted</term> and dregs of metals contracted during the solidification of **Mercury**. It is a certain superfluity that, being foul and impure during the ripening <term>digestion; in alchemy, a process of slow heating to mature or "cook" a substance into a higher state</term> of **Mercury** into metallic form, could not withstand the freezing <note>original: *congelationem*; in this context, it refers to the process of a liquid substance becoming a solid metal.</note>. This is because it was not of a uniform nature, nor was it proportional to **Mercury** in a way that allowed it to be solidified and ripened into a metal. 

Some Philosophers have called this dross "combustible sulfur," because it cannot endure the trial <note>original: *examine*; the cupellation or refining process used to test a metal's purity in a furnace.</note> of metals; instead, it vanishes or is separated into dregs. I will offer this example: blood in sentient beings and moisture in plants take on different roles during solidification. Some parts of the blood are proportional to the flesh; therefore, they can be thickened and turned into flesh, retaining the consistency and the name of "flesh." 

However, certain parts of the superfluous moisture reside in the pores; these are not converted into solid flesh at all. Thus, they are cast out through sweat or by medicines and are separated from the true flesh. There are far fewer superfluities in the "sanguine" <note>referring to the healthy, blood-rich "complexion" or temperament in medieval medicine.</note> complexion than in others. In a similar way, we must speak of **Gold** and other metallic species: depending on whether the **Mercury** was purer or more impure in its first solidification, it contained and pulled in more or fewer natural superfluities or dross. 

For this reason, a difference arises during the solidification of **Mercury**, which defines and produces diverse metals. Whatever part of the metallic species is made of **Mercury** is said to be incombustible and inseparably permanent. Even if it is made "volatile" <note>capable of being vaporized or moved by heat.</note> by the Alchemist's art in fixed bodies, it remains naturally inseparable in its elemental proportion. But whatever dross was contracted within the **Mercury** and mixed into it from the start—this occurs during the freezing by heat in the first composition of **Mercury** as it matures into a metallic species. Therefore, being rejected as a foreign substance <note>original: *heterogenea*; meaning "of a different kind," as opposed to the "homogeneous" or uniform nature of pure Mercury.</note> from the "mercuriality" or uniform nature of **Mercury**, it is removed by the trial and separated from the metallic species. In those other metals, many superfluities and drosses prohibit and hinder the contact or adherence of the mixture of those metals—or rather, their frozen **Mercury**—with other raw **Mercury**. 

For those superfluities, as has already been said, are not of the primary composition of **Mercury**, nor of its natural or proportional homogeneity. And although they might be part of the mixture, they are nonetheless not part of its true proportion; for whatever is part of a thing's "proportion" <note>In this context, proportion refers to the essential ratio of elements that defines a specific substance.</note> is not superfluous. Therefore, they cannot be inseparably mixed with **Mercury**—not only with **Mercury** being coagulated by art <note>referring to alchemical solidification</note>, but not even with **Mercury** already coagulated, because the nature of the mineral quality in that same metallic species is joined with them. Since such drosses, when tested by the trial of fire <note>original: *examen ignis*; the refining process used to test a metal's purity in a furnace</note>, are something combustible and therefore separable. ### ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

...remaining [impurities] of those metals which they have accidentally encountered, with coagulated **Mercury**, or with other crude **Mercury**? This is because a simple nature will rejoice and be perfected by adhering to another simple nature that is similar and identical to itself in its primary homogeneity <term>homogeneity; the quality of being uniform in kind or nature</term> and elemental proportion. 

As has been stated, **gold** is nothing other than **Mercury** thickened by its own digestion <term>digestion; the alchemical process of slow, constant heat to mature a substance</term> and elemental action. Therefore, although in the earth there is a difference in maturity between **gold** and **Mercury** (because **gold** is more mature than **Mercury**), there is nevertheless no diversity in their underlying matter. 

For this reason, whatever **gold** has acquired through the digestion of maturity, that same **Mercury** can also acquire for itself without any external help. However, in order to shorten and contract the labor, the **Art** <note>original: "Ars"; referring to Alchemy as the "Great Art"</note> joins **gold** to **Mercury**, as has been said. From these two seeds, it artificially effects and generates the very same thing that nature, by its own action, created from a single seed within the minerals. Throughout this process, the identity of the matter is always preserved, though the power of the action differs from that of nature. 

And therefore, just as nothing foreign to its nature enters into the first composition of this work, it likewise does not multiply anything that is not of its primary disposition. For this reason, some people falsely believe that the **Philosophers’ Stone** is composed of diverse things, or of all things, and that it is nourished by these instead of the aforementioned seeds—even if many different names have been given to it. Nor does this Philosophical work "eat" or convert into itself anything foreign to its nature, because it does not vegetate <term>vegetate; the biological process of growth and nutrition found in plants</term>. 

Therefore, although there is a body and a soul or spirit in the said **Philosophers’ Stone**, it is not "vegetably animated" like trees and plants. For this **Stone**, like all minerals, belongs to the **first imposition** <note>In medieval philosophy, "impositions" refer to the hierarchical levels of complexity in creation; the "first" being the simplest mineral state</note> as previously mentioned, and not to the second or any higher imposition. Trees and plants belong to the **second imposition**, just as sentient beings belong to the third, fourth, fifth, or final imposition. In these four latter impositions, mixed things "vegetate" (grow and consume), for in them the elements are transformed through many transmutations...

## BERNARD OF TREVISO

...and having been altered many times, they are more subtle; therefore they are more active and perfect, even if they are not more durable or permanent in their mixture. This is because the elements within them are not of a fixed composition but are prone to dissolving; for this reason, they take in nourishment **vegetatively** <term>vegetatively; in the manner of a plant, growing from within through biological or "vital" processes</term>. 

Our **Stone**, however, like all minerals, is of the **first imposition** <term>first imposition; a term referring to the primary, non-living state of mineral matter</term>. It does not grow like a plant, nor is it nourished vegetatively. Instead, its nourishment occurs through the **apposition** <term>apposition; growth by adding new material to the outside of a substance, like a crystal growing in a solution</term> of a nature similar to its own, rather than through biological growth. 

For example, as is shown by experience, this **Philosophical Stone** is nourished by "feminine sperm" <note>original: "spermate fœminino"; in alchemy, this usually refers to the refined Mercury or the "Mother" substance that receives the "Male" seed of Gold</note>—specifically, from **Mercury** applied to it in a way that is unifying, imperceptible, and compounding—all mediated by the digestion of heat. 

It takes what is similar to itself and assimilates it through addition, not through biological multiplication. For this reason, it emerges heavier in quantity and more active and perfect in quality. Neither fire nor heat multiplies our **Stone** as if it were its proper food, for heat is not part of its primary composition; rather, fire heats it as an external influence <note>original: "extrinseco accidenti"; an outside factor or accidental property rather than an internal substance</note>. 

How, after all, could flame or fire multiply the **Stone** itself or make it heavier on its own, when it cannot be fixed and permanently mixed with it, nor does it share its primary composition or form? Therefore, nothing nourishes and multiplies the said **Stone** toward the generation of its own form except for the "feminine sperm," which nourishes it by means of heat. It nourishes it not **vegetatively**, but through **addition** and mixture. 

He who multiplies and nourishes in this way will not go astray, because this nourishing substance is converted into the very same species as the **Stone**. One could, of course, increase the **Stone** and its weight by adding foreign substances, but this would occur outside its natural species and could not be converted into it. 

Such weight would be contrary to nature; that is, it would not result in the same species or a unity of one species. Instead, it would be a mere collection and accidental composition of different species, which could be separated again through testing <note>original: "examine"; likely referring to the "assay" or "trial" by fire to check for purity</note>.

But when the **Philosophers** <note>In alchemical texts, "Philosophers" usually refers to the ancient and medieval authorities such as Aristotle, Geber, or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> say that the **Stone** is made from "every thing," they mean that it is made from the **four elements** <term>four elements; the classical building blocks of matter: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth</term> which are **anatized** <term>anatized; from a Greek root meaning to "equalize" or "proportionately balance" elements so they no longer conflict or dominate one another</term> with one another through proper and natural digestion. Every thing that can be created or destroyed is made from these four elements. 

Therefore, the Philosophers use this comparison to say: our **Stone** is procreated from "every thing"—that is, from every element. For if even one of them were "killed" <note>original: "mortificato"; in alchemy, this refers to stripping an element of its external qualities to reach its essence</note> or destroyed, the entire proportion of **Goldenness** <term>Goldenness (aureitas); the essential quality or "soul" that makes gold what it is</term> would perish, along with its species. 

And although in the broad range of things that can be changed, anything might be generated from the four elements mixed in either actuality or potentiality, it is not said of just any such product, but specifically of our **Golden Stone** (or other things properly **anatized**), that it is made from "every thing." This is primarily because in those things produced not through "anatization" but through a simple balance of elements, not all elements are present in their active state; rather, they exist in their specific balance of acting and being acted upon. Some elements are present only **potentially**—whether as active or passive—while others are present **actually**. 

But in the **Philosophical Stone**, which is **Gold**, since it is an **anatized** work of nature, all four elements—active and passive—are present **actually** and remain in equal proportion. For **Goldenness** is nothing other than the four elements **anatized**. This does not mean that the form and matter are called "anatized," but rather the potentiality and the act. That is to say: they are not anatized and balanced in **quantity** (by weight or size), but in **quality**. This is because the active part does not exceed the passive in its action, nor does the passive exceed the active in its "suffering" <note>In classical physics, "passion" or "suffering" refers to the state of being acted upon by an external force</note>. 

For there is an equal proportion of measures in gold, or in our **Medicine**: double hot, double moist, double cold, and double dry. All are present in the "act of action and passion"—namely, Fire, Air, Water, and Earth—as was said before. All these are said to be **anatized** and balanced in **quality** and not in **quantity**, because they are equally active and passive, and therefore they remain durably within the gold. For in gold, the passive permanently consists within the active; and conversely, the passive...

### BERNARD OF TREVISO

...does not rise up into an active state. Nor is it necessary that the elements be equalized <term>anatic; from a Greek medical term meaning "in equal parts," here referring to the balancing of elemental powers</term> in quantity—that is, that there be as much of the matter of fire as there is of the matter of earth. For if that were the case, fire, in addition to its own inherent quality, would be everywhere; it would not be of an activity equal to the passive earth, but of a far greater power. 

For this reason, in **gold** there is much more of the heavier and more passive element—namely, the matter of **Earth**—rather than the lighter and more active elements. This refers to quantity: in gold, the quantity of **Earth** is greater than that of **Water**; the quantity of **Water** is greater than that of **Air**; and the quantity of **Air** is greater than that of **Fire**. Because of this, gold is the heaviest of all metals. 

Yet, within this unequal proportion of quantity, there exists an equal and balanced <gloss>anatica</gloss> proportion of qualities: the **Hot**, the **Dry**, the **Moist**, and the **Cold**. Each of these qualities is present in gold, as has been stated previously. The cause of this great weight is the lasting solidity of the Earth and Water, and the way the Water dissolves into a single nature <note>original: "homogeneę"</note> with the Earth; for this Water dissolves homogeneous Earth. 

Furthermore, the cause of the weight is their intrinsic mixing through their smallest parts <term>per minima; a phrase meaning the elements are mixed at the most fundamental, microscopic level possible</term>. This is because the Water does not allow the Earth to have any pores or gaps, both in gold and in **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. 

This is different in the other metals. In their solidification <note>original: "congelatione"</note>, because of the dross <term>scoria; the impure, stony byproduct of smelting or metallic growth</term> rejected by the mercurial nature <note>original: "mercuriositate"</note> and mixed with those same metals as a foreign substance, tiny pores are formed imperceptibly. From these pores comes lightness, which is nothing other than the absence of matter; porosity is the opposite of gravity, which is nothing other than the solid placement of matter. Therefore, if there were as much of the matter of Fire in its solidity as there is of the matter of Earth in an equal measured quantity, Fire would be just as heavy as Earth.

Now, the cause of the weight of **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for lead</note> is its immature solidification. It has not yet rejected the dross to its outer parts, which is why pores are formed; however, at the same time, the pure remains mixed with the impure. This is similar to what is found in raw quicksilver, where the thickening <note>original: "inspissatio"</note> and coagulation are still weak. For this reason, Saturn (or lead) retains the weight of its quicksilver, not because of the purity of its solid matter—as is the case with gold—but because of its coagulation or its immature "cooking" <term>coction; the alchemical process of "ripening" a metal through heat and time within the earth</term>.

Therefore, if in this **Great Work** you do not wish to destroy Fire and Air, you must preserve the heat of the compound in a distinct and balanced <gloss>anatica</gloss> proportion. If, however, you do not wish to destroy Air and Water, then you must foster the moisture in that same compound,

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

So, in the same way, you preserve water and earth, or earth and fire, in the said work; it is necessary to properly preserve the cold and the dry through the craftsmanship of the **Philosophical art**. Because if any of these are destroyed, the proportional form and species of <term>goldness; original: "aureitatis"; the essential, metaphysical quality that makes gold what it is</term> perishes. For this reason, the Philosophers say our stone is composed of *every thing*: that is, from every element—the element indeed being preserved intrinsically for itself, and acting as a component in its own right. Therefore, all elements are the principles, both in act and in potentiality, of all alterable things that are to be composed; for that reason, they are called "all things." 

Furthermore, my honored Doctor, for the sake of your honor, it is necessary for you to understand the sayings of the Philosophers according to **nature’s possibility**, and not according to the mere sound of words. For they have treated this sacred and hidden art, and its secrets, under similarities, fables, riddles, and obscure words; they hid them by deliberate effort, lest they be revealed to the unlearned, the impious, and the unworthy. 

Finally, to proceed to the other points of your letter: I have understood that the artifice of your stone is indeed made from gold, but I cannot grasp it in my mind from your writings, because you do not prescribe the first origin of that composition. Therefore, there is no need to treat it more extensively until you have taught the composition and operation more clearly. Nor, indeed, do I believe the **Elixir** or the **Philosophical Stone** consists of the signs appearing in it, nor from the properties of the "nutritive vegetation of the flame" which you attribute to it, as has been clearly shown from what was already said. 

When I received your work and the gift of such a great secret sent to me, I recognized your zeal toward me and your unmerited trust in me. Therefore, I keep that stone for the sake of your friendship and guard it as a most welcome gift, intending to write more to you about it once you have declared its nature more clearly. 

However, because you say that in your stone there are three things—**body, spirit, and soul** (which is clear to you as an expert and operator)—the Philosophers, when they said those three things of natural art were in their stone, understood them through similitude and experiment. For they called the **Earth** the "body" and its "bones," because it is the binder of the compound, preventing the fluid elements from their raw fluidity <note>This refers to the "fixation" of volatile substances, where solid earth prevents liquids or gases from escaping</note>, having fire with it symbolically in its dryness.

<meta>This page continues Bernard of Treviso’s explanation of alchemical terminology, specifically how the "elements" of the Philosopher's Stone are metaphorically compared to the human body, soul, and spirit. It clarifies that while alchemists use biological terms, the Stone is a homogeneous mineral substance, unlike the heterogeneous human body.</meta>

->BERNARD OF TREVISO<-

They called water and air **spirit**, because these are the moistening elements that dissolve the earth. They called air and fire the **Soul**, because these are the elements that ripen and "digest" <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance to mature or transform it.</note> the entire compound. They named them this way by analogy to the human form. Just as in a body of balanced flesh there must be bones to support the frame, so too in the flesh there must be the vitality of the "vegetable accidents," which are called its **spirits**. 

This is in opposition to the errors of the Pagan Philosophers, who thought that the vital spirits were something distinct from the established body and the parts that compose it. Similarly, in human flesh, there must be an **informing soul** that digests the "brutal acts" <note>Referring to basic animal instincts or raw physical impulses.</note> in a man and performs the work of the intellect within him. 

But in our **Philosophical Stone**, one must think differently. In the Stone, "earth" has the name of **bones**, while water and air receive the name of **spirit**. Nor is there a "soul" in it, except insofar as it contains air and fire—a fact I understand you know perfectly well. But the Philosophers divided it in this way: for by means of a "crude spirit," they extracted a "digested spirit" from the dissolved body. What remained for them was a <term>fixed ash; original: "cinis fixus"; the solid residue that remains after heating and does not vaporize</term> which required further dissolution. In this ash, they found a stony, incombustible oiliness and gumminess, which they called the **soul**. It is this soul which "vivifies," joins, <term>waxes; original: "incerat"; the process of softening a substance to a waxy, fusible state</term>, and makes the natures united. In the spirit, they separated the natures; in the oil, they reunited them. 

For our Stone does not have a "formable form," such as a vegetable or sensitive <note>In medieval philosophy, "sensitive" refers to the soul of animals which possesses senses, as opposed to the "rational" soul of humans.</note> form. Rather, it only has a "formed form," which is the elements themselves, because it is **homogeneous** <note>Meaning it is uniform in composition throughout.</note>. The human body, and the bodies of other sentient beings, are **heterogeneous**, because bone, flesh, blood, marrow, hair, and nails are recognized as being different within them. This is quite different in **gold**, in which whatever is found within it is discovered to be of a single species. 

Therefore, venerable Doctor, the Philosophers speak in these analogies for the sake of the administration of the art and the operation of nature. It is not because there is literally a soul in the stone—except metaphorically (as you skillfully understand)—nor a spirit, nor a body in the sense of a "formable form" as is found in man and other sentient creatures. 

**Truly I say to you** <note>original: "Amen dico tibi"</note>, that the **oil** is what naturally "waxes" and joins the natures, and naturally introduces the medicine into...
