...is referred to the Elixir: because in this work, the Elixir precedes **azoc** <note>In this context, azoc refers to a refined mercurial spirit extracted from the initial mix</note> and not the other way around: just as water, oil, and spirit precede the soul. For from the Elixir, **azoc** is drawn out and extracted, just as oil is from water, and not vice versa; as is mentioned elsewhere. 

For example: just as in the medical art, pure spring water is joined with the meat of a chicken in a simple and first <term>decoction; the process of boiling a substance to extract its essence</term> through <term>elixation; original: "elixationem," the act of boiling or seething</term>. From this first stage of boiling, there emerges a broth and a decoction that is perfect and good; namely, because the moist, watery parts and the "airy" essence of the chicken have been dissolved into the said water—even though other elements are also present there in actuality. 

However, so that a much more perfect medicine may be made, and one more noble for restoring health to a sick human body, the chicken meat (which was boiled with the water and already changed into broth) or a part of it, is pounded and distilled with a stronger boiling. From this comes a broth and decoction that is much more noble and potent, participating in the nature of the whole chicken. This is because in this second boiling, not only the moist parts of the chicken are dissolved, but also the hot parts—that is, the airy and fiery parts—are melted and mixed into the broth itself. Therefore, the entire virtue and power of the chicken is extracted into that liquid by such a boiling. 

Similarly, it happens in the **Philosophical work**, because the crude mineral spirit—acting like the water—is joined with its own body, dissolving it in a first boiling. From this, it is named **Rebis**: because it is composed of a twofold and double thing <note>original: "ex re bina"</note>, namely from male and female seed. This means it comes from the "dissolver" and the "thing to be dissolved," even though the matter and substance are essentially one. 

Hence the verses:

> The thing **Rebis** is two joined, yet remains one,
> It is dissolved so the first things are either the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> or the seeds of the **Moon** <note>Silver</note>.

Moreover, from these two things dissolved together, the **Elixir** is composed: that is, the "tinted water." 

Hence the verses:

> **Elixir** in Greek is called a "part" in the second art,
> For from the lye <note>original: "lixis," a play on words between Elixir and lye/water</note> clean bodies are made by themselves.

From this Elixir, my honored Doctor—as if from the first broth of a simple boiling—**azoc** is extracted, namely by a stronger and repeated distillation. This **azoc** reflects and participates in the nature of its body (which is hot) from which it is extracted, and it retains that body's virtue within itself, such as its oily nature, which is hot and moist: because it is fire and air in actuality; although in it there are...

...all elements in essence and composition. Therefore, from the aforementioned metals, medicines can be composed by various methods to cure the diseases of sentient beings <note>refers to humans and animals</note>; however, these are irrelevant to the **Work of the Philosophers**, just as the Elixir relates to **Azoc** <note>original: "Azoc"; a term often used in alchemy to refer to the essential mercurial spirit or the "mercury of the philosophers"</note>. This is to say: the spirit, the vital part, and the fleeing soul are neither sheer nor transparent, nor are they clear like a tear from the eye, nor is it just any dissolving spirit—even though they are of higher natures relative to one another according to their degrees. For example, the soul is higher than the raw spirit, even though they share one form. 

Because the soul lies hidden under the appearance of the dissolved spirit before it is thickened again (for the soul always appears as **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> when extracted from the body), so after the thickening, the soul and spirit lie hidden under the appearance of the body. Your Reverence saw an experiment of this principle in the powder once sent to the King, to whom you are the physician. In that experiment, **quicksilver** was found in the form of **quicksilver**; but if it had remained at the bottom and been coagulated, it would certainly have taken on the same appearance as the powder. 

That powder, however, shall be called a **tincture** <term>a substance capable of staining or transforming the "color" and nature of a metal</term> in name only, and not a medicine of metals, because it was not yet fully **fixed** <term>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate when exposed to fire</term>, even though it would be perfectly effective as a human medicine. But the **fixed medicine** exceeds this human medicine in power beyond all doubt, both for the metal and for the human. This transformation cannot happen in a clear and transparent sheer liquor. 

For even if the aforementioned **Elixir** and **Azoc** (that is, the spirit and the soul) reflected and possessed transparency, the earth would have already, in its proper proportion, released the water and been separated from it—the very water which thickened and coagulated its parts, created opacity in the Elixir and Azoc, and caused the metallic form to remain solid and capable of freezing. For in the restraining of fixed metallic species, it is necessary that the restraining agent acts upon that which is to be restrained, and the freezing agent upon that which is to be frozen; this cannot happen in the aforementioned sheer and clear water. 

However, it happens differently in vegetables, in which simple and sheer water is thickened into the vegetables themselves through **decoction** <term>the process of boiling a substance to extract its essence</term>. Yet, that water eventually vanishes and evaporates when tested by fire because it is not permanent or fixed in its composition. This is because it did not naturally possess a **homogeneous earth** <note>earth of the same nature or kind</note> joined with it in its composition, as **quicksilver** does; such earth is the cause of permanent fixation in homogeneous things. Therefore, simple water cannot be fixed through freezing with vegetables...

...vegetables, just as **Mercury** is with metals. Therefore, if **Mercury** should take on a transparency in the **Work of the Philosophers**, it will by right remain an irrepressible substance; nor will it be congealed upon the **latten** <term>laton: a brass-like alloy of copper and zinc, often representing the base metallic body in alchemy</term> into a metallic form, species, and proportion. For such a substance carries with it—and within itself—no means of its own congealing, namely the "earth" within the "water." This earth (as has been said) is **Mercurial**, and it is the primary cause of thickening, coagulation, and fixation. If, therefore, that "water" remains so far outside the metallic proportion, how can similar species be procreated from this composition? 

Those people also err who think they can extract a clear, transparent water from **Mercury** and perform many wonders with it. For even if they were to perfect such a water, the work would be of no use; it would not suit its nature or proportion, nor could it restore or build up a perfect metallic species. For as soon as **Mercury** is changed from its primary nature, it is immediately prevented from entering our **Philosophical Work**, because it has lost its **spermatic nature** <note>the "seed" or generative potential inherent in the metal</note> and the nature of metals.

From these points, therefore, it is known how much truth your opinion contains, and in what ways it is contrary and foreign, when you say: "It is necessary (as I think) for perfecting the supreme **Elixir** to have a **gum** <note>original: "gumma"; refers to a thick, resinous stage of the alchemical matter</note> in which all things necessary to it are present, containing the four elements; and it is a most clear water, like a spiritual tear from the eye," and so on, which you claim makes pure gold become a spirit. 

For "body does not penetrate body"; rather, it is a subtle, spiritual, congealed substance that penetrates and colors the body. Let it be as you say, my honored Doctor: that natures are not joined except by a **gum**, or by an oily and proportionately balanced thing having a spiritual nature, yet with the elements fixed and enclosed within it. To this "gumminess" the entire **Philosopher’s Stone** is ultimately reduced through a light **inceration** <term>inceration: the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a soft, wax-like consistency</term>. In this state, it reflects all the elements, standing like bronze and the nature of bronze, and standing moreover as a subtle spiritual substance, penetrating and coloring metallic bodies. For this **Stone**, in its first raw spirit that is to be sublimated, did not lose its species (that is, the species of that same spirit), nor does it lose its primary nature even when it becomes a great and perfect **gum**. Therefore, oil and gum have nothing to do with this **Stone**, except as elements brought into balance...

Yet he, speaking secretly in a philosophical manner under this "chaff," describes the truth openly, philosophically, and learnedly. # BERNARD OF TREVISO

...although he was a revered and ingenious Doctor, in this art he perhaps conducted experiments without the underlying doctrine of causes. As for his claim that in the first purification, the **raw spirit** <note>the volatile, gaseous part of a substance</note> is **sublimated** <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a gas and then collects again as a solid, used here to describe purifying Mercury</term> from lesser salty minerals, and his claim that Mercury itself—which is cold and wet by nature—is made into a powder that is hot and dry by nature; this is of no use to our Philosophical work. 

Even if it were true that he could make such a powder from Mercury as he describes—namely, one dried and heated through sublimation from salty minerals—those purifications are vain and irrelevant; indeed, they are harmful to the completion of our work. For although lesser minerals <note>non-metallic minerals like salts or vitriols</note> share a nature with metals, they do not share the same species or proportion. Both greater and lesser minerals arise from the same subterranean birth or placement, and are universally of one and the same origin, and therefore of the same nature. However, they differ in proportion, quality, and species, or form. 

Therefore, if Mercury is distilled and dried with these lesser minerals, its internal nature becomes confused and disproportionate; it is hindered and rendered useless for the effect of the **female seed** <note>original: "spermatis foeminini"; in alchemy, Mercury is often cast as the "female" or "lunar" seed which must be joined with the "male" or "solar" seed of Gold</note>, and it is made invalid for the work of metals. For as soon as it is turned into the form of a powder—unless it is derived from its own **body of the Sun or Moon** <note>Gold or Silver</note>—it undergoes a drying that is useless for the Philosophical work. 

However, I do not deny that drossy and unclean Mercury can and should be sublimated or purified once or many times according to proper Philosophical experience, using simple salt to remove the external mineral dross and impurity. Yet, this must be done while the **fluidity** of the Mercury always remains unharmed, and its **radical moisture** <term>humido radicali: the fundamental, life-giving "sap" or essential liquid within a substance that allows it to be transformed without being destroyed</term> (that is, its "mercuriality") remains uncorrupted, for this is part of its natural proportion. 

For the Mercurial species and form must remain uncorrupted in such a work, as has been said before; its outward form should not be reduced to a dried-out powder. Because a corrupted outward appearance shows that the internal nature is confused, unless the form of generation were to alter it, as is clearly seen by those distinguished in the work through the appearing way of nature. -> DE TRANSM. METAL. <-

...which are joined and mixed together through their innermost parts by **amalgamating** <term>amalgamatio: the process of combining Mercury with another metal to form a soft paste</term>. From this process, [the Mercury] is frequently relieved and reunited, casting off and losing its superfluities without its essential nature being confounded. Afterward, however, it is suited to the **Philosophical Work** <note>the "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> and is capable of dissolving metallic species; yet it is not greatly altered internally for the Philosophical Work unless it is changed by the fixed bodies dissolved within it.

Therefore, it must be noted universally that as soon as Mercury is turned into a powder of any kind—beyond its natural state for dissolving a body—it will immediately be useless for the Philosophical Work.

There are certain deceptive **sophists** <note>alchemical frauds who used chemical tricks to mimic the appearance of precious metals</note> who, having joined **copper** <note>original: "venere", referring to Venus, the planetary name for copper</note> to themselves or added other species, perform a "sophistic" work. That is, they give a color to imperfect copper, but it is not a natural color; they induce an appearance, but not a species—that is, a true **transmutation**. This is just as one who paints a dead image or carves one from wood: it only appears to be, but is not. And just as much as a living man differs from his image or painting, so much does their work differ from the Philosophical Work. 

Hence, this mixture does not endure the **test of fire** <note>original: "examine ignis"; a method of assaying metal by intense heat to see if it oxidizes or remains pure</note>, even though it is mineral in nature; for nature does not draw it from a balanced digestion, nor has that art boiled it vehemently enough to alter the mixed natures. Therefore, that metal appears to be **tinctured** <note>stained or colored on the surface to look like gold or silver</note> only on the surface and not permanently throughout its interior. One must not cling to the experiments of these deceptive sophists, because the truth of the natural art refutes this useless sophistic work and shows it to be false.

And if it is argued by way of persistence that, just as through the purifications of the dross of Mercury, the aforementioned **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist often cited by later writers</note> dried it in its nature by sublimation; so also (as you say) through **revivification** <note>the process of returning a chemically altered substance back to its original liquid metallic state</note> he re-moistened it, and rendered that Mercury hot and moist, and conformed to its body in nature. This, indeed, does not stand in the way, my revered Doctor, nor does it attack the truth of the Philosophical art; rather, the error in the natural art appears more clearly. For, as is clear, Arnaldus teaches—if you look at the sound of his words—that Mercury thus dried through boiling water...

<header>BERNARD OF TREVISO</header>

...into which it is cast, to be **revivified** <term>reuiuificari: the process of restoring a metal to its liquid or metallic state after it has been powdered or oxidized</term>; and [Arnaldus] says it is made hot and moist, whereas first, having been **sublimated** <term>sublimatus: purified or changed in state by heating a substance into vapor and collecting it as a solid</term>, it was hot and dry. But what true Philosopher would say that Mercury or any other metal is changed in its nature’s internal quality by simple water—however hot and boiling it may be—or that it acquires its natural moisture and is thus revivified? Therefore, Mercury acquires nothing in this revivification, because common water does not **digest** <term>decoquit: literally "cooks down," an alchemical term for the slow application of heat to mature a substance</term> nor alter it: because it does not penetrate or enter it; and what does not penetrate and enter, does not alter: because everything that is to be altered must first be thoroughly mixed.

Indeed, such water can wipe away certain **dross** <note>original: "scorias", referring to surface impurities or slag</note> floating on the Mercury, but it cannot infuse a new quality into it. For whatever nature Mercury retained when reduced to powder and **mortified** <note>original: "mortificatus", an alchemical term for "killing" a metal, or stripping it of its outward metallic properties like luster and fluidity</note> through sublimations, it will entirely keep that same nature when revivified by water. 

I wish this to be said out of reverence and honor for the aforementioned **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist whose works Bernard frequently critiques</note>; but I contemplate and defend the truth of nature and experiment. Furthermore, my honored Doctor, so that I might satisfy your letter with this response and bring it to an end, I humbly pray that you bear what I have briefly discussed with a good and fair mind; for I have done this not by way of refutation, but only by way of disputation. If indeed I have replied anything to you which causes you **doubt** <note>original: "scrupulum", literally a small sharp stone, used figuratively to mean a hesitation or unease of the mind</note>, may you receive it prudently with a fair and good mind, or signify it to me in letters, and I shall satisfy you to the best of my ability, by the gift and teaching of the most true Teacher, our Lord Jesus Christ, the blessed Son of God, forever and ever.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'V' decorated with intricate scrolling foliage patterns, beginning the main text.</image-desc>As the venerable *Ramon Lull* <note>original: "Raymundus Lulij"; a major 13th-century figure whose name was frequently attached to alchemical texts to lend them authority</note> says: The intention of nature in performing our mastery <note>The "mastery" refers to the "Magisterium" or the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> is that the Stone must be divided into the four elements, so that each one by itself, according to the requirements of nature, can be purified. And this is the preparation of things which precedes the operation of the perfect preparation, and is properly called the *Separation of elements*, since it divides all impure parts from the pure parts, so that with the lighter and purer parts, our perfect preparation may successively occur through natural conjunction. This occurs through the bringing back together of the moist with the dry—substances prepared immediately and directly through the benefit of the separation of elements. Otherwise, the moist would not love the dry, nor the body the spirit, if it were not first well washed of their infections by means of distillations and calcinations <note>the process of reducing a solid to powder through high heat</note>, solutions, and coagulations. For through the separation of elements, the falsity of its burning sulfurousness is burned away, which came to it through the original stain of our "menstrual" matter <note>original: "menstrualis"; in alchemy, this refers to the base solvent or the raw, unrefined matter at the start of the work, often described using biological metaphors</note>, which is the corruption of our stone. Therefore, the earth of the bodies is calcined after the extraction of the air <note>original: "æris"; representing the volatile or gaseous state of the matter</note>, so that it may be perfectly purified from false sulfurous qualities and burnings. Therefore, it is clear that if the corruptible matter had not been placed there through the corruption of the stone, it would never need to be purged.

And since it is thus necessary that after the corruption of the stone, the compound of that stone be purified of all its filth—after its separation into the four elements through distillation and calcination—before the <term>Mercury<note>Mercury here refers to the "Philosophical Mercury," the spiritual/liquid principle of the stone, not necessarily the common metal</note></term> is joined with the body to begin the real preparation, which is the creation of our stone.

For this dryness fixes the matter, because the dryness of fire provides the tint <note>original: "tingit"; to color or transform the substance</note>. However, that which is manifest <note>original: "manifesto"; the external, observable properties</note> is coldness and humidity. It is necessary, therefore, to have a proportion between these, so that the coldness and humidity are tempered with heat and dryness, ensuring they do not flee from the fire. Act, therefore, so that the humidity and coldness receive the heat and dryness which were hidden, so that they become one single substance.

Indeed, that coldness and humidity is a watery and burning smoke which destroys the "blackness" <note>The "nigredo" or black stage of alchemy, representing putrefaction</note>, and that stone is of one virtue and nature in its hidden state, and another in its manifest state. For in this composition, are not the works of the planets and their images active in their proper places and times, just as they are in a fetus? For in the fetus, in the **first month** when the seed is received into the womb, **Saturn** works by coagulating and constricting the matter with his coldness, and thus, by nature itself, it is coagulated into the first mass.

In the **second month**, **Jupiter** works by digesting the matter with heat into a certain crude mass, which is called an **Embryo** <term>Embryo: the early stage of development before distinct limbs are fully formed</term>.

In the **third month**, **Mars** works by acting on the matter with his heat and dryness, dividing and sequestering that mass, and arranging the limbs.

In the **fourth month**, the **Sun** <note>original: "Sol"</note> works, who nourishes the spirits, and the offspring begins to live.

In the **fifth month**, **Mercury** works, who creates the openings and the pores <note>original: "spiracula"; breathing holes or vents</note>.

In the **sixth month**, **Venus** works: for she disposes and ordains the eyes, the eyebrows, and the testicles.

In the **seventh month**, the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note> works with her coldness and humidity; she labors to expel the infant, and if it is born then, it can live. But if it is not born, it becomes weakened.

And in the **eighth month**, **Saturn** works again by constricting; the fetus is formed in the womb, and if it were born then, it could not live.

But in the **ninth month**, **Jupiter** works again by nourishing with heat and humidity; he restores strength to the fetus, and thus it is born completely and lives well.

Therefore, it should be known that for three months water preserves the fetus in the womb. Air also nourishes for three months, and fire guards for just as many. When these are completed, the blood of the one being nourished in the navel, once it is cut, goes to the breasts and there takes on the whiteness of snow <note>The author is comparing the biological change of blood into breast milk to the alchemical change of colors, specifically the transition to the "white" stage or *albedo*</note>. It should be known that there are four principal regimes <term>regimina</term><note>The "regimes" are the different stages of heat and chemical treatment directed by the alchemist</note> of our stone: namely, **dissolving**, **washing**, **joining**, and **fixing**.

**To dissolve** is to divide bodies and create the matter. **To wash** is to bury <note>original: "inhumare"; to place the vessel in a warm environment like a "bath of Mary" or fermenting dung</note>, to distill, to ascend, and to descend. **To join** is to impregnate, to whiten, and to redden. **To fix** truly is to ferment and to wed <note>original: "desponsare"; the "chemical wedding" or permanent union of the volatile and fixed parts of the stone</note>. Dissolving converts the stone into its primary matter—that is, its water; washing converts it into air; joining into fire; fixation into spiritual and tinging earth. Whence Aristotle says:

> When you have water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth: then you will have the full art.

Because the four elements are then well and perfectly prepared, the master of the work and the fire accomplishes all these things in a single vessel, in four degrees—namely, the four types of colors of conversion, as will be discussed below.

Fire, according to Avicenna <note>A Latinized reference to Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval European alchemy</note>, is dissolved so that it may be converted into Mercury, and divided into four elements, so that it may have its first origin: and so that the sulfur of the Philosophers may be extracted from the body, and pure quicksilver <term>argentum viuum</term> may be held above the earth, from that matter out of which gold and silver are made beneath the earth. And those things, once joined together, are cooked until they become one—standing, penetrating and deepening, tinging and permanent. One part of this substance converts a million parts of Mercury, or of any imperfect body...

And it must be noted that there is no other thing in this science except this alone: namely, that if clean, pure quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term> has been coagulated by the power of "non-burning sulfur," that will be the best thing which Alchemists can receive, so that from it they may make their gold, as Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica* was the foundational scientific text for the Middle Ages; Book IV discusses how heat and cold act on matter to create minerals</note>. This is because the best sulfur, clear with redness, cannot reach the state of gold unless it was first white, since the yellow color <note>original: "citrinum"</note> is composed of much white mixed with black.

Therefore, the Philosophers first handed down the composition of white sulfur for silver, and afterwards of red sulfur for gold: because gold cannot be made unless it was first silver. However, white sulfur is obtained from the purest substance of quicksilver, because it contains within itself everything we need. Therefore, the artist must be of a constant will and should not use many different things, but rather intend only toward the completion of the work. For our art is perfected within the very multitude of things.

Because this art is very difficult to know, we intend to give teaching concerning its secrets: first concerning Mercury and its water; concerning the body, spirit, and soul; and concerning their operations, which are not entirely unknown or hidden to many.

Once this has been duly prepared, the entire work is perfected. Because **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"; in alchemy, this is not just the liquid metal but the "spirit" or "principle" of all metals</note> heats and cools, dries and moistens, and performs contrary works according to its diversity and the manner of its management. Therefore, the entire secret consists in its management. Thus, it is necessary for the operator to know its management well and without error, since by the same operation it does not work contrary effects in the same degree, insofar as it is itself; but the contrariety of the operation must proceed from itself being so disposed, and not from another—namely, through a sublime solution, and congealing, and the mixing of its water with the **Water of the Sun** <note>original: "aqua Solis"; a reference to gold in its dissolved, spiritual, or "mercurial" state</note>, with purified **Gold** <note>original: "Sole"</note>. Before its congealing, it performs only a single operation: if it is cast upon copper, it merely tints it <note>this refers to "surface whitening" or "silvering" which alchemists considered a superficial, false transmutation</note>, and it does not bring about a different temperament than it had before. All of this is as far as appearance is concerned, not as far as true existence; for through the examination by fire, the tincture can be separated from the body—notwithstanding a fixed tincture—just as **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> is separated from **Gold**. But in the true transmutation of copper or another metal, a true union of the colored and the colorant is required, along with a true transmutation of all the elements of the colored thing and the coloration. The second step will be the fixing of the color and the induction of a new form, which is followed by its own proper coloration.

Therefore, the principles that **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in early alchemy, known for his "Mercury-Sulfur" theory</note> handed down—through them, the true medicine cannot be made, nor through the sayings of the Philosophers in the ***Turba*** <note>The *Turba Philosophorum* (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages</note>, as I firmly hold.

Furthermore, the ***Turba*** says: that the medicine must be composed of four elements; consider its temperament. Therefore, the ***Turba*** does not speak here except of the base works—that is, of the foundation. For so says **Geber**: "Where we have spoken most openly and plainly, there we most hide the science."

Wherefore it should be known, according to the authors, that there is **one stone**; if anyone wanders from that one in the beginning, he will find weariness in the end.

This "one," however, is not one in number, but in kind: just as male and female are sufficient for procreating offspring without any other addition. And so the **Philosopher's Stone**, composed of two, is sufficient for the intended medicine—namely, the spirit and the soul, which are

...are **the Sun** <note>original: "Sol"; alchemical gold</note> and **the Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; alchemical silver</note>: and some say that to these two a third is added, namely the "body." For just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does our stone <note>original: "lapis noster"; the goal of the alchemical work</note>. However, there are diverse opinions on this point: for some say that one of these is both spirit and body, and they deceive men regarding the addition of a third. Others say that the "third" is actually the composite formed from the two, because it does not resemble either of the starting components, and it is called by the name "the one of all bodies." Others say that a body truly must be joined to these two, because the work will then be stronger, and their operation will be finished in a shorter time. But whichever opinion is held, the number [of essential principles] is not increased. For clarity, it should be noted that **Sulfur** <note>original: "Kibric"; an Arabic-derived term for alchemical sulfur, the "father" or active principle of metals</note> is the father of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> and of all things that can be melted. And this is said to be that "one thing" which is both precious and cheap. Indeed, **Quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, which is its son, is different and foreign in its temperament from the father; yet they relate to each other as father and son. Even if a third thing were added to these two—namely, a metallic body—the number would not be multiplied because of this, nor would the names change, because a metallic body is itself composed of these two. It is therefore clearly established that its composition, in whatever way you repeat it, consists of two things. And it must be known that after these two are joined, they are always called by a single name. However, this "one thing" which is spoken of by the Philosophers is called by the names of all things in this world. Because of this, everyone goes astray—partly due to the multitude of names, and partly due to ignorance of the proper proportions. Likewise, when you hear anything regarding the **Ferment of the Philosophers** <note>original: "fermento Philosophorum"; a substance that acts like yeast to "leaven" or transform base metals into gold</note>, understand nothing other than the "perfect body"—that is, the most perfectly cleansed and sublimated body. And yet, let no one believe that he can join the spirit and the soul to the body merely through grinding <note>original: "contritionem"</note> or through a simple solution. Take the example of quicksilver joined to lead: it seems to be mixed, but in truth it is not, because it is separated by the violence of fire. But what the Philosophers say—**"Dissolve and congeal"** <note>original: "Solve & coagula"; the fundamental axiom of alchemy</note>—is undoubtedly understood as the solution of the body and soul into water, and the congealing causes the soul and spirit to be mixed with the body. Therefore, if the soul and spirit were perfectly joined to the body through only a simple solution and congealing, the Philosopher would not have said: Again...

...dissolve and congeal, and again dissolve and congeal, so that the tincture of the stone <note>original: "tinctura lapidis"; the concentrated essence that transforms base metals into gold</note> may grow firm, provided they could be joined together in the congealing. Know therefore for certain that the more often it is dissolved and congealed, the more the soul and spirit are joined to the body and are retained by it; and for this reason, at every turn, the tincture is multiplied.

And here a greatest secret must be known: that the red and white stones <note>referring to the White Elixir for silver and the Red Elixir for gold</note>, made from the elements of other things, can be joined with the perfect Elixir, and then they add to its tincture, and not otherwise.

Another secret also: that sharp waters <note>original: "aquæ acutæ"; corrosive solvents like mineral acids</note> are made, with which the body is dissolved with the souls and spirits in a perfect solution; and afterwards it is congealed, God granting it. Nevertheless, all parts of our stone are grown together and share the same essence. However, the operation of this stone is described as manifold by the Philosophers <note>the "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities</note>. For some rectify each part individually, and compose them, and afterwards bring them to perfection; and this operation is varied in many ways, and is laborious and difficult and subtle, therefore many err in it: because the assistance—that is, the aid of it—demands many extraneous things. 

Nevertheless, the operation of this stone is a single path, and is perfected in a single vessel. Yet the fire is not uniform in its total action. And therefore, so that this treatise may suffice and be of benefit to students: I say that the internal fire of this work is like the heat of the Sun in the Greater World <note>the Macrocosm or the universe at large</note>. For the Sun in the time of Spring is moderate and light in heat; otherwise, the plants which are tender would be dried up and would bear no fruit at all. Moreover, this heat enters the plants until they grow little by little; and the more they grow, the more the heat of the Sun gradually increases and is augmented daily, until the crops turn white. And Spring being finished, Summer begins; and because the Sun is then stronger, thereafter it is strongest until the end of Leo <note>the zodiac sign associated with the peak of summer heat in July and August</note>, until all things receive their due form and perfection. 

And blessed be God who has wonderfully ordained these things by His wisdom. In a similar way, therefore, this stone is to be governed. For some say that the heat of the first regimen <note>the first stage of the chemical process</note> ought to be like that of a hen brooding over her eggs to bring forth chicks. Others, however, say that it ought to be like the natural heat digesting food and nourishing the body; others, like the heat of dung <note>original: "calor fimi"; decomposing organic matter was used in laboratories to provide a steady, gentle, low-temperature heat</note>, because this heat is tempe-

### PHILOSOPHY

...measured: others [say] as the heat of the Sun existing in Aries <note>the sign of the Ram; in astrology, the Sun's "exaltation" where its power begins to surge in spring</note>, because the Sun has its dominion and exaltation there: because there it begins to rise and warm moderately.

And for this reason some have said that we ought to begin with the Sun being in Aries and the Moon staying in Taurus: which things were all said to indicate a moderate heat for the first action of this work. And although the action of this stone is unique—namely, decoction <note>the process of heating a substance in a liquid to extract its essence</note> with natural fire—nevertheless the state of this heat is varied in three ways: because first there will be a moderate fire, and it lasts until blackness <note>original: "nigredo"; the stage of putrefaction and death of the matter</note>; and also until that is converted into whiteness <note>original: "albedo"; the stage of purification</note>. This blackness lasts perhaps 46 days, or more or less, according to the diligence of the operator and the guidance of fortune: and this heat is likened to the heat of the Sun passing from Aries into Taurus. When a certain whiteness appears, let the fire be increased gradually until the perfect drying or waxing <note>original: "inceratio"; the process of softening the stone to a wax-like consistency so it can absorb liquids</note> of the stone; and this heat is likened to the heat of the Sun in Taurus, running into Gemini.

But when the stone is dried and reduced to ash, the fire is again strengthened until the stone turns most perfectly red <note>original: "rubedo"; the final stage of the Great Work</note> and is clothed in a royal garment by the fire.

And this heat is likened to the heat of the Sun in Leo. For this is the house of its own dignity. Then let it be continued until it becomes a poison <note>original: "venenum"; in alchemy, this refers to a substance of such extreme potency that it "infects" or transforms everything it touches, like a medicinal tincture</note>.

For then our dragon <note>a common alchemical symbol for the volatile matter or mercury</note>, shining in solar fixation <note>original: "fixatio solaris"; the point where the substance becomes stable and no longer evaporates under heat</note>, is adorned with the radiance of the heavens and the power of the earth. From here, indeed, the Philosopher's Stone, overcoming all things and digesting all things, corrects and amends all defects in the body. Its names are multiplied according to the multitude of appearing colors. For in the first regimen, when it is black, it is called Earth, and Saturn, and by the names of all black and earthly bodies. Then, when it is whitened, it is called living water <note>original: "aqua viva"; often referring to the purified, "animated" mercury</note>, and by the names of all waters, salts, alums, and things possessing whiteness. But after it is turned yellow <note>original: "incitrinatur"; the stage of "citrinitas" or yellowing, which bridges the white and red stages</note> and is sublimated and refined, then it is called Air, yellow oil, and by the names of all spiritual and volatile things. Finally, when it turns red, it is called Heaven, red sulfur, gold, carbuncle <note>a deep red gemstone</note>, and by the names of all red, precious, and beautiful things, whether in stones, animals, or plants.

Here it should be noted that our water is called the **Male**; and the earth is called the **Female**, which is the thickness <note>original: "spissitudo"; the physical density or material body</note> of the stone, and thus the earth becomes spiritual, airy, and subtle; and this thickness or earth is called **our bronze** and **our lead** <note>In alchemy, the prefix "our" (nostrum) indicates that the author is referring to a philosophical or purified version of a substance, not the common metal found in a mine</note>.

It is necessary, therefore, to govern it gently, so that the sulfur becomes incombustible <note>original: "incremabile"; meaning a substance that has been so purified by fire that it can no longer be consumed or destroyed by it</note>, together with the water in which it resides. For the water dissolves and whitens it. But some say that one of these—namely, the dregs remaining at the bottom, which is called the **smoke**—is the earth, and the other which ascends from the earth—namely, from the dregs—is the **heaven**. Therefore, the heaven must be repeated over the earth until the earth becomes heavenly and spiritual, and the heaven becomes earthly and is joined with the earth; then the work is completed <note>This describes the process of distillation and circulation, where vapors rise (heaven) and condense back into the solid matter (earth) until the two are perfectly unified</note>. And it must be known that since the body is coarse and the spirit is subtle, they cannot generally be mixed together unless the body is first made so subtle by the spirit that the body itself equals the spirit in its fineness. Then such a mixture occurs that fire cannot separate or overcome, even if it were to act upon it continually for a thousand years: because they are mixed by their smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; an early concept of mixing at the molecular or atomic level</note>, so that by no ingenuity, after they have once embraced each other, can they be separated. For in this way the **dragon** will die, and not without it; that is, unless it is killed along with him. And this dragon—that is, the **sulfur**—is extracted from the body through the mastery of the art, and it is our secret sulfur. 

When, therefore, you wish to test the medicine, place the weight of one grain of wheat upon a glowing plate of copper, and if, entering with a little heat, the plate is diffused through the whole, inside and out, it is perfectly tinting; and if it perseveres in the fire, it is the stone, and then it is perfect. And thus it is clear that there are three things which complete our **Elixir** <note>a medicinal or transformative substance</note> which we have made: the first joins them, and two compose the medicine. Thus, there are three joined in one body. But it must be noted that if the medicine is dissolved again and governed in all things as before, thereafter there will be no end to its power of tinting <note>original: "tincturæ"; the ability of the stone to change the color and nature of base metals</note>. It constricts the pores of **Luna** <note>the alchemical name for Silver</note>, making it heavy, and in other bodies it will cause the dross and stench to exit, and it tints them most perfectly, and finally will change them into gold or silver: and thus through our art occurs the true alteration of one nature into another.

But here it must be known, that every alteration of minerals toward the perfection of minerals stands in a higher degree...

...of spiritual things. We are not speaking of angels, nor of celestial intelligences, but of a higher degree of the perfection of all metals, and this is found in the **mineral spirit**: for minerals correspond to minerals, and vegetables to vegetables, so that there is no opposition between them, but rather the greatest harmony. This is because this spirit is of the golden ore, and it does not differ from gold except in this: that gold itself is "fixed" <note>original: "fixum"; in alchemy, a 'fixed' substance is stable in fire and does not evaporate</note>, whereas the spirit is not fixed.

Thus **our gold** is not the gold of the common people <note>original: "aurum vulgi"; common metallic gold used for coins or jewelry</note>, because ours is spiritual. It dissolves all imperfect bodies, separating the pure from the impure, since nature only receives what is of its own nature and rejects what is alien—which is a sign of its perfection. And therefore, this substance dissolves, separates, divides, purifies, and enlightens all bodies; it tints them and transmutes them into the finest gold. This is because it is a fixed body made spiritual, according to different methods of "digestion" <note>Digestion refers to the application of gentle, consistent heat over a long period to mature a substance</note>. For first it was silver before it was gold; therefore gold is that which is most fully digested, etc.

### *The first step of the Ladder of the Wise begins.*

Concerning the way those being born are produced from the born. Bacon <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1214–1292), an English philosopher and friar to whom many alchemical works, like the *Mirror of Alchemy*, were attributed</note> says in the *Mirror of Alchemy*: No one is born except from a male and a female, nor is any sprout produced except from heat, moisture, cold, and dryness. Therefore, there is nothing in the "work" <note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) is the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> except that which is truly luminous, like the purest **Sun** <note>original: "Sole"; in alchemy, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold and the active, masculine principle</note>, which illuminates all lights with its own light. It illuminates the air and warms the earth; by its heat it generates and nourishes animals, plants, and stones, and it casts out the darkness of that **Mercury** <term>Mercury: Here refers to 'Philosophical Mercury,' the volatile, feminine principle or the 'spirit' of the metal</term> and of other imperfect bodies when it is "projected" <note>Projection is the final stage of alchemy, where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transmute them</note> upon them, as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous of the Arabic alchemists; here citing a work on the *Essence and Procreation of the Sun*</note> says.

Because it is sulfur, radiating and shining in its clearest and purest substance, it illuminates and radiates not only in the day, but even in the night and in the darkness; and similarly, it illuminates all things in which there is splendor and greatness by its light.

Indeed, all these things are from its own work when they are clothed in its garments.

Therefore, let him who seeks it make peace between it and its wife, so that they are not separated from one another, but...

...they are mixed inseparably. When they have been killed (as will be more fully evident), let them be raised again in a new, incorruptible resurrection, so that they may be immortal thereafter. For after their resurrection they shall be clothed in glory and eternal strength, and then all who know their secret will rejoice in great prosperity. From these things, the greater world of nature is created, consisting of sulfur, magnesia, *Ceduae* <note>original: "Ceduæ"; an obscure alchemical term often representing the element of Air or a specific mineral vapor</note>, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, and similarly the spirit of sulfur; in the same way, there is the hidden spirit of this science. Magnesia is earth, *Ceduae* is air, quicksilver is also water and a flowing body. Therefore, truly join these natures—namely the male and female, the hot, cold, moist, and dry—and nourish them with "living water" <note>original: "aqua viua"</note>; its spirit and light are considered the tincture. Cook the work; compose it from whichever bodies it is made. For among the Philosophers it is called the "Water of Wisdom," by which the wise practitioner of the art joins it, so that nature may be altered and converted into another nature, and nature may appear through nature. Therefore, join the two natures until you draw the natures to yourself, and it becomes a most lucid and clear thing, which shines and is illuminated after it has been fitted into its great and most excellent perfection.

Indeed, such a great perfection is not reached unless the **Ladder of the Wise** <note>original: "scala sapientum"</note>, which is composed of twelve steps, is first ascended.

The first step is **calcination** <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or to change its physical state, usually resulting in a fine powder</term>, which is the highest purgation of our blessed, rhythmic stone, the restoration of heat, the preservation of innate moisture, and the induction of solution. And everything calcined is "fixed" <note>original: "fixum"; in alchemy, a 'fixed' substance is stable in fire and does not evaporate or change further</note> in its own kind. And so the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note> are calcined philosophically with the "first water," so that the bodies may be opened and become spongy and subtle. This allows the fecund water to better enter to perform its work, which is to exalt the earth into a **miraculous salt** <note>original: "salem mirabilem"</note> by its own attractive power alone. This fecund water is a "non-natural fire," by whose power the completion of this mastery is achieved—

...And from here, speaking of fires, Raymond <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher to whom many influential alchemical works were attributed.</note> says: It must be noted that here lie contrary operations: because just as fire against nature <note>original: "ignis contra naturam"; a chemical heat or acidic solvent that performs actions opposite to the usual laws of nature.</note> dissolves the spirit of the fixed body into "cloud-water" <note>original: "aquam nubis"; likely referring to a vapor or a distillate.</note>, and constrains the body of the volatile spirit into congealed earth; so, by contrast, the fire of nature congeals the dissolved spirit of the fixed body into a globose earth; and through fire against nature, it resolves the fixed body of the volatile spirit—not into cloud-water, but into the water of the Philosophers <note>original: "aquam Philosophorum"; the essential solvent of the alchemists.</note>. This is because the fixed part of nature's fire returns to a volatile state, and the spiritual body becomes a spirit, and the moist becomes dry, and the heavy becomes light, and the spirit becomes moist according to the form of cloud-water and a constrictive weightiness.

Unnatural fire <note>original: "ignis innaturalis"</note> is the fire of a bath <note>original: "ignis balnei"; a water-bath or bain-marie.</note>, or of manure <note>original: "quiliniij," likely a corruption of "fimi"; heat generated by fermenting dung.</note>, or of the grape-harvest <note>heat from fermenting grape skins.</note>, or of a horse, or any other heat produced by diligent industry.

Elemental fire <note>original: "ignis elementalis"</note>, however, is that which is nourished by combustibles and feeds a flame. Once the secrets of these fires and the principles of our true medicine are known, one easily arrives at our mastery.

Hence, if it is asked from what things our medicine is made: I say that it is elicited by art from those things in which it dwells potentially by nature. And according to Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician and philosopher whose works formed the basis of medieval chemistry.</note>, our medicine is elicited from those things in which perfection or the proximity to the first matter <term>first matter (prima materia): the fundamental, formless substance from which all things originate</term> is found. It is not, however, drawn from imperfect or foreign things, because the imperfect cannot bring about perfection, nor can the unclean purify. And because it is proper to extract these natures from their root, Aristotle says: Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of metals cannot be transmuted unless they are first reduced to their first matter and form, which are the parts of primary essentiality, and this knowledge is inherent in all bodies. However, raw materials are not entirely necessary for our work; rather, the center of the Philosophers' Stone is the neutrality of extremes. For it is said that the "sperm of metals" <note>original: "sperma metallorum"; the generative essence or seed of metallic growth.</note> is contained in the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note> of the earth; the extremity of one side, below, is the metal which is created by nature in the heart of the earth; and on the extremity of the other side, above, is the completed elixir <note>original: "elixius"</note>, upon which art works through the mediation of nature above the earth.

->### THE SECOND STEP<- <note>original: "Secundus"; inferred from the catchword on the previous page.</note>

...through the middle ground, where a state of neutrality is sought, it is necessary for the body to be brought back to its center through Art <note>the alchemical practice</note>, which imitates nature as far as it can; yet in some respects Art is weaker, and in others it corrects nature.

Thus it should be known that the intent of our transformation is to begin where nature left off. This is because the origin of nature’s work—which is watery within for all homogeneous substances—extends divisibly to three degrees of extremity: namely, to the height of perfect bodies, the depth of perfect things, or to the breadth of their neutrality—specifically by making the dead live and killing the living, whose quickening is deadly <note>A classic alchemical paradox: the "living" metal must be destroyed or "killed" to be reborn in a more perfect state.</note>.

Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says: Every whole is composed of three parts, which is why it can be a work of nature. First, to draw out the natures, collect them, purify them, and join them proportionally in a watery form, and furthermore to congeal them—a process entirely forgotten by human memory.

But regarding the artificial operation, we strive to work spiritually from a contrary sense as mentioned above: yet still by imitating nature—that is, by killing the living and spiritually raising the dead, and preparing them toward an "ultra-perfect" external state. Thus, if the quantity of water is equal to the quantity of the sulfur itself, or gradually greater—specifically as much as is sufficient to incorporate it—gold or silver is generated from them, depending on the length of the decoction <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of long-term heating or "cooking" the mixture.</note>.

It must be known that we do not take the substance from which the bodies themselves are made, but rather we take that which belongs to its own essence—the essence of all things. Once we have learned from what source that "all" is generated, it must be nourished by the same. And our Mercury is not the common Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi"; ordinary quicksilver used by tradesmen, as opposed to the "Philosophical Mercury" of the alchemists.</note>, but it is a Mercury that kills [other] Mercury by its very scent.

And according to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prominent theologian and scientist to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>: Our Mercury is made from perfect bodies and not imperfect ones: that is, with the "second water," after the body has been properly calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note> by the "first water." From these is then made the "alkali water" <note>original: "aqua alcali"</note>, which is congealed with quicksilver, for these are our "pearl-ash" <note>original: "cineres clauellati"; a source of potassium carbonate.</note> and our "burnt soda" <note>original: "soda nostra combusta"; sodium carbonate.</note>.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding the artificial operations of alchemy. ->PHILOSOPHY<-

### The second step of the Ladder of the Sages is Solution:

Which is the revelation of the hidden, the thinning of coarseness, and the reduction of a hard, dry, earthy thing into a certain liquid substance. Whence the Philosopher <note>likely Aristotle</note> says: **Work nothing until all things become water.** And that water is the **Mercury of the Philosophers**, which and no other we must use; yet it is not produced until the sum of the volatile overcomes the sum of the fixed. This water, according to Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note>, the father of Philosophers, is said to be unique though made from conflicting things; it is called **Magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in this context, a symbolic name for the "First Matter" or a primal substance, not the modern chemical element</term>, containing within itself the spirit, soul, and body of ash. It is "unequal" in its name because nothing is like it, and it is suited to manifest the hidden nature. Its secret is not found in other things, because according to the Philosophers it is called *celestial water*, and there are conflicting things within this one water. Turn therefore thing into thing, and you shall have the mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the completion of the alchemical process.</note>.

And in this solution, while the earth is disturbed, "the mountains shall be carried into the heart of the sea" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the dissolution of solid minerals into a liquid state</note>, and then the form is destroyed; but once one form is destroyed, another is immediately introduced. For every quality coming upon another quality makes it such as it was not before, because a natural quality cannot be given unless it remains under some form, containing qualities within itself either in action or in potential.

Wherefore **Avicenna** <note>original: "Auicenna"; Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher</note> says: *The subsequent quality draws its being from the quality which preceded it.*

Moreover, the **solution of the stone** is its reduction into the mineral water from which it was composed, with nature operating. Indeed, this stone does not bear fruit until it comes to nothing, like running water. From this, therefore, in the process of dissolving, it is fitting that the reduction take place; it is easier and more suitable to be reduced finally to neutrality, and afterwards to its first watery nature, or otherwise to some other subtle state. And what can be done by fewer means is done in vain by more. Wherefore the Philosopher says: *If you can complete it from Mercury alone, you will be a seeker of a most precious work.* And know that it is not a foreign thing into which it must be converted through the natural mastery, just as is evident in frozen ice, which when it is dissolved, turns into water; it is evident, therefore, that it was water beforehand. Wherefore he says: **Unless everything be turned into water...**

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Ladder of the Sages," specifically focusing on the second step: Solution. It transitions from the definition of the alchemical water (Magnesia) to the practical philosophy of how art assists nature in achieving perfection.</meta>

-># THE LADDER<-
<page-num>86</page-num>
<meta>catchword: thickened-</meta>

perfection shall in no way be reached. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: **Nature is not mended except in its own nature**, the refinement of which nature is achieved by the skill of art; yet art within nature does not correct what nature cannot. Therefore, nature must be assisted by art in that which was omitted by nature. For that which nature is only able to perfect in the depths over cycles of thousands of years, we—through the industry of the highest art—are able to perfect more than completely in a shorter term, even in a single year; and thus nature is aided by skill, and skill by art.

For Aristotle says: **If I did not see gold and silver, I would say for certain that Alchemy was not true; unless I saw the perfection of the work of nature through contemplation, I would not consider Alchemy to be true.**

It should be known that there are many modes of solution, yet of all of them only one solution is necessary to us, which is only to be made (as I have said) from itself, with itself, and so on: raw, clear, and without violence.

Whence the Philosopher <note>A common title for Aristotle in medieval texts, though here it refers to an alchemical authority</note> says: A raw solution is better than a cooked one, a dewy one better than a dry one, a voluntary one better than a violent one, a temperate one better than a hasty one, a fragrant one better than a foul one, a clear one better than a thick one, and a black one better than a red one.

And therefore, in every solution, one must be deeply cautious against the vitrification <term>vitrification: the process of turning into glass, which renders the alchemical material "dead" and unable to transform</term> of the matter along with the odors and flavors of the imperfect bodies, and also lest the generative power of that form be suffocated in any way by burning corrosives. Therefore, assist the **solution** by the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; referring to Silver or the feminine, cooling principle</note>, and the **coagulation** by the Sun <note>original: "Sol"; referring to Gold or the masculine, heating principle</note>. The digestion of this solution is very necessary for us.

And our **digestion** is called: the thinning of moisture, the destructive ripening, the loosening of things bound together, the awakening of disposition, and the enabling of separation, which can be done in diverse ways, as shall be said later.

But as Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were highly influential in Europe</note> says: To dissolve the body and congeal the spirit is our first work, because the body is not dissolved unless the spirit is congealed. Nor is the spirit congealed except with the solution of the body. For if they are joined together at the same time, each acts upon the other, just as water acts upon the earth mixed with it; therefore, you shall refine it in its own manner.

For the earth is not refined unless the water is thickened, nor is it thick-

...water is thickened, unless the earth is refined. For thus, between the congealing <term>congelatio: the process of a liquid becoming solid</term> of the spirit and the dissolving <term>solutio: the process of a solid becoming liquid</term> of the body, there is no difference in time, nor is it a different work, because each acts upon the other in its own manner. For action and passion <note>the act of doing and the state of being acted upon</note> do not result from things that are contrary in species but similar in genus and nature; one of the contraries, being in excess, destroys or alters the remainder. The body, when mixed with humidity and placed for a long time over a slow fire, is dissolved: because the humidity turns back upon it and dissolves it. The body, by its cold and dry nature, closes, retains, and thickens the moist, incinerating the dry; yet the humidity cannot leave the body unless it absorbs itself along with the fire.

For when the proper heat works through putrefaction <note>the breakdown of matter, often identified by a blackening of the substance</note>, the moist is turned into the dry. And therefore, when you have dissolved the body, you congeal the moist, and this occurs with a delay; this delay is chiefly due to the four warring elements, so that peace may be made between them, etc.

### The Third Step of the Ladder of the Sages.

The aforementioned four warring elements, distinct among themselves, are afterwards separated in this third step of the Ladder of the Sages through rectifying distillation <note>a process of purifying a liquid by repeated evaporation and condensation</note>; and therefore this step is called "our separation." This is the separation of the watery vapor from the dregs, or its purification, the thinning of its density, the extraction of the gross parts, the division of those things which are joined, the production of principles, and the segregation of like parts.

Whence the Psalm <note>A reference to Psalm 78:16 or Deuteronomy 32:13</note> says: *He brought forth water from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone*: because it must be done in proper baths <term>balneum: a water bath or "bain-marie"</term>, and afterwards in dry stoves <term>stupha: a dry heat chamber or "sweat-room"</term>, according to the requirements of reason. From these, the phlegm <note>the watery, tasteless part of a distillate</note> is first separated and evacuated in the baths. Then these four principles are separated from the beginning according to the required signs, and especially Luna <note>the Moon, representing Silver or the "white" alchemical principle</note>, the male prior to the female; thus, with their matter left at the bottom in the first distillation, you shall reserve the yellow sapphire <note>original: "saphiram citrinam," likely referring to a yellow-colored liquid or essence</note>. Afterward, the orpiment <term>auripigmentum: a golden-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</term> is rectifyingly separated, both from its moisture and by itself, in a dry stove as many times as necessary, until no "midday redness" <note>likely a reference to a specific red vapor or the "rubedo" stage</note> rises, and the orpiment remains clear and white.

This is the preparation that many are ignorant of; for the Philosophers have hidden the preparation of the stone, which is the key to the art and to the most difficult of matters.

Prepare, therefore, by preparing and purging; separate by rectifying <note>rectificatio: the purification of a substance by repeated distillation to achieve its purest form</note> while seeking the mastery of the work. Divide the stone into two principal parts: namely, into the upper part, ascending upwards, which is spiritual and aerial; and the lower way, which is earthly. And yet, these two parts are of a single nature, the division of which is necessary to perform the miracles of a thing of one nature—that is, the generation of the Philosophers' Stone. For the lower earthly part is its nurse and leaven <note>fermentum: a substance that "ripens" or transforms the rest of the material, much like yeast in bread</note>, fixing the whole stone in place; and its upper part is the soul, giving life to the whole stone. To perform this division in the Philosophical furnace specified below, a proper, nourishing, and continuous heat is required, specifically for ten or fifteen days. The longer the heat is maintained, the better the "digestion" of the water is perfected, from which our brass <term>aes: literally "brass" or "bronze," but here referring to the base metallic matter of the stone</term> is born.

And all brass is sulfur, but not all sulfur is brass: because the sulfur of nature is contained within other sulfurs. And all gold is brass, but not all brass is gold: just as every man is an animal, but not every animal is a man: because...

...from the genus to the species, as Plato says, is not a good logical consequence <note>original: "non est bona consequentia." For this water of ours is the key of the art, and the head of the work; and the spirit, soul, and body together compose our "bronze" <term>aes: while literally 'bronze' or 'copper,' in this context it refers to the 'base matter' of the alchemical work</term>. And when you have obtained water from air, and air from fire, and fire from earth, then the perfect separation is achieved. For you obtain fire from earth through rarefaction <note>the process of making a substance less dense</note>, calcination, and liquefaction; and you obtain earth from fire through congealing and thickening.

And when you have a tempered substance—that is, one with equally balanced qualities—within the Philosophical vessel <term>vas Philosophicum: the specialized glass flask or retort used in alchemy</term>, place "natural fire" beneath your vessel. By its heat, all things must be warmed and drawn toward the center of the fire. Once these things have been raised toward "heaven" <note>referring to the top of the distilling apparatus</note>, gathered together, and settled upon the "summits of our mountains" <note>the upper parts of the vessel where vapors condense</note> for a short time, that air becomes the generation, turning all things into its own nature. Its light parts yield to the heavy parts; the light parts which previously triumphed now descend with them and in them—within that "heavenly dew"—down to the earth, to be multiplied infinitely.

...a coupling of things encompassing each other, a re-folding of things dispersed, an equalization of principles, and an arrangement of opposition.

For the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, one of the most famous medieval alchemical texts</note> says: Arrange the airy substance through discernment, so that earth may be held from two natures, and water, as predicted, from two bodies: because in this way the subtle is separated from the gross, and the rare from the thick. Clearly, what we have said before must be performed gently and with great ingenuity—that is, with the proper and nourishing heat. For in our work, no water is necessary except that which is white; nor any oil, except that which is white and clear of any yellowness <term>citrinitas: the "yellowing" stage of the alchemical process, which here must be avoided or purified</term>; nor any earth, except that which is pale and whitish. For then the earth is capable of binding, the water of dissolving, and the air of coloring in abundance.

And there are two earths and two waters in our work. The first earth is that which remains at the bottom in the first distillation; it is properly pale, and our rectification <term>rectificatio: the process of purifying a substance by repeated distillation</term> is performed upon it, once the oil has been separated from this earth (as was mentioned above, though somewhat vaguely), and similarly from the water. Again, the oil is distilled by itself, and then what remains at the bottom is called fire, which is sometimes called the "Second Earth." Aristotle <note>The author attributes these views to Aristotle, though they stem from "Pseudo-Aristotelian" medieval alchemical traditions</note> speaks of these two earths—namely, earth and fire—which together are calcined into a white state. He also speaks of the "vinegar-like" liquids, which are the two waters: namely, water and oil. And sometimes the author takes the name of one for the name of the other, so that unworthy seekers might wander from the path of truth.

Again, Aristotle says: Join to it two operative virtues—namely, water and oil—and by rectifying the water and the air, the earth and fire will also be rectified. I have added this here because I said too little regarding separation in the previous chapter. And for the sake of those who are accustomed to "de-flower" books <note>original: "libros deflorare"; a metaphor for skimming or picking out choice parts of a text without understanding the whole</note>, I have done this so that they might not find everything they require placed in an orderly fashion in a single chapter. But regarding the conjunction <term>coniunctio: the fourth stage of the alchemical Great Work, where separated elements are reunited</term>, I say that there are three modes of joining. The first is "dyptative" <note>likely referring to a relationship between two distinct categories or opposites</note>, such as between the agent and the patient, the rare and the dense, the male and the female, sulfur and Mercury, or matter and form.

Whence the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says: "The generation of nature is contained only in matter and form." Likewise, he says elsewhere: "It is enough for the operator of this art to reduce a thing to the simple purity of rarity and density, though not individually in the elements." Therefore, join Sabricus <note>also known as Gabritius, representing the solar/male principle</note> to Beya <note>the lunar/female principle; their union is a central alchemical allegory</note>, so that they may give birth <note>original catchword: "gnant", from "gignant"</note> between themselves...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Ladder" of alchemical stages, moving from the preparation of the "earths" and "waters" into the specific theory of Conjunction—the union of substances. It categorizes these unions by number: twofold, threefold, and fourfold.</meta>

...beget <note>original: "gnant", likely "generant"</note> their own kind, whose seed shall be multiplied like the stars. And thus it is clear that a **twofold conjunction** <term>dyptatiua coniunctio: a pairing of two distinct substances, often masculine and feminine</term> is sufficient in the Great Work <term>magisterium: the "Mastery" or the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>.

**Threefold conjunction**: that is, the union of the trinity is made from body, spirit, and soul. For according to the Philosophers, just as the soul is the bond of the spirit, so also the body is the bond of the soul, because the spirit penetrates, the body fixes <term>figit: the process of making a volatile substance stable so it can withstand heat</term>, and the soul joins them together. Thus this trinity is a unity in essence: because they are coeternal and equally balanced.

**Fourfold conjunction** is called the "correction of the principles," so that one of them may be fulfilled in the other; wherefore, for the most praiseworthy conjunction, it is necessary that the four elements in our work be in a composition that is liquid, fresh, lukewarm, and properly proportioned.

Since equality does not arise from three, but from four opposing things that communicate in nature. And just as a woman has fifteen veins and a man has five <note>This refers to symbolic ratios of masculine and feminine principles or medieval physiological theories</note>, so the **Sun** <note>Sol: representing the masculine principle or gold</note> in conjunction will first have three parts of its water, and his wife <note>representing the feminine principle, Mercury or Silver</note> nine; when the male has ascended upon her, he will hold her tail in his beak <note>A symbolic image of a closed, circular system where the substances consume and transform each other</note>. This must stand in the required **Philosophical vessel** <term>vas Philosophicum: the sealed glass container used for the work</term>, placed in the **Philosophical furnace** <term>furnus Philosophicus: the alchemist's kiln, designed for constant, regulated heat</term>, and finely sealed; it should stand with the aforementioned moisture placed beneath it. And it should be known that the seed is never placed into the womb <note>matrix: the vessel where the "conception" of the Stone occurs</note> unless it is done simultaneously, and the womb is immediately closed until the light is brought forth.

And when it has stood in **eclipse** <note>eclipsis: the "nigredo" or blackening stage, where the matter dies and putrefies before being reborn</note> for five months, with the darkness receding and a clear light arriving, the heat should be increased moderately—especially on the "days of abstinence"—until the radiant Sun arises. Then it should be nourished continuously in triple heat, because then it does not fear the punishments of the battling fire.

And thus the body is the cause of retaining the water, and the water the cause of saving the oil from burning, and the oil the cause of retaining the fiery tincture <term>tinctura: the transformative essence or "dye" of the Stone</term> for the sake of the appearance of color; and so the thick will strive to retain the subtle, and the spirit will strive to be submerged and melted into the bodies.

And then like applauds its like, because of the great desire for material adherence and the sulfurous form. Whence **Yometras** <note>original: "Yometras"; likely a reference to a specific alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Hermes or Geber</note> the Philosopher says:
