### On the separation of the elements in our stone, to be understood philosophically.

Rhasis the Philosopher <note>original: *Rasis*; referring to the 9th-century Persian physician and alchemist Rhazes</note> says: Know for a truth that the Philosophers never intended for our stone to be divided into four elements separately, as the foolish alchemists do. This is clearly shown by what Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: Know for a truth that the elements are not divided in our stone according to their physical substance, but rather according to their virtue <note>original: *virtutem*; meaning their essential power or internal properties</note>; for a pure and simple element is not found anywhere except in its own natural sphere. Nevertheless, it is a fact that the active and passive qualities of the elements can be separated and divided from one another according to which quality predominates. For example, when "viscous water" and its substance—in which coldness is the dominant force—is separated, then it is said that "water" is separated. But when a more dense substance in which heat dominates is separated, then it is said that "air" and "fire," or an airy and fiery substance, are separated. He who can grasp this, let him grasp it; and he who cannot, let him not meddle in this science and art. Therefore, in conclusion: Our water is extracted from the substance of the hand <note>original: *manus*; this may be a printer's error for *magnes* (magnet) or *minera* (ore), though "hand" was sometimes used metaphorically for the operator's initial material</note>, and not from another, because there is a greater tincture <note>the coloring principle or soul of the stone</note> in them. As for the earth, I do not care what its color or substance is, so long as it is subtle, clear, and fixed, etc.

### On the true Philosophical putrefaction of our stone.

Arnold says in his *Rosary*: In our work, putrefaction <note>the process of breaking down a substance through heat and moisture, often associated with a blackening phase</note> is necessary, because nothing is ever born, nor grows, nor is animated, except after putrefaction. For if the matter has not been putrefied, it can neither be melted nor dissolved. And if it has not been dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing. Our putrefaction, therefore, is not filthy or unclean, but is the mixing of water with earth, and earth with water, down to the smallest parts <note>original: *per minima*; a term referring to the most fundamental, indivisible particles of matter</note>, until the whole body becomes one. Hence says Morienus the Philosopher <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note>: In the putrefaction of our bronze <note>original: *aeris*; a term for the metallic starting material</note>, the spirits are united with the body and are dried within it. And unless the water were dried with the earth, the colors would not appear. Also, our putrefaction is nothing other than dea... <note>original catchword: *mor*; likely completing the sentence as *mors* or "death," referring to the symbolic death of the base matter</note>

# THE GAME

And our putrefaction <note>original: *putrefactio*; the stage of the alchemical process involving the breakdown or "decay" of the matter.</note> does not happen without the moist and the dry, because the earth is contained within dryness and cannot rise by itself. The reason for this is that heavy things cannot ascend higher, nor can light things remain below with heavy things and be thrust down without their companion; rather, each is the beginning and the end of the other. Concerning this, King Hali <note>original: *Hali Rex*; likely referring to the 10th-century Arabic author Khalid ibn Yazid or Haly Abenragel</note> says: Know that unless you sublime the body until it becomes water, the water will not putrefy in its entirety; nor can it be congealed, except by fire. For fire congeals the mixture of our stone. And likewise, we dissolve the bodies so that the heat may cling to their innermost depths. And thus fire alone changes water and earth from their own natures and colors.

->*How our water is blackened from its nature, hear John of Auster.*<-

John of Auster <note>original: *Iohannes Austri*; likely referring to the medieval alchemist John of Garland, also known as Johannes de Hortulana</note> says: Our bronze <note>original: *Aes*; a term used for the base metal or "body" of the Work</note> is indeed, first, the more it is cooked, the more it is dissolved and blackened, and it becomes a more subtle and spiritual water.

Secondly, the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened and dried, and it becomes of a greater whiteness <note>term: *albedo* (the second major stage of the work, representing purification)</note>.

Thirdly, the more it is cooked, the more it is colored and reddened, and it becomes the tincture of the intended redness <note>term: *rubedo* (the final stage of the work, representing perfection and solar power)</note>. Furthermore, that it is necessary for our stone to first become black is proven thus: because the generation of one thing does not happen except through the corruption of another. But the corruption of putrefaction does not happen except through heat acting upon the moist.

But heat acting upon the moist first produces blackness; wherefore it is clearly evident that the beginning of our work is blackness and the "crow's head" <note>original: *caput corui*; a traditional alchemical term for the perfect blackness of the *nigredo* stage</note>. Therefore the Philosopher says in the *Assembly* <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts</note>: When you see blackness coming upon that water, know then that the body is liquefied. Then it is necessary to continue a light fire over it, until it has conceived the dark cloud which it brought forth. The entire intention of all the Philosophers is and was that the body, now dissolved into a black powder, should enter its own water and become entirely one; and pure water receives the water as its own nature. Hence the Philosopher of the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius Philosopher*; referring to the author of the *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> says: It is necessary to boil that blackness of the water with a light fire, until it is blackened in its own water—that is, until the whole becomes water. For then water is mixed with water, and water embraces water.

Yet they are not diverse natures, nor many; rather, there is only one nature, having within itself all the natures and things which suffice for our art: because by one order, nature begins and ends its work.

-> *Hear the Rosary regarding how our stone must be turned red.* <-

Unless you first whiten our bronze, you are unable to make it red: because no one can pass from one extreme to the other except through the middle. This is to say: no one can come from black to yellow <note>original: *citrinum*; the stage of *citrinitas* or yellowing that traditionally follows whitening</note> except through the white, because yellow is composed of much white and the purest black. Therefore, whiten the black and redden the white, and you will have the Mastery <note>original: *magisterium*; the completed successful alchemical process</note>. For just as the year is divided into four parts, so also is our blessed work.

It emphasizes that nature works as a unified whole and outlines the necessary progression from black to white to red.</summary>

# OF CHILDREN <note>original: *PVERORVM*; part of the title *Ludus Puerorum* or "The Children's Game."</note>
<page-num>125</page-num>

For first there is Winter, which is cold & humid & rainy. The second season is Spring, which is warm & humid & flowering. The third season is Summer, which is warm & dry: that is, red. The fourth season is Autumn, which is cold & dry, and the time of gathering fruit. By this arrangement we tint natural things until they bring forth fruit according to our wishes: because now Winter has passed, the rain has gone, and the night has receded, and flowers have appeared in our land, and the time of pruning has arrived. <note>This passage paraphrases the biblical Song of Solomon 2:11-12, used here to poetically describe the successful transition from the difficult "winter" of the black stage to the "flowering" of the white stage.</note> But when we stand upon the white rose, we shall obtain this effect alone: by converting metallic and sick bodies into white through art and operation. And when you see that surpassing whiteness, be joyful and certain that within that whiteness, the redness is hidden. And it is not necessary to extract this redness, but to govern it with fire alone, until the whole becomes red. And thus it follows clearly that the color of redness is created especially from the completion of digestion. For blood is not generated in a man unless it is first diligently cooked in the liver <term>original: *epate*; in pre-modern medicine, the liver was believed to be the organ where the "second digestion" occurred, turning white nutrients into red blood</term>, and after that redness, you should by no means add water or any other thing until it is cooked down to the completion of the redness. For in the time of summer and fruit, an inundation of rainwater corrupts the fruit; therefore, it is necessary to burn with a dry fire without moisture until it is reddened with a perfect redness. Therefore, do not stop, even if the red is somewhat slow to appear. Because just as the first digestion of the stomach whitens everything, so the second digestion which takes place in the liver reddens everything. Therefore it is clear from what was said before that by increasing the fire after the whiteness, you will have the redness from the foremost colors; however, in the middle of those colors, the yellow <term>original: *citrinum*; a transitional stage known as the *citrinitas*</term> will appear. But that yellow color is not stable: because after the yellow, the red soon arises. With its appearance, our work is complete: for then it will have the power of the male, and it converts every incomplete body into true gold-producing matter <term>original: *solificum*; literally "sun-making," referring to the alchemical association between the Sun and Gold</term>.

Hence the Philosopher says: If there should be pure and clear sulfur with redness, and if there should be in it the fieriness of a simple, non-burning substance, it will be the best thing that Alchemists can receive, so that from it they may make gold, etc.

# GAME <note>original: *LUDUS*; refers to the title of the work, *Ludus Puerorum* or "The Children's Game."</note>
<page-num>126</page-num>

### Again on the natural, reciprocal, and circular proximity of the elements to one another.

Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and philosopher widely cited in alchemical texts as an authority on nature and minerals.</note> says: It should not be kept silent that in all things which relate to one another circularly through generation, the transition of the whole is easier, because they share a commonality in many things.

This is why gold is made more easily from silver than from any other metal: therefore, nature has well ordained that the elements should communicate their qualities to one another circularly, so that circular transmutations might be made from them, and the circular transmutation of the elements might occur. For example, earth communicates its dryness to fire, fire communicates its heat to air, air its humidity to water, and water communicates its coldness to earth, and earth again its dryness to fire. And thus, circularly, the matter of earth desires to be under the form of fire: because fire, as if naturally thirsty, acts upon the earth and converts the matter of the earth into its own form. Again, that same matter of earth desires to be under the form of air, which air is as if naturally sensing the fire. And therefore it acts upon the fire and the earthy matter. And the fire, which had made the earth into its own form—then that matter naturally desires to be under the form of water: Water, sensing this, acts upon the air and upon that matter which was fire, air, and earth, and thus converts it into its own form. Then that matter naturally desires to be under the form of water: water, sensing this, acts upon the air and upon that matter which was fire, air, and earth, and thus converts it into its own form. <note>The text repeats this sequence, likely to emphasize the continuous, cyclical nature of the elemental "appetite" or desire for transformation.</note> When, therefore, that matter has been fashioned in all the forms of the elements, it naturally desires all of them at once. The elements, sensing this and as if naturally quarreling <note>original: *rixantia*; a common alchemical metaphor describing the "struggle" of opposing qualities like hot and cold as they reach equilibrium</note>, all wish to be together at once: because they are active, passive, and contrary. From that contrariety and quarrel, the elemental forms are destroyed, and they remain under the [unified] elemental form. But as for itself: that is, through circular transmutation, the matter of the elements is made into an elementated substance <term>original: *elementatum*; a medieval philosophical term for a compound body where the four elements have been perfectly balanced and unified</term>.

Hence, the blessed Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274); while primarily a theologian, many alchemical treatises were attributed to him in the later Middle Ages.</note> says the following concerning the form of the elements joined in the same body: "I have seen and I have done it through the art cooperating with nature. For I took a certain sulfur, which was of a fiery nature, and I transmuted it..."

<summary>This page explains the theory of elemental circulation, arguing that matter naturally "desires" to move through the forms of fire, air, water, and earth to reach a balanced, "elementated" state. It cites Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas to validate the possibility of transmuting metals like silver into gold by mimicking these natural cycles.</summary>

[I transmu]ted <note>The start of this sentence is completed from the previous page's context.</note> it into pure water, which I again changed through the art into air and into water; and when I wished to change it into earth, so that the earth might become purer, I found a certain **red stone**, most clear, transparent, and shining. And in it, I beheld all the forms of the elements, and even their oppositions within that matter of the stone—I know not by what power this happened, unless by appetite <note>original: *appetitu*; in alchemical philosophy, this refers to a natural inclination or "desire" of matter to reach its most perfect form.</note>.

For from the redness, I saw the form of fire; from the transparency, the form of water; and from the brightness, the form of air.

Wherefore Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says in his own tenth [chapter]: "Most blessed father, Hermes the Philosopher <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: That metals consist of the four elements, and each element in its own matter abounds from the four elements, since a simple element <note>A "simple" element is a pure, theoretical element (like pure Fire), which does not exist in the physical world alone.</note> is not given to us to act upon. Also, in the matter of metals, it is necessary that the elements have one common matter of bodies, which is common to the form of the elements, so that they can be changed through them."

And that same matter which was of water, may be of air, earth, and fire. There are, therefore, four qualities or virtues proceeding from the being of the elements, and any of these can be said of the elemental matter: and these virtues are **heating**, **cooling**, **dryness**, and **humidity**. And two of these qualities are active, namely hot and cold; but two are passive, namely moist and dry. There are, therefore, two elements by comparison to elemental things—namely fire and water—which are active, and two that are as it were passive, like earth and air. They are active and passive among themselves to the extent that they communicate in nature.

Hence it is that one element communicates its quality to another, so that by thus circulating, it can convert the quality of that element into itself, and it is changed. It is also to be known that it is common to all metals that their matter is very close to one another in nature, in virtue, and in power.

Hence Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great, a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> says: Because he learned in the works of nature by his own sight that "living waters" <note>original: *aquæ viuæ*; often a term for mercury or the "first matter" of metals.</note> flow from a single origin; and in one part there was gold, and in another silver, which were nevertheless one single matter, but the location was different in its heat. Therefore, the diversity of the place where the metal was purified brought about the diversity according to its species <note>i.e., whether it became gold or silver depended on the "baking" conditions in the earth's crust.</note>.

### *Recapitulation of the whole work of Alchemy, and of our stone, according to the intention of all the Philosophers.*

Plato says: The craftsman of our work must first dissolve the stone: then coagulate it, since our work is nothing other than to perform a perfect dissolution and coagulation. Whence the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (The Rose Garden of the Philosophers), one of the most famous illustrated alchemical texts.</note> says: Unless everything is turned into water, it by no means reaches perfection. Therefore, it is sometimes necessary to use some mixing and grinding in the whole governing of our work, but only to deal with the **permanent water** <note>original: *aqua permanens*; a technical term for the transformative liquid or "universal solvent" that does not evaporate when heated.</note>, whose power is **spiritual blood**: that is, the tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a substance capable of infusing its color and properties into another body, effectively transmuting it.</note> without which nothing is made. For in our operation, the body is converted into spirit, and the spirit into body. For thus the things mixed are brought back into one and unite with each other. For the body incorporates the spirit through the tincture of blood: because everything that has spirit also has blood.

For every thing whose root is earth and water becomes "dying." This is to say, earth becomes water, and the qualities of water overcome it; such is the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit, and vice-versa. For they have one operation: because one is not dissolved unless the other is coagulated. Therefore, in the beginning of the work, you should unite the **Sun** <note>The Sun (*Sol*) represents the masculine principle, heat, and Gold.</note> by means of the **Moon** <note>The Moon (*Luna*) represents the feminine principle, moisture, and Silver.</note>, and coagulate by means of the Sun, for from this the effects will appear, because the lower part is pressed down, since naturally the higher things rule over the lower.

Hence says King Hali, the Philosopher <note>Hali (Khalid ibn Yazid) was a legendary Umayyad prince and one of the earliest figures associated with the translation of alchemy into Arabic and then Latin.</note>: These both—namely the dissolution of the body and the freezing <note>original: *congelatio*; used here synonymously with "coagulation" or "solidification."</note> of the spirit—shall be in one operation, and one does not happen without the other. The reason is that when the body and soul are joined together, each of them acts upon its partner. For example, when earth and water are joined together, the water strives to dissolve the earth with its moisture; by its power and the property within it, it makes the earth finer than it was before, and renders the earth similar to itself in body, so that it becomes water. And conversely, the water is thickened with the earth and becomes like the earth in density, because earth is thicker than water. Therefore says Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a dominant medieval scholar credited with many alchemical works.</note> in the *Secret of Secrets*.

Know that between the dissolution and the coagulation of the spirit, [there is] no <meta>catchword: iam (now/already)</meta>

It highlights the necessity of "permanent water" or "spiritual blood" to act as the unifying agent between the physical body and the spirit.</summary>

Therefore, Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a renowned physician and alchemist.</note> says: The work of our stone is its own dissolution, knowing that the matter of the stone can in no way be destroyed without remaining under some form. For these are the signs of the perfect dissolution and **putrefaction** <note>The process of breaking down or "rotting" the material, considered the first essential stage of the Great Work.</note> of the body: because heat acting upon the moisture first converts it into blackness, which blackness is the **Raven’s Head** <note>original: *caput Corui*; a traditional term for the *nigredo* stage, representing the death of the old matter before its purification.</note>; and this is the beginning of our work. And thus the stone is dissolved into water, which water is called our **Mercury**, and the Mercury of the Philosophers.

Hence King Hali <note>referring to Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince and early alchemist.</note> says: The composition of our mastery is the joining or marriage of the congealed spirit with the dissolved body: and their union and their passion <note>In alchemy, "passion" refers to the suffering or transformation the substances undergo when exposed to fire.</note> take place over the fire. For heat is its nourishment, and the soul does not love the body, nor is it joined with it in a complete union, except through the transformation of both, and this happens by the power of fire and heat, through the conversion of their natures. Hence Morienes <note>A legendary hermit and alchemist said to have been the teacher of King Khalid.</note> says: Our mastery is nothing else but the extraction of water from the earth. And conversely, the pouring of water upon the earth, until the earth putrefies with its water; which, when it has been putrefied and cleansed, the whole mastery is well-directed, God helping. Hence Plato says: Take our stone, and fit it into thin tablets, and place them in our vessel well-closed, and roast them with a light fire until it is thickened. And know that the whole mastery is nothing other than making a perfect dissolution and coagulation: that is to say, first to dissolve, then—so that the water may be congealed—to boil it down in the heat of the Sun.

### The method for projecting the red stone follows.

Melt half an ounce of Mercury and half an ounce of Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, each separately: then put your medicine <note>The "red stone" or elixir for gold.</note> upon the molten Jupiter, and let it stand thus mixed in the crucible for a little while, so that they may be well incorporated. And there ought to be three crucibles: one in which the medicine is mixed with Jupiter; in the second there ought to be raw Mercury, a half part or two. The third crucible should be empty. Then the medicine with Jupiter in the crucible should be cast into the other empty crucible. Then immediately the Mercury should be emptied into the crucible where the medicine is with Jupiter, so that it may be well moved and thoroughly mixed. Then set the whole away from the fire, and allow it to cool outside the fire. But the other crucibles should always stand by the fire. And when the Mercury has been cooled, the medicine should be emptied into the empty crucible. Then let the other crucible in which the medicine was be emptied, and the Mercury added. And thus one must always proceed, until the medicine has congealed the Mercury: once it is congealed into a **red glass**, diaphanous and transparent, place one weight of this red glass upon 44 weights of molten Jupiter, and it will be a very good proportion. And you shall do with it in the same order as you did above in the projection of the white medicine. ->*The following concerns the manifold virtue of our stone, and its ineffable medicinal effect, operation, and multiplication.*<-

Menander the Philosopher <note>A name often cited in alchemical collections like the *Turba Philosophorum*.</note> says: When you have reached the end of our work, you will not need to repeat our labor, since its action is stronger than the action of fire. This is because it consumes everything, which artificial fire does not do; for artificial fire requires wood and plants and consumes them, yet it does not consume all parts of things, but leaves behind ashes and charcoal. But the medicine of our stone leaves nothing behind in things; rather, it totally converts a thing from its own form into its own essence. For our medicine is like a spark of fire, which is increased in the act; and it is increased in quantity, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy.</note> says. Indeed, it is increased and multiplied to such an extent that the operator must eventually cease from the action for a time, overcome by the sheer exhaustion of the task. And this is the poison <note>original: *venenum*; used here to describe the stone's transformative potency which "kills" the base form of a metal to "vivify" it into a higher state.</note> about which the Philosophers boasted, with which they vivified stones whose natures were diminished, and brought them back to a tempered nature. Therefore, honor our stone. Hermes says: When our stone has reached its limit, nothing seems more subtle than it.

Do not wonder, therefore, if the super-celestial bodies <note>The planets and stars, believed to be made of incorruptible "Aether."</note> are in themselves incorruptible, since incorruptibility has been found here in nature among the lower things, and it is subject to none of the other lower bodies.

For if our stone were to stay in the fire until the very last day <note>The Day of Judgment at the end of time.</note>, it would never be consumed, nor would it be changed. And the same Hermes adds, saying: When I reached its end, such joy came to me as I never had in all the days of my life, seeing that such an essence could be held in these lower realms without elemental matter.

->*How our medicine of the stone cures all diseases and infirmities, and the method of using it.*<-

The method of using the medicine is as follows, according to all the Philosophers. If you wish to use our medicine by consuming it, then take a weight equal to two gold ducats <note>original: "florenorum ducatorum," a common gold coin used here as a unit of weight, roughly 7 grams.</note> of our elixir for every one pound of some confection <note>A "confection" was a medicinal preparation, often a paste made with sugar or honey.</note>, and eat a weight of one drachm <note>Approx. 3.5 grams.</note> of that confection in winter. If you do this, it drives away all bodily infirmities, from whatever cause they may have arisen, whether hot or cold <note>A reference to the "humoral" theory of medicine, where illnesses were caused by an imbalance of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>. It will preserve health and youth in a man; it makes a young man out of an old man and causes gray hairs to fall out. Likewise, our Philosophical poison <note>The term "poison" (venenum) is used paradoxically here to mean a substance so potent it "kills" the disease or transforms the base nature of the body.</note> cures leprosy instantly. It dissolves phlegm, purifies the blood, sharpens the sight and all the senses, and improves the intellect in a marvelous way beyond all the medicines of the Philosophers. Therefore, our medicine is beyond all price, since all things were made for the sake of man, etc.

The aforementioned treatise was transcribed from a very ancient book by a certain doctor residing in the famous city of Leipzig <note>original: "Lypsiæ."</note>. This ancient book once belonged to Charles IV, Emperor of the Romans <note>Charles IV (1316–1378), Holy Roman Emperor, known for his patronage of Prague and interest in the sciences.</note>, by which he also caused our stone to be labored upon and most perfectly completed. He also erected and founded many monasteries of various orders and many outstanding collegiate and cathedral churches, etc. <note>The text implies that the Emperor’s legendary wealth and many building projects were funded by alchemical gold.</note>

# HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF THE ROSE-
### GARDEN OF THE PHILOSOPHERS,
### *composed and compiled into one most diligently.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>Those who desire to possess the truest knowledge of the greater science of the Philosophical art should inspect this little book <note>original: "libellum," a common way for authors to modestly refer to their manuscripts</note> most diligently and read it through very often, and they shall attain the desired success. Hear these things, sons of the ancient Philosophers, for I am pleased to proclaim them with as loud a voice as I am able. For I come to reveal to you the principal state of human affairs, the most secret of all secrets, the treasure of the whole world; I shall make it manifest, not falsely nor mockingly, but most certainly and most kindly. Wherefore, show me such devotion in listening as the mastery of doctrine <note>original: "doctrinae magisterium"</note> I bring to you: for indeed, concerning those things which I have seen with my own eyes and touched with my own hands, I can now offer you a more correct testimony. I speak somewhat more confidently than many deceitful boasters, who, after much expense and labor at last, find no result for themselves but a miserable one. Therefore, I speak to you clearly and openly, so that the skilled as well as the unskilled may be able to understand the secret from this mastery <term>magisterium: the finished alchemical work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>. Nor can anyone rightly assault me with blasphemies: for since the ancient Philosophers wrote as obscurely as they did confusedly—so that they are not only not understood, but do not even seem to agree—in order that they might either deceive those seeking this most precious art or deter them from their purpose. I, however, removing all deceit and obscurity, will plainly place before your eyes every truest experiment, together with the opinions of the Philosophers brought forward for this purpose to explain it best, so that the matter under discussion may become more open and be more clearly understood.

Wherefore we first make it known that all those operating outside of nature are deceivers and labor in a matter that is not proper. # ROSARIUM

Once this is known, he does not need many things, but only one; nor does it require great expenses, since there is but one stone, one medicine, one vessel, one governance, and one disposition. 

And you should know that the art is most true. Furthermore, the Philosophers would never have studied to express such diversities of colors and order unless they had seen and touched them. Wherefore we repeat this: All those working outside of nature are both deceived and deceivers. Therefore, let our practice and intent be in nature: because our stone is of animal, vegetable, and mineral nature. Be of one will in the work of nature, and do not presume to try now this, now that, because our art is not perfected in a multitude of things. For however much its names may be varied, it is still always only one single thing, and from that same thing: for nothing is introduced into nature that is not of its own nature within it. 

Wherefore it must be necessary that the active and the passive are, in their genus, one and the same thing: but in species, they are another and diverse, according to <term>Mercury: In this context, Mercury is not just the metal but the transformative "spirit" or "moisture" that acts as the universal solvent and the feminine principle in the alchemical marriage.</term>, by which a woman is distinguished from a man; because although they agree in one genus, they yet have a distinct difference between them, just as matter and form differ. For matter undergoes the action, but form acts by making the matter like itself. 

Therefore, matter naturally desires form, just as a woman desires a man, and the base desires the beautiful <note>original: "turpe pulchrum." This is a reference to Aristotelian physics, where "base" or "unformed" matter has a natural inclination to reach its "perfection" by receiving a "form."</note>. In this way, the body more freely embraces the spirit, so that it may arrive at its perfection. By knowing the natural roots, therefore, you will better perform your work from them: because I cannot express our stone in any other way, nor name it by any other name. ### PHILOSOPHY

...and spirit: and it is converted from nature into nature, up to the final degree of its perfection.

They have also said that our stone is made from one single thing, and it is true: for the entire <term>mastery<note>original: "magisterium," referring to the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work"</note></term> is performed with our water: for this very water is the <term>seed<note>original: "sperma"</note></term> of all metals, and all metals are dissolved into it, as has been shown.

Therefore, the reduction of bodies into <term>prime matter<note>the original, undifferentiated substance from which all things are made</note></term>, or into <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argentum viuum"</note></term>, is nothing other than the resolution of congealed matter. Through this, the "lock" is opened by the entry of one nature into another. Whence the Philosophers said: The Sun is nothing other than mature quicksilver. For in Mercury there are only two elements in an active state, namely earth and water, which are passive. However, the active elements, such as air and fire, exist within it only in potential. But when these things in pure Mercury are led from pure potentiality into act, according to proper <term>digestion<note>the process of refining a substance through gentle, consistent heat</note></term> and proportional <term>decoction<note>boiling or heating to extract the essence</note></term>, then gold is created. For this reason, in gold, the four elements are fitted together in equal proportion: and therefore, mature and active sulfur is present there. Our art, however, assists nature by administering mature Gold to the Mercury, in which (as has been said) there is mature and perfectly digested sulfur—derived from nature, through the work of nature.

And note that your door should be well and firmly closed, so that he who is within cannot fly away; and, God granting, you will thus arrive at the result.

And see according to nature how bodies are regenerated in the bowels of the earth. # ROSARY

### Geber on the investigation of truth.

In our volumes, we have considered the secret and natural powers and the properties of natural things. Through our own experience in finding and investigating this matter, we have reached an entirely certain conclusion. For we have found nothing else but this: that those substances from which our <term>medicine<note>original: "medicina," the "Philosopher's Stone" or "Elixir" used to heal "sick" (imperfect) metals and turn them into gold.</note></term> is drawn for the purpose of transmuting bodies, must possess these specific properties of quality within themselves.

**First**, it must contain within itself a most subtle and incombustible earth, which is suited for being fixed in every way alongside its own <term>radical moisture<note>original: "radicali humore," the fundamental, life-giving fluid of a substance that acts as the "glue" holding its parts together against the heat.</note></term>.

**Second**: it must have an airy and fiery moisture, joined so uniformly that if one part is volatile <note>meaning it evaporates or reacts to heat</note>, the other part is as well. This moisture itself surpasses all other moistures, enduring the heat of the fire until the completion of its sufficient thickening—the "ash" <note>original: "cineris," likely referring to the solid state reached after calcination</note>—remaining inseparably attached to the earth without evaporating.

**Third**, the natural disposition of the moisture must be such that, by the benefit of its <term>homogeneity<note>original: "homogeneitatis," the state of being of the same kind or nature throughout.</note></term> across all its different properties, it keeps the earth joined to it by the conversion of both. Because they are powerfully balanced in their mutual likeness and total union—bound together by an inseparable connection—they allow for a good <term>fusion<note>original: "fusionem," the ability of the substance to melt and flow like wax or liquid metal, allowing it to "soak" into other metals.</note></term> after the final stage of preparation.

**Fourth**, this homogeneity must be of such pure essence—and artificially cleansed of every combustible or burning substance—that it does not burn the things it joins with, even in the smallest parts, but rather preserves them from burning.

**Fifth**, it must possess a clear and splendid <term>tincture<note>original: "tincturam," the coloring power or essence of the Stone, which "stains" or "dyes" base metal into gold or silver.</note></term> within itself—white or red, clean and incombustible, stable and fixed—so that fire can by no means change it, nor can burning sulfurs or sharp, corrosive acids destroy or deceive it.

**Sixth**, the entire completed compound must be of such subtlety and tenacity of matter that, after the final application at the end of its <term>decoction<note>original: "decoctionis," the process of long-term heating or "cooking" the alchemical mixture until it matures.</note></term>, it remains in a state of very thin fusion, like water, and possesses a deep penetration into the very depths of the thing to be changed.

<summary>This page outlines Geber's six essential criteria for the alchemical "medicine," emphasizing the need for incombustibility, stability, and the perfect union of "earth" and "moisture." These qualities allow the Stone to penetrate and transform metals without being destroyed by fire.</summary>
<keywords>Geber, investigation of truth, alchemy, the medicine, transmutation, radical moisture, homogeneity, tincture, decoction, fusion, incombustibility</keywords>

...stable, which exists at the completion of any fusion, and by its proximity and affinity, it naturally adheres to its own <term>smoke<note>original: "fumo." And these are: oiliness, tenuity of matter, affinity, radical humidity, purity, clarity, fixing Earth, and Tincture.

The first of these differing properties is **Oiliness** itself, which, during <term>projection<note>original: "proiectio," the act of casting the alchemical medicine onto base metals to transform them.</note></term>, provides a universal fusion and "opening" of the medicine. For the very first thing required after the projection of the medicine is its sudden and suitable fusion, which is perfected and incorporated through its natural <term>oiliness<note>original: "oleagineitate." In alchemical theory, this "oil" allows the solid stone to melt and flow like wax so it can mix with the molten metal.</note></term>.

The second is **Tenuity** of matter—or its spiritual subtlety—which is thin or flowing during fusion like water, penetrating into the depths of the substance to be changed. This is necessary because, immediately after the medicine melts, it must be able to enter the body of the metal.

The third is **Affinity** or proximity between the <term>Elixir<note>A term used interchangeably with the "medicine" or "stone."</note></term> and the thing to be transmuted. This provides the power of "clinging" when it meets something similar to itself, allowing it to be retained. This is necessary because, thirdly, after the medicine has entered the metal, it must immediately adhere to it properly.

The fourth is **Radical Humidity**, which is also fiery; it congeals and consolidates the retained parts by clinging to what is like itself. It creates an inseparable union of all similar parts forever. This is necessary because, fourthly, after the parts have adhered to one another, they must be consolidated by this viscous and essential radical moisture.

The fifth is **Purity** and purified **Clarity**, which grants an eminent splendor during the process of combustion. Once the parts are consolidated, the "putrefied" parts that are left over are not joined to them; thus, the active power of the fire burns away all foreign superfluities that have not been consolidated. Therefore, <term>putrefaction<note>original: "putrefactio." In this context, it refers to the separation of the "clean" from the "unclean" through a process of breaking down or "rotting" the impurities.</note></term> follows immediately and is necessary.

The sixth is **Fixing Earth**, which is tempered, thin, subtle, and fi...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the "proper matter" for the alchemical work, specifically focusing on the nature of quicksilver (mercury). It seeks to correct common misunderstandings regarding the writings of Geber, a foundational authority in alchemy.</meta>

# THE ROSARY #
<meta>catchword: of salts</meta>

Common quicksilver adheres in bodies, which is false. For they think they understand the chapter of **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath and the most influential figure in medieval alchemy.</note> regarding quicksilver, where he says: "While searching in other things, we have not found in our discovery anything else that is more befriended by the natures of bodies than quicksilver, etc." But all of this must be understood regarding **Philosophical quicksilver**. For it alone adheres in bodies, and the ancient Philosophers could find no other thing—nor will the moderns find another thing—that adheres to bodies, except Philosophical quicksilver. Since common quicksilver does not adhere in bodies; rather, the bodies adhere to that quicksilver. And this is true through experience, because if common quicksilver is joined with any body, the quicksilver remains in its own nature or recedes, and does not turn the body into its own nature; and therefore it does not adhere to bodies, but the bodies adhere to it. 

Because of this, many are deceived in working with that common quicksilver. Because **our stone**, namely the <term>Western quicksilver<note>original: "argentum viuum occidentale." A poetic name for the primary solvent or "First Matter" of the alchemists.</note></term> which preferred itself to gold and overcame it, is that which kills and makes alive. Know therefore that quicksilver that has been <term>coagulated<note>Turned from a liquid into a solid state.</note></term> and <term>mortified<note>original: "mortificatum." In alchemy, this refers to a process of symbolic death and decay, where a substance is broken down to its base essence before it can be purified and "reborn."</note></term> in its own nature, is the father of all the wonders of this mastery of ours, and it is both spirit and body: that is, a spiritual body, because it rises through <term>sublimation<note>original: "sublimatione." The process of heating a substance until it becomes a vapor and then collecting the purified solid that forms as it cools.</note></term>. And this is what Geber said: "The consideration of the true thing which completes everything, is the consideration of the chosen ones of the pure substance of quicksilver." 

But it is often asked from what things this substance of quicksilver can most especially be drawn out: And we, in answering, say that it is drawn out from those things in which it is found. Therefore, son, consider and see where that substance is made, and take that one and no other, if you desire to arrive at the true understanding, etc. I say to you in the charity of Christ, that we have in no way been able to find—nor likewise have the Philosophers been able to find—any thing enduring in the fire, except alone that perfect <term>unctuous humidity<note>original: "vnctuosa humiditas." A "fatty" or oily moisture that does not evaporate or burn away when heated; it was considered the essential "glue" and life-force of metals.</note></term> which cannot be burned. And when that is prepared as it should be, it leads all bodies that it touches to the truest solar completion <note>The transformation into gold.</note>, and over all bodies, and most especially <term>the Moon<note>original: "Lunam." The alchemical symbol for silver.</note></term>.

The root of the art is the <term>soap of the wise<note>original: "sapo sapientum." A metaphorical term for a substance that cleanses or prepares the metal for transformation.</note></term>, and it is the mine of all things.

Whoever wishes to investigate the secret of this art, it is necessary for him to know the <term>first matter<note>original: "materia prima." In alchemy, this refers to the primordial, formless base substance required to begin the creation of the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term> of our bodies, otherwise he will be frustrated in his labor.

The first matter of bodies is not the **common Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius vulgi." And understand it in this way: "unless a grain of wheat"—that is, the grain of the body—"is cast into the earth"—that is, into its first matter, which is the unctuous vapor or the **Mercury of the Philosophers** and the wise, etc. And such a vapor is called the **Stone** known in the chapters of books, and the principle of the matter of our operation, and the **unctuous sulfur**, from which in the completion is extracted the <term>fifth essence<note>original: "quinta essentia." And they say that it must be in a temperate place for three days, so that the heat of the fire and the fumes may evaporate. And therefore from this I conclude, that every good and perfect medicine of Alchemy and **Elixir**, or powder, must be in the manner of salt, and becomes salt, and has the virtue of salt, and is of the most sluggish fusion and penetration, when projected upon bodies...

Son, first before all things I advise you to fear God, in whom is the vision of your disposition, and the help of every solitary person.

The practitioner of this <term>science<note>original: "scientiæ." **Aristotle**: Oh, if God only recognized a faithful mind in a man, He would surely reveal the <term>secret<note>original: "arcanum." A profound secret of nature that cannot be discovered by reason alone but requires divine favor.</note></term> to him.

Whence the *Rosary* says: Common salt dissolves gold and silver, and increases the redness in gold and the whiteness in silver, and changes copper from corporality to spirituality, and with it, bodies are re-calcined. Whence the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumen luminum," an alchemical work often attributed to the Persian physician Rasis.</note> says: If the almighty God had not created this salt, the Elixir would not be perfected, and alchemical study would be in vain.

Note, there are four Mercuries, namely: raw Mercury, sublimated Mercury, Mercury of <term>Magnesia<note>In alchemy, "Magnesia" is not the modern chemical magnesium, but a term for the "mother" or "womb" of the stone, often described as a dark mineral earth.</note></term>, and unctuous <note>oily or fatty</note> Mercury. But Magnesia is the full moon. The **Mercury of the Philosophers**: that is, the matter in which the Mercury of the Philosophers is contained. And it is that which nature has worked upon a little, and formed into a metallic shape, yet left imperfect.

Thus he says: It should be noted that there is a certain thing called the "medium of ingress," which is neither perfect nor entirely imperfect. Because nothing can be made from nothing, and what nature has not perfected in itself, the craftsman—by aiding nature—can lead back from imperfection to perfection. And it is called the stone of invisibility, the holy stone, the blessed thing. **Geber.** <note>Referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous figure in early Arabic alchemy.</note>

Quicksilver does not possess combustibility. Its purification is therefore the removal of earthiness and wateriness through ingenuity; if it be pure, the power of white, non-burning sulphur will coagulate it into silver: and that is the best thing, so that by art the Elixir for silver might be made from it.

concerning this nature or craft, we have an example in bread. **Another Philosopher:** Nothing can be made out of the perfect, since the species of things that are perfect in their nature do not change, but rather are corrupted; nor can anything be made entirely from the imperfect according to the art. ### Saint Thomas Aquinas: 
The matter of the stone is a "thick water." However, the active agent is heat or cold congealing that water. 
### The same author: 
And you should believe that those stones which proceed from animals are more precious than others.

### Light of Lights: 
Yet no kind of stone can be prepared without **green and liquid duenech** <term>duenech: an Arabic-derived alchemical term often referring to antimony or vitriol</term>, which is effective and is born in our mines.

Son, contemplate the highest worldly things, which are on the right and on the left, and ascend to where our stone is found, and onto that mountain which bears every kind of pigment and spice, and likewise the mineral.

### Malchamech: 
The stone that is necessary in this work is from a living thing. You will find it everywhere—on the plain, in the mountains, and in the waters—and both the rich and the poor possess it. It is the cheapest and yet the most expensive; it grows from flesh and blood—how precious it is to the man who knows it! 

### From the Treasury of Philosophy: 
The Philosophers have said that our stone is made of spirit, body, and soul, and they speak the truth. For they called the imperfect body the "body," the ferment the "soul," and the water the "spirit," and they did so rightly. For the imperfect body by itself is a heavy, weak, and dead body. Water is the spirit, cleansing, refining, and whitening the body. The ferment is the soul which grants life to the imperfect body, which it did not have before, and leads it into a better form. The body is **Venus** <note>Associated with copper</note> and female; the spirit is **Mercury** and male; the soul is the **Sun** and **Moon**. The body must be liquefied into its first matter, which is Mercury. 

### As Morienus says: 
Our Mercury is not obtained except from liquefied bodies—not by common liquefaction, but only by that which lasts until the spouses are joined and united in a true marriage, and this continues until the **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"</note>. 

### Morienus says: 
Take the **phlegmatic** and the **choleric**, and grind the **sanguine** <note>These terms refer to the "Four Humors" or temperaments of ancient medicine, here applied to alchemical substances</note> with them until the sanguine becomes a heaven-tinting substance.

# THE ROSARY

**Hermes:** <note>original: "Hermes"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> Understand, children of the wise, that this most precious stone cries out: Protect me, and I will protect you; grant me my right so that I may help you. For my **Sun** <note>The active, masculine principle or gold.</note> and my inward rays are within me, but the **Moon** <note>The passive, feminine principle or silver.</note> is truly my own, and my light surpasses every light, and my goods are more sublime than all goods. I bestow many joys, riches, and delights upon those who desire them, and when I seek something out, they recognize me: I make them understand, and I cause them to possess divine power.

I beget light, but darkness is part of my nature, unless my metal were dry. All bodies have need of me, because I liquefy them: I wipe away their rust <note>original: "rubiginem"; in alchemy, this refers to the impurities or oxidation on the surface of metals.</note> and I extract their substance. Therefore, when I and my son are joined together, nothing better or more venerable can be created in the world.

->*The arrangement of the vessel suitable for our work, according to the tradition mentioned by a certain man named Ferrarius.*<- <note>likely referring to Efferarius, an alchemical author from the 13th or 14th century.</note>

Let there be a round glass bowl <note>original: "concha vitrea"</note> whose base is small in the manner of a platter. And in the middle of its joint, let a glass band be formed surrounding it. And above that band, let a round wall be cast, equally distant from the wall of the bowl to the thickness of the lid of the bowl itself, so that the wall of the cover fits easily into this space without pressure. The height of this wall should be equal to the height of the bowl's wall, or a little more or a little less. 

Let two covers be formed equal to the measure of this hollow of the two walls, whose length should be equal, and each should be two large palms <note>A unit of measurement based on the width of the hand.</note> in size, and their shape should be the same, namely pyramidal. In the tops of which let there be two equal holes—one in one and the other in the other—into both of which a single hen's feather could fit. 

The whole purpose of the vessel is that its cover can be removed at the will of the craftsman, and that the joint be clever, so that without any **sealing clay** <note>original: "lutatione"; 'lute' was a paste used to hermetically seal laboratory apparatus.</note>, no exit is open to the spirits—that is, to **Mercury** and **lazmer** <term>lazmer: an obscure alchemical term, likely derived from Arabic, referring to a specific volatile spirit or vapor</term>. The specific intention for this is that the lower bowl with its joints should enter halfway into its cover.

# PHILOSOPHY

**Hermes:** <note>original: "Hermes"; the legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note> The Dragon does not die unless it is killed with its brother and its sister—not by one alone, but by both together, namely by the **Sun** and the **Moon**. <note>The Sun and Moon represent the masculine/active and feminine/passive principles, or gold and silver.</note>

**The Philosopher:** <note>original: "Philosophus"; likely referring to a specific authority like Geber or Morienus, often cited generically in such texts.</note> Mercury <term>original: "Mercurius"; in alchemy, the "living" spirit of metal.</term> never dies unless it is killed with its sister: that is, it must be congealed with the Moon or the Sun. Note that the **Dragon** is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> extracted from the bodies; having in itself body, soul, and spirit, regarding which he says: The Dragon does not die unless with its brother and its sister: that is, the Sun and the Moon. That is to say, it dies with the extracted sulfur having in itself the nature of moisture and coldness by reason of the Moon. With these, the Dragon dies: that is, the quicksilver extracted from those same bodies from the beginning, which is the **permanent water** <term>original: "aqua permanens"; a stable alchemical solvent that does not wet the hands.</term> of the Philosophers, which is created after putrefaction and after the separation of the elements; and that water is called by another name, **stinking water**. <note>original: "aqua fœtida"; a term for the initial, impure stage of the dissolved matter.</note>

Hence the Philosopher says: This stinking water carries with it everything that the offspring needs. **Aristotle** says in the second book of *Physics*: It is ridiculous to make the perfect into something better by making it imperfect. <note>original: "Ridiculum est ex perfecto facere imperfectum melius."</note>

**Bonellus the Philosopher:** <note>Bonellus is one of the speakers in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early Latin alchemical text.</note> The **Brass** <term>original: "Aes"; not common brass, but the "matter" of the stone.</term> that I spoke of before is not the brass or the tin of the common people, but it is our true work. Because it is necessary for it to be mixed with the body of **magnesia** <note>In alchemy, magnesia refers to the "mother" of the stone or a crude mineral form of the matter.</note> so that it may be cooked and ground with the **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; here referring to a potent alchemical solvent.</note> until it is destroyed. However, you must have much water of this "son of the art," and this continuously until you have added the water in parts, and the greatest part of the earth has been dissolved. **Avicenna:** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina, the famous Persian polymath.</note> That which becomes spiritual ascends upward in the vessel. But that which is thick and coarse remains below in the vessel. And unless you have so blackened and destroyed the body until the water no longer wishes to mix with it, or be received by the earth, you shall achieve nothing. For when it becomes a **spiritual powder** in the vessel, it stays below. Therefore, unless you turn everything into spiritual powder, you have not yet ground it enough. And what you do in the white body, do also in the red: because this medicine is one in essence, and similarly one in its mode of acting.

**Verses:**

> *Care for nothing more than turning the Brass into pure water,*
> *The tincture of the gum from things fixed in the fire.*
> *It is dissolved in a certain fire, the stone is fixed frozen water,*
> *When it returns to its first form, thus understand the rule,*
> *Then our brass will be like the Stone of the Philosophers.*

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the components of the Great Work. ->ROSARY<-

### On the Salt of the Philosophers.

There are three stones, and there are three salts, out of which the entire **mastery** <term>original: "magisterium"; the completion of the alchemical Great Work.</term> consists: namely, the mineral, the vegetable, and the animal. And there are three waters: namely, the Solar, the Lunar, and the Mercurial. Mercury is mineral; the Moon is vegetable, because she receives into herself two colors, whiteness and redness. And the Sun is animal, because he receives three things: namely, constriction, whiteness, and redness; and he is called the "great animal." <note>The Sun (Gold) is called the "great animal" because in the alchemical worldview, it is seen as a living, perfected entity that possesses a "soul."</note> And **Sal Ammoniac** <term>original: "fal Armoniacus"; ammonium chloride, used as a flux.</term> is made from him; and the Moon is called vegetable, and **Salt Alkali** <term>original: "fal Alkali"; an alkaline salt, like potassium carbonate.</term> is made from her. Truly, Mercury is called the mineral stone, and common salt is made from it.

Likewise: When the Philosophers saw the matter of this art dissolved, they called it **Sal Ammoniac**. And when it was putrefied, then they said: "Our stone is vile, and is found in the dunghill." <note>A common alchemical paradox: the most precious substance comes from the lowliest, most rejected matter.</note> And many have dug, and worked in dung, and found nothing. And when it was converted into water, both rich and poor have it, and it is found in every place, and at any time, and in every thing, though the search burdens the seeker. And when it was whitened, they called it **Arsenic**, and by the name of every white thing, and **virgin’s milk**. <term>original: "lac virginis"; a term for a white, milky liquid or suspension produced during the work.</term> And when it was red, they called it **sulphur**, **hyacinth**, and **blood**, and by the name of every red thing.

**Gratianus:** <note>An authority often cited in alchemical florilegia like the *Rosarium*.</note> From every thing ash can be made, and from that ash salt can be made, and from that salt water is made, and from that water Mercury is made, and from that Mercury, through various operations, the Sun is made.

**Arnoldus:** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> This ash, indeed, lacks fusion <note>It does not melt easily.</note>; however, so that it may enter and **tinge** <term>original: "tingat"; to dye or transform the color and nature of a metal.</term> the metal, a "liquefaction" or "sweat" is returned to it, according to the method passed down by the Philosophers. What then is that method? Is it by dissolving it into water? Certainly not; for the Philosophers do not care for waters that wet the hands <note>original: "aquas tangentia adhaerentibus"; literally "waters clinging to things they touch."</note> and such-like moistures.

**The Philosopher:** <note>A generic title for an authority, often Aristotle or Geber.</note> Whoever wishes to alter bodies and spirits and change them from their nature, must first reduce them to the nature of **salts and alums** <note>original: "falium & aluminum"; alums are astringent mineral salts used to fix dyes and stabilize substances.</note>; otherwise he will accomplish nothing. Then, let him dissolve them.

**The Philosopher:** Salts and alums are those things which are produced by our works. Whence **Arnoldus** says: He who would have a fusible salt...

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose writings formed the basis of both medicine and alchemy in the Middle Ages.</note> says: If you wish to be enriched, prepare salts until they are pure water: for salts are converted into the spirit of fire: Salts are the roots of your work. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" founder of the alchemical tradition.</note> says: All salts of whatever kind are contrary to our art, except for the salt of our **Lunaria** <term>original: "lunariæ"; likely referring to a specific lunar solvent or "moon-plant" used symbolically.</term>. Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says: The reason that the work is not found in common salts or alums is this: he who seeks from nature what is not in it has already been misled. The Philosopher says: The salt of metals allows **Mercury** <note>The liquid principle of all metals.</note> to be dissolved into pure water under the heat of dung <note>Alchemists used the steady, gentle heat of fermenting manure—a "philosopher’s furnace"—to facilitate slow chemical changes.</note>. And that coagulated mixture will be the perfect medicine.

Note, every salt well prepared returns to the nature of **Sal Ammoniac** <term>original: "sal armoniacus"; ammonium chloride, prized for its ability to sublimate and act as a bridge between solid and spirit.</term>, and the whole secret lies in the preparation of common salt. Note: Roman Vitriol <note>Iron(II) sulfate or copper(II) sulfate; a key ingredient for producing acids.</note> has the nature of the stone of metals, and it is hot and dry. Likewise: Alum appears to be a coagulated Mercury, but it lacks its full completion, being hot and moist; and it is called "the peer of one": that is, Mercury. He therefore who understands salt and its solution knows the hidden secret of the ancient wise men. Place your mind, therefore, upon salt, and do not think of other things. For in salt alone is hidden the science and the primary secret, and the most hidden mystery of all the ancient Philosophers.

Calidius: A lesser fire rules all. An element is the first of things that can be composed; hence neither earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire is a pure and simple element among us, because they are mixed with one another, and especially in that part where they join together. # ROSARY

...the quintessence <term>original: "quinta essentia"; the fifth element, thought to be a pure, incorruptible substance that binds the other four elements</term>: this is because it is extracted from all elemental things, and there is no elemental motion <note>The instability or tendency toward decay found in earthly matter</note> within it, as there is in other elemental bodies. Therefore, the Stone is called "every thing": because it has within itself and of itself every thing necessary for its own perfection. It is found everywhere because of its participation in the elements; it is called by every name because of the noble and wonderful variety of its colors; it is most vile through putrefaction <note>The "blackening" stage where the material appears to rot</note>, and most precious through its power. Among the Philosophers, this Great Work <term>original: "magisterium"; the master-process of alchemy</term> is covered and hidden. Our Stone is called "one thing" when the substance of the body and the water are prepared inseparably, so that one cannot be separated from the other. Our Stone is said to be made of combustible matter, yet Mercury alone is the incombustible and airy spirit, and therefore it must be present in the Great Work. 

Likewise: The Stone which the Philosophers seek—in which are the first elements of minerals, the tincture <term>the coloring principle</term> and the lime <term>original: "calx"; the powder left after a substance is heated or "burned"</term>, the soul and spirit with the body, the fixed and the volatile—is Mercury. This is not just any mercury, but that one upon which Nature has performed its first operations toward a metallic nature, but left imperfect. If you extract this stone from the thing in which it is found, and begin to work upon it toward perfection, starting exactly where Nature left off, you will find perfection within it, and you will rejoice.

Quicksilver <term>original: "Argentum vivum"; literal mercury</term> is worth nothing by itself, but when it is "mortified" <note>killed or chemically transformed</note> with its hidden body, then it is valuable and lives an incorruptible life. This body is of the nature of the Sun <note>gold</note>; therefore it is necessary that it converts all the quicksilver into the nature of the Sun, just as leaven <term>original: "fermentum"; like yeast in bread</term> converts the whole mass of dough into the nature of the leaven, and not the other way around: for the thing dominated is always transformed into the nature of the thing dominating. Our Stone is called "Mercury" by all the Philosophers, but it is not "born" as many think <note>i.e., it is not naturally occurring in this state</note>, but is extracted from the body. The Philosopher’s Stone is made of three: namely, the Sun, the Moon, and Mercury. That is: create Mercury from the Sun and Moon in its true being, without using the common mercury of the masses, but through the Philosophical way. 

Note: This stone is one in the whole world, and whoever wanders from this one thing at the beginning of the work labors in vain. In the whole world there is no other thing necessary in our work except this stone given to us, the Sons of the Sun <note>A traditional name for alchemists or those enlightened in the art</note>. <header>THE ROSARY</header>

### Aristotle, King & Philosopher.

I have never seen any living thing grow without putrefaction; unless it becomes putrid, the alchemical work will be in vain.

**Morienes:** This earth, together with its water, putrefies and is cleansed; when it has been cleansed, with the help of God, the whole work will be directed.

**Parmenides the Philosopher:** Unless the body is destroyed, shattered, and putrefies, and is converted into a substantial substance <note>referring to the breakdown of the physical form into its essential elemental state</note>, that hidden power can neither be extracted nor joined to the body.

**Baccho the Philosopher:** When natures are corrupted and putrefy, it is then that they give birth. **Plato the Philosopher:** We have an example in the egg, which putrefies first, and then the chick is born, which becomes a living animal after the whole has been corrupted.

**Plato:** Note that without corruption, generation cannot occur; therefore, you should labor in putrefaction. **The Philosopher:** The corruption of one is the generation of another <note>original: "Corruptio unius, generatio est alterius"; a fundamental Aristotelian principle used here to explain that the "death" of the base metal is required for the "birth" of the gold</note>.

**Hermes:** The second step is to putrefy and to grind. Its arrangement, therefore, is first to make it black and let it putrefy. **Plato:** The first regimen of Saturn <term>Saturn: the planet and god associated with lead, melancholy, and the color black; here it signifies the first stage of the work</term> is to putrefy and expose it to the Sun. The composition, indeed, is completed in four nights.

**Democritus:** Be neither lazy nor too swift in putrefying the stones and the bodies that have been placed and joined together; pay attention to your work, and you will succeed. **Rosinus to Euthycia:** Take a sea animal, dry it, and let it putrefy. **Morienes:** Nothing grows or is born except after putrefaction. If, however, there is no putrescence, it can neither be melted nor dissolved, and if it is not dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing.

**Morienes:** Our Stone is the preparation of the mastery itself, and it is likened in its order to the creation of man. For the first is coitus <note>the joining of the male/female principles</note>, the second is conception, the third is pregnancy, the fourth is birth, and the fifth is the nourishment that follows. O dearest one, understand these words of Morienes, and you will not err in the truth. Open your eyes, therefore, and see that the seed <term>original: "sperma"; the generative, life-giving essence or "mercury" of the philosophers</term> of the Philosophers is living water: but the earth is the body.

<summary>This page features a collection of quotes from legendary authorities like Aristotle, Plato, and Hermes, all emphasizing that "putrefaction"—the symbolic death and rotting of the material—is the absolute prerequisite for alchemical rebirth. It frames the alchemical process as a biological cycle similar to the development of a chick in an egg or the stages of human reproduction.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical explanation of the "Black Stage" or putrefaction. It transitions from the previous page's focus on decay to the specific mechanics of how the "body" (earth) and "spirit" (water/sperm) unite to form a single substance, often described through the metaphor of sexual union (coitus) and conception.</meta>

<page-num>167</page-num>
-> PHILOSOPHY. <-
Ll 4

...imperfect body <note>The OCR reads "pus," which is a fragment of the Latin *corpus* (body)</note>, which is rightly called the mother: because she is the mother of all elements. Therefore, when the sperm <note>In alchemical texts, "sperm" refers to the active metallic seed or the "mercurial" liquid</note> is joined with the earth of the imperfect body, it is then called coitus <note>original: *coitus*; the alchemical "intercourse" or chemical union of opposites</note>; for then the earth of the body is dissolved into the water of the sperm, and they become a single water without any separation.

Whence **Hali** <note>likely referring to the Arab alchemist Hali Abbas or Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: The solution of the body and the coagulation are two things, but they have a single operation. For the spirit is not coagulated <note>thickened or solidified</note> except through the solution of the body. Nor is the body dissolved except through the coagulation of the spirit. When the body and soul are joined, each acts upon its like. For example: When water is joined to earth, the water—by its moisture and power—strives to dissolve the earth: for it makes the earth finer than it was before, and renders the earth like unto itself: because water is more subtle than earth. The soul performs the same action in the body. And in the same way, the water is thickened by the earth, and becomes like the dense earth, because earth is thicker than water. Therefore, between the solution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit there is no difference, nor any distinct work in any respect, such that one could happen without the other. Just as there is no separate point in time when water and earth are joined where one can be distinguished or separated from the other in their combined action. Just as the male sperm is not separated from the female sperm in the hour of their union: so their end is one, their deed is one, and one and the same operation is perceived in both at once.

Therefore **Merculinus** <note>a medieval alchemical poet often cited in the Rosarium</note> says:

> *He calls the mixture of things a union and a procreation,*
> *The seeds are mixed like milk, appearing as one when combined.*

The second stage is **conception**, when the earth is dissolved into a black powder; and it begins to retain a little bit of Mercury within itself: for then the male acts upon the female: that is, the **azoth** <term>Azoth: the essential transformative agent in alchemy, often considered the "Mercury of the Philosophers" or a universal solvent</term> acts upon the earth. Therefore **Arisleus** <note>The protagonist of the alchemical "Vision of Arisleus"</note> says: Males do not give birth among themselves, nor do women conceive alone. For generation comes from males and females, and especially from a composite of the two.

For when the males lead the females, nature rejoices, and a true generation occurs: but if nature is joined to an alien, unsuitable nature, it brings forth no true seed. This is what **Merculinus** says:

> *That which was like milk, the conception changes to blood,*

**Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>: Whatever color appears after the blackness is praiseworthy in the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: *Turba Philosophorum*; one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among pre-Socratic philosophers</note>. And when you see your matter blacken, rejoice: for it is the beginning of the work. The same author says: Therefore, burn our <term>copper</term> <note>original: *æs*; here referring to the base material of the work, not necessarily common copper</note> with a gentle fire, like a nurse tending eggs; do this until the body is established and the <term>tincture</term> <note>The transformative essence or "dye" that changes the properties of the metal</note> is extracted. I am the black of the white, and the red of the white, and the yellow of the red, and certainly I am a teller of truth and not lying. And know that the "head of the art" is the **crow**, which flies without wings in the blackness of the night and the clarity of the day. For from the bitterness existing in its throat, coloration is received; from its body, redness; and from its back, pure water is received. Understand therefore the gift of God, and receive it, and hide it from all who are foolish. For it is hidden within the caverns of metals, whose stone is wondrous and animate <note>living or possessing a soul</note>, its color splendid, its mountain sublime, and its sea open. Indeed, we confess that in the **Philosophical Stone**, after a true purification, the greater part is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury</note>. And because of this, it is not burned, except by accident. And that is a most precious saying. All of this, however, is done by nature, and it is not to be believed that it is possible to do this through any artificial craft, as some fools have thought and still think. For the Philosophical Stone is found already created by nature, and by God most high it needs nothing more than for that which is superfluous in it to be removed. Therefore, let the matter itself be prepared so that what is pure may be drawn from it, and the earthy and dreggy parts removed. Whence **Tudianus** the Philosopher says: Know that our stone is airy and volatile; in its manifest <note>outwardly visible</note> form it is cold and moist, but in its hidden <note>internal</note> form it is hot and dry. And that coldness and moisture which is manifest is a watery smoke—corrupting, blackening, and destroying itself and all things—which flees from the fire. But the heat and dryness which is hidden is "hot and dry gold," and it is a most pure oil, penetrating into bodies and not fleeing: because it is the heat and dryness of **Alchemy** that tints <note>tinctures/transforms</note>, and nothing else.
