<meta>This page continues the technical description of the "Black Stage" (nigredo), moving from the metaphorical "Crow" described on the previous page to the chemical and philosophical requirements for "Putrefaction." It establishes the specific proportions and heat sources needed to ensure the body of the metal is broken down so it can be reborn.</meta>

<page-num>169</page-num>
# PHILOSOPHY #
<sig>L l 5</sig>

Therefore, ensure that the watery coldness and moisture, which is on the outside, is equal to the heat and dryness, which is hidden: so that they may come together and be joined at the same time, and together become one thing—penetrating, tinting, and deepening. These moistures, however, must be destroyed by fire and the stages of fire, with a gentle temperament and a suitable and moderate digestion. **Philosophical Putrefaction** <note>original: *Putrefactio Philosophicalis*; in alchemy, this is not biological rotting but the chemical breakdown of a substance into its base components</note> is nothing other than the corruption or destruction of bodies. For once one form is destroyed, nature immediately introduces another better and more subtle form for itself. Putrefaction is the same as the breaking down of the rotten: for through putrefaction every thing is digested, and a "breaking" occurs within the rotten; that is, between the foul and the pure. For a pure body, once putrefied, immediately grows and multiplies into its own likeness—just as is evident in a grain of seed, which, after it has remained for many days under the heat of the earth, swells so that the Pure part of it may grow and multiply, while the foul part vanishes. Therefore, putrefaction is also necessary in our work for the reasons mentioned above.

Conception and betrothal take place in the putrefaction at the bottom of the vessel, and the generation of those things begotten will occur in the "air," namely in the head of the vessel: that is, the <term>alembic</term> <note>The cap or "head" of the distilling apparatus where vapors condense</note>. The body does nothing unless it putrefies, and it cannot putrefy except with <term>Mercury</term>; for one part of the body, it seems that thirty-six parts of water <note>In this context, "water" refers to the liquid solvent or Mercury</note> must be taken for the sake of putrefaction. Let the putrefaction be done by the slowest fire of warm, moist dung, and by no other means: so that nothing rises. For if anything were to rise, a separation of parts would occur, which ought not to happen until the **male and female** are perfectly joined and one receives the other—the sign of which is the appearance of a perfect solution on the surface through skill. And although the <term>azoth</term> <note>The essential transformative agent, often symbolized as the "mercury of the philosophers"</note> appears white in the first mixture or conjunction because the female overcomes it with her color, nevertheless, in the putrefaction, both are blackened by the benefit of the fire. Through the fire increasing the heat within the moisture, the blackness putrefies; this is the **tincture**, and therefore it must be preserved. A great secret.

The nature of gold putrefied in <term>strong water</term> <note>original: *aqua forti*; usually referring to nitric acid, used here as a potent solvent to break down the "body" of gold</note> excels all natures. Therefore, in the composition of the stone, it must be noted that no stone excels the **mineral stone** in virtue. The Philosopher says: **Make a circle of the male and female.**

<meta>This page follows the discussion on putrefaction and the breakdown of substances. It moves from the necessity of "corruption" to the philosophical and geometric logic of the Great Work, specifically how the union of opposites (Gold and Silver) leads to the creation of the Philosophers' Stone.</meta>

<page-num>170</page-num>
-> THE ROSARY <-

-> [Make a] round, and from it extract a quadrangle, and from the quadrangle a triangle: make a round circle and you will have the **Philosophers' Stone**. <- <note>This famous geometric instruction represents the "Squaring of the Circle," a metaphor for balancing the four elements (the quadrangle) and the three principles of sulfur, mercury, and salt (the triangle) to return to a unified, perfected state (the circle).</note>

**Geber** <note>original: *Geber*; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational 8th-century alchemist</note> proves in the *Book of Examinations* that if **Gold** <note>original: *Sol*, literally "The Sun"</note> and **Silver** <note>original: *Luna*, literally "The Moon"</note> are incorporated together with skill, they are not easily separated. And thus one desires the other, because one is dry and the other is moist. And after one is joined to the other, they embrace with such a strong bond and contain each other so completely that one cannot be easily torn from the other. This will be much stronger if one of them is spiritual—that is, medicinal—and thus capable of "tinting" <note>the ability of the Stone to transform other metals through its spiritual essence</note> by reason of its spirituality. **Gold** is gold in its current state <note>original: *actu*</note> and is the matter itself; but if it is spiritualized, it is transformed from a fixed state into potentiality, from matter into form, from a passive thing into an active agent, from female into male, and from a reborn thing into a **creative force** <note>original: *res naturans*; a philosophical term referring to nature as an active, self-generating power</note>. Therefore, since there is no matter of gold—no gold that was not first silver, as the Philosopher says—if such a form is joined to its own matter (that is, to Silver), they will certainly embrace most greedily; and the greater perfection completes the lesser perfection. This occurs naturally and amicably, because every nature desires to be perfected and naturally shrinks from being destroyed.

It should be known that, according to **Avicenna** <note>original: *Auicenna*; the Latin name for Ibn Sina, a Persian physician and philosopher</note> in his letter to Hasen concerning the hidden thing: the intention of those working in this art—or rather, the intention of the art itself, according to the possibilities of the nature of things—is to bring the form and nature of one thing upon the matter of another. For example: to clothe copper with the form and nature of silver, or lead with gold, and so on for the others. For since the "form" is the essence of each individual thing (as is stated in the second book of *Physics*), when a thing is stripped of its form and another is brought upon it, its nature is undoubtedly transmuted from its original species. Thus we say that the name **Alchemy** <note>original: *Alkimia*</note> in Greek signifies **Transmutation**. And for this reason, we say Alchemy is the science of the transmutation of things from their forms and species, according to the divine forms of things.

<summary>This page explains the philosophical and geometric logic of alchemy, defining the art as the transmutation of forms and the union of Gold (Sol) and Silver (Luna) to create a perfected spiritual body.</summary>

...things are the four elements. Know, however, that the said colors appear in our dissolution:

I ask: in what amount of time can this <term>blessed stone</term> <note>The *lapis benedictus* or Philosopher’s Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note> be made? To which it is answered that a certain author, the Philosopher **Lilius**, <note>Likely referring to the author of the *Lilium Philosophorum* (The Lily of the Philosophers), a widely cited medieval alchemical treatise.</note> testifies that he completed his mastery in eight days; and some say seven; and some say three months; and others say four; others say half a year; and others say one year. And **Mary** <note>Mary the Prophetess, an early alchemical authority often credited with inventing the water-bath or *balneum Mariae*.</note> says she did this in three days. To this I say that the cause of this diversity—namely, the brevity or the prolongation of the process—could be due to a deficiency in the power of the water of **Mercury**. Or perhaps because one was working with the **Sun** <note>Gold.</note> and the **Moon**. <note>Silver.</note> And some of them added more, and others less. 

The Sun, however, is fixed and does not flee, and they worked with these alone. Wherefore, because of its inability to be fixed and its <term>impatience of fire</term> <note>A poetic way of describing volatility—the substance's tendency to evaporate or "flee" when heated.</note>, when it was mixed with the Sun through fusion, it caused the Sun to ascend for a great part. And when it ascended, they thus called it the water, the soul, and the spirit, saying that their water was not <term>common water</term> <note>original: "aqua vulgi," meaning ordinary water found in nature, as opposed to the specialized chemical solvent of the alchemists.</note>, nor common Mercury. And then the earth remained at the bottom; then they returned that water over the body, and again made it ascend by the power of fire, and again mixed it with the earth until it carried the whole earth with it in its belly. 

Wherefore a certain man says: *The wind has carried it in its belly.* <note>original: "Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo," a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the volatile spirit carrying the fixed essence.</note> Wherefore it was necessary for them to have a large quantity of the said water. And then the spirit of the body was fixed. They therefore repeated this **sublimation** <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then allowing it to condense back into a solid form.</note> until the whole remained fixed and was unable to ascend. And then the spirit was fixed in the body, and the Moon was incorporated into the Sun and mixed through its smallest parts; and thus the operation was complete. 

Hence the said diversity in the process could have been caused by adding more of the fixed body than of the non-fixed, or vice versa; because when there was more of the non-fixed, it ascended more quickly, and when there was more of the fixed, it ascended more slowly.

But what do you say about this which the Philosophers say, namely: *Our gold is not common gold, and our silver is not common silver.* <note>original: "Aurum nostrum non est aurum vulgi, & argentum nostrum non est argentum vulgi." This is a standard alchemical disclaimer that their materials are "philosophical" or purified versions of metals, not the metal found in coins.</note> I say that they call the water "gold"—that which, by the power of fire, ascends to the higher parts. And truly that gold is not common gold; for the common people would not believe that it could ascend to the higher parts.

# PHILOSOPHY

...superior parts <note>The start of the page is a fragment of a word from the previous page, likely "superiora" (higher parts).</note> because of their fixation. Know, furthermore, that it has been the custom of the Philosophers—by God—to always falter or intentionally mislead at the most critical point. They hide the matter, sometimes through symbols and figures, sometimes through metaphorical words, and sometimes through false and foreign practices. When they felt they had spoken the truth, they would then claim they had spoken only figuratively. Thus **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose works emphasized secrecy and coded language.</note> says: "Wherever we have spoken openly, we have said nothing; but where we have placed something under an enigma and figures, there we have hidden the truth," etc. Hence it is said:

> Salts and alums are not the stone, but helpers of the stone.
> He who has not tasted the flavor of salts will never come 
> to the desired <term>Ferment of the ferment</term> <note>The 'ferment' is the catalytic substance (like yeast in bread) that allows the Stone to transform base metals into gold.</note>; for it ferments what is finished through excellence. As is the above, so is the below. 
> Burn in water, wash in fire. Cook and recook, and 
> cook again. Bury very often and always coagulate. 
> Kill the living and resuscitate the dead. And do this seven 
> times. And you will truly have what you seek. If you know the regulation of fire, 
> **Mercury** <note>Quicksilver, representing the volatile or liquid principle of matter.</note> and fire are sufficient for you. Verse: 
> *Our copper is enough if you know it well, even if you know nothing else.* <note>original: "Aes nostrum bene si scis sufficit, si cætera nescis."</note>

-> *From the ancient booklet by **Hortulanus** on the* <-
-> *Epistle of Hermes, he says:* <-

Only he who knows how to make the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> understands their words regarding the stone. For the Philosophers have endeavored to clearly manifest this art to the worthy, and to hide it from the unworthy. And so, regarding the strength of their intention, they always spoke the truth, but regarding the literal sense of the speech, they did not. They said, for instance, that the Philosopher's Stone is made from an egg, because in an egg there are three things similar to the three things that make up the stone. **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy are attributed.</note> says: "Its father is the **Sun**, its mother is the **Moon**." And thus he hints that two things already enter into the composition of this stone, and **Hortulanus** <note>A 14th-century alchemist known for his commentary on the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> proves this. Because the water of the **Sun** <note>Gold.</note> is volatile, and its body is fixed; and conversely for the **Moon** <note>Silver.</note>. And then those words were declared, spoken by Geber and other Philosophers: "Make the fixed volatile, and the volatile fixed, and the fixed volatile." For they urge multiple solutions, because the entire work stands in dissolution. Likewise, when he says, "That which is above is also that which is below," here by "above" is understood the more worthy, and...

...through the lower and less noble part, <note>original: "per inferius indignius"</note> so that specifically one might be made out of those three, or from the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>In alchemy, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, or the masculine and feminine principles of nature.</note> one thing may be made, whose parts are equal; and this conjunction is called the **sublimation of the Philosophers**. And it is called sublimation, exaltation, or dignification, because the **Moon** and **Mercury** are dignified. For when the union has been made in such great dignity, the Moon is as the Sun and Mercury. Likewise, when the <term>fixation</term> <note>Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire.</note> is made—which is called the **dead body**—the Sun is as lowly as Mercury; the text intends this, and this is the "ascending and descending" of the Philosophers.

Also: The **Stone** is said to possess the four elements, which **Arnolphus** <note>Likely referring to Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a physician and alchemist.</note> explains. Because when the <term>solution</term> <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> is made, it is called one element, namely **water**. And when the body is impure, it is called the second element, namely **earth**. And when the said earth is <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to a powder or ash by heat.</note>, it is called **fire**; and when the Stone is dissolved again, it is called **air**. Also, the Stone is said to have a body, a soul, and a spirit. By **body** is understood the impure body, as mentioned above. By **soul** is understood the <term>ferment</term>, and by **spirit** that which acts in <term>projection</term> <note>The final act of the alchemical work, where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note>, because by another name it is called the **Fifth Essence** <note>original: "Quinta essentia," the pure, celestial element beyond the four earthly elements.</note>; which this composition has acquired, and it possesses the true power of converting.

Also: the aforementioned stone is called **Rebis** <note>From the Latin *res bina*, meaning 'double-thing' or 'two-fold matter', representing the union of opposites.</note>: that is, one thing which is made from two things: namely, body and spirit, or from the Sun and Moon, and from the cleansed and fermented body. Also: it is called the stone **"found everywhere"** because of its true composition: for when those three—Sun, Moon, and Mercury—are joined together, the power of the stone is throughout the whole, in both the mountains and the plains: that is, in the bodies, and in Mercury, and in the sea: that is, the dissolved water. And the **"fliers"** receive help from it. The fliers are <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Liquid mercury.</note> and the imperfect bodies, which are converted into the Sun and Moon; and it is called **Scorpion** <note>original: "Scorpio"</note>: that is, poison: because it kills itself and brings itself to life: because that triple thing, cast upon quicksilver, brings it to life: because it makes it a true body. And in this way, the sayings of all the Philosophers can be further explained. And yet, it is called mineral quicksilver by the Philosophers, but the matter of the Philosophers' Stone is **water**, and it is understood as the water of those three, as **Ortulanus** <note>Also known as Hortulanus, a 14th-century alchemist famous for his commentary on the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> proves. Nor should there be more...

# PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>177</page-num>

...nor fewer: and he says that the **Sun** is masculine, the **Moon** feminine, and **Mercury** is the sperm. But so that generation and conception may occur, it is necessary that the male be joined to the female: and beyond this, the seed is required. Thus, before <term>fermentation</term> <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "medicine" is stabilized and given the power to transform other metals.</note> can occur, there must be conception and impregnation. When the matter is multiplied, it is said that the infant grows in the mother’s womb, and then it is fermented. **Ortholanus** <note>A 14th-century commentator on the Emerald Tablet.</note> and **Arnold** say that the soul is then infused into the body, and the **Crowned King** is born.

Likewise, in the book of the *Assembly of the Philosophers*, <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note> this doctrine is held: **Dissolve the bodies and imbibe the spirit.** <note>original: "Soluite corpora & imbibite spiritum."</note> They use the word "bodies" in the plural because there must be at least two. They use "Spirit" in the singular because it is necessary that there be only one. And there is no sperm without the material of the bodies except for **Mercury**. When it is said, "Imbibe the spirit," it refers to that operation which fixes the **Mercury**; thus the **Stone** is multiplied, and multiplied again—that is, the process is reiterated.

Likewise, when **Mercury** <term>mortifies</term> <note>To "mortify" means to kill or strip a substance of its outward metallic form, often turning it into a black powder.</note> the matter of the **Sun** and **Moon**, the matter remains like ash; this is called by the Philosophers "Sifting" <note>original: "Cribratio"</note> and "contrition." Regarding this ash, it is said in the books of the *Assembly* and of **Arnold**: **Do not despise this ash.** Likewise: The aforementioned ash, which consists of those three, is called by the Philosophers the **Impure Body**, because it must be decocted <note>Boiled or heated in solution.</note> and <term>calcined</term> <note>Reduced to a white powder through high heat.</note> until it reaches whiteness. Therefore **Morienus** <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist said to have taught the secrets of the Stone to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says in the *Assembly*: **Unless you cleanse the impure body, and return it rendered white, and place the soul into it, you have directed nothing in this mastery.**

And thus two things are held: namely, the calcination of the **Stone** itself, and the fermentation. **Calcination** means the reduction of the stone into the form of white ash, or earth, or white lime, through the operation of the spirit, which is done by "our fire"—that is, by the water of our **Mercury**. Likewise: when it is said "the tinted thing tints," <note>original: "tinctum tingit"; a classic alchemical maxim meaning that the perfected medicine (the tincture) has the power to color or transform other bodies.</note> it is understood that if this calcined, dissolved, and coagulated medicine is fermented to white, it becomes the **Moon** [Silver]; with the **Sun** [Gold], it becomes the **Sun**. Likewise: **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), considered the father of chemistry.</note> proves this regarding the "medicine of the third order" and says literally: because for both the white and the red, there is one and the same path with the **Sun** and **Moon**, though they differ in fermentation. This medicine of the third order is twofold—namely, Solar and Lunar—and yet in essence, it is one.

...and the method of acting is one. However, there is an addition of <term>citrinity</term> <note>original: "citrinitas," the yellowing stage of the alchemical process that follows the white stage.</note> or of a lemon-yellow color, by which the medicine is perfected from the substance of fixed sulfur <note>Sulfur that has been rendered non-volatile by heat.</note>; that is, that both medicines [the white and the red] are begun with the **Sun** and the **Moon**. The **Sun** is understood in two ways: in one way as the "water of the Sun," and in another as the "body of the Sun," as stated above.

Also, when it is said that all colors appear, it is true: because before fermentation, during <term>calcinations</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder.</note>, dissolutions, and fixations, all colors appear. Also: the author of *The Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumen luminum," a title of an alchemical treatise often attributed to the Persian physician Rhazes.</note> says thus: "And know that those things are the same which whiten and redden from within and without: namely, the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and **Mercury**." These three things, when dissolved and fermented, he calls **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum."</note>, saying: "**Quicksilver** has within itself body, spirit, and soul." In the same place, the cause is such: cook the male and female together until they are coagulated and become the **Stone**.

Also: It should be noted that our **Elixir** is not made except from minerals. And further I make known that the **dragon** <note>In alchemy, the dragon often represents the raw, volatile matter or the "mercurial" energy that must be subdued or "killed" to be transformed.</note> does not die unless he is killed along with his brother and sister—and not by one alone, but by both together. The brother is the **Sun**, and the sister is the **Moon**.

Finally, **Arnold** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemical writer.</note> says: "Because whatever the Philosophers have said about the Stone, they have spoken the truth. For they spoke by the power of the word to hide it from the unworthy. But they spoke by the power of intention to the worthy, and always the truth; and the Philosophers know that such matter must be handed down mystically, just as poetry is told through fables and parables. And when the Philosophers speak of great things, they do not mix in parables nor fables [without purpose]," as **Macrobius** <note>A 5th-century Roman grammarian and philosopher whose works were highly influential in the medieval period.</note> says.

Alphidius says: Take the whiteness, and cast away the blackness. Democritus: Purify the tin with an exceptional washing, extract from it its blackness and its obscurity, and its brightness will appear. In the work of Sorin: Dissolve with a white fire until it appears like a naked sword, and make the body white by whitening it. Rasis <note>The Latin name for Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine and alchemy.</note>: When water is mixed with Air, it whitens it from within. This whitening is called by some "impregnation," because the earth is whitened. For when water dominates, the earth grows and multiplies, and the increase of new offspring is generated from there. Alphidius: Then it is necessary for you to wash the black earth and whiten it with hot fire. Whence Hali <note>Likely Haly Abenragel, an Arab astrologer and alchemist.</note> says: Take that which descends to the bottom of the vessel; and wash it with hot fire until its blackness is taken away and its thickness recedes, and make the additions of moisture fly away from it until it becomes an exceedingly white <term>calx</term> <note>A powder or residue left after a metal or mineral has been consumed or "revived" by fire; here, it refers to the purified state of the matter.</note> in which there will be no stain. For then the earth is fit and purified to receive the soul. Whence Merculinus says:

> Confirming what has changed, impregnation promises an opening <note>original: "Firmans mutatum prægnatio spondet hiatum"</note>
> Those who are well-impregnated are bound in harmonious peace. <note>original: "Qui bene prægnantur, concordi pace ligantur."</note>

Whence Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist who reportedly taught the secrets of the Stone to King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says: This earth with its water putrefies and is purified; when it has been purified, with the help of God the whole mastery will be directed. Hermes also says: <term>Azoth</term> <note>A term for the "Universal Solvent" or the essential mercurial spirit of the work.</note> and fire wash the <term>laton</term> <note>original: "latonem." This refers to the base, "black" metal or the impure "body" of the Work which must be cleansed to reach the white stage.</note> and take the blackness away from it.

Therefore the Philosopher says: Whiten the laton, and tear up your books, lest your hearts be torn. For this is the composition of all the Sages, and also the third part of the whole work. Join therefore, as is said in the *Turba* <note>Referring to the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note>, the dry with the moist: that is, the black earth with its water, and cook it until it is whitened. Thus you have water and earth by themselves, and the earth whitened with water: that whiteness is called "Air."

Solomon, in the seventh [chapter] of Wisdom: He proposed to have this science instead of light, and above all beauty and health. In comparison to that precious stone, he did not compare it [anything else]: since all gold is as small sand, and silver shall be esteemed as clay in its sight. The things desired in the world cannot be compared to this. <note>original: "Longitudo dierum & sanitas in dextera eius..." This entire opening passage is a paraphrase of Proverbs 3:16–18, attributing the qualities of Wisdom to Alchemical Science.</note> Length of days and health are in her right hand; and in her left hand are glory and infinite riches. Her ways are beautiful and praiseworthy operations, not to be despised, and her paths are moderate and not hasty, but achieved through the persistence of long-lasting labor. She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and an unfailing light; blessed are those who hold her fast, because the knowledge of God shall never perish, as Alphidius testifies, saying: "He who finds this science, his food shall be lawful and eternal."

**Aristotle**: O, how wonderful is that thing! For it has within itself all that we seek, to which we add nothing and from which we take nothing away; rather, in the preparation alone we remove what is superfluous.

**Arnoldus**: <note>Referring to Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> The <term>materia prima</term> <note>The "First Matter," the primitive, formless base substance required to begin the Great Work.</note> of metals is a certain smoky substance, containing within itself an unctuous humidity, from which substance the craftsman separates the Philosophical humidity. This is fit for the work and shall be as clear as a tear; within it dwells the metallic <term>quinta essentia</term>, <note>The "fifth essence" or quintessence; the purest, most concentrated medicinal or spiritual force within a substance.</note> and that is the "placable metal." In it is the medium for joining the tinctures, because it possesses both the nature of <term>sulphur</term> and the nature of <term>argentum vivum</term>. <note>Literally "living silver," or Mercury. In alchemy, Sulphur (the soul/heat) and Mercury (the spirit/moisture) are the two primary principles that must be balanced.</note>

**Geber**: <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy.</note> O, how useful is this thing! For we use it as a raw medicine; yet after that thing has been cooked and digested, it is the greatest poison above all poisons. <note>Alchemists often spoke in paradoxes: the medicine that heals is also a deadly poison if handled incorrectly or taken in its "raw" (unrefined) state.</note> **Gratianus the Philosopher**: In Alchemy there is a certain noble body which moves from master to Master; in its beginning there will be misery with vinegar, but in the end joy with gladness. **Astanus in the Turba**: <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts translated from Arabic.</note> Take that black spirit which does not burn, and with it dissolve and divide the bodies. He says the same: it is entirely fiery, dissolving by its own fieriness, and dividing all bodies with its equals. **The Rosary**: <note>Referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical series.</note> Whoever wishes to enter our Rosary and see there and possess roses both white and red without that "vile thing" with which our secrets are unlocked, he is like a man who wishes to walk without feet. For in that vile thing is the key by which the seven metallic gates are opened, and without that vile thing, the precious work is never perfected. The <term>ablutio</term> <note>Ablution or washing; the process of purifying the matter until it turns from black to white.</note> is the termination or the cleansing of the blackness, until it becomes perfectly white.

...white, and the red fully red. For <term>Azoth</term> <note>original: "Azoth"; the essential transformative agent or universal solvent, often identified with the spirit of mercury.</note> and fire pluck out the darkness of the fire.

**Mortification** is the separation of hardness from the body: because the soul is then dead, while the body is alive by reason of heat and dryness. For everything possessing heat has life. And for this reason, <term>Alchemical lime</term> <note>original: "calx Alchimica"; the powdery residue left after a substance has been "killed" or purified by intense heat (calcination).</note> is said to possess life: because the Philosophers have striven to kill their imperfect life and restore a perpetual life.

**Revivification** is by reason of nourishment—namely, of its own perfected moisture—and the restoration of the rectifying humidity by the removal of the imperfect moisture itself.

### FROM A CERTAIN CHARTER
-> the torn letter <-

Now I manifest to you by natural knowledge, in this my purpose concerning the Stone of all Philosophers and the hidden one, which is a stone adorned with a triple garment: the stone of riches, the stone of charity, the stone of relief from all poverty, and the stone of healing from all languor. And in it is contained every secret; it is called a divine mystery given by God, and in the world there is no thing more sublime after the rational soul.

You must note diligently: I have told you that our stone is adorned with a triple garment: that is, it is to be divided into three parts: into body, soul, and spirit. Therefore the dead body, because it lacks a soul, is dark.

If you wish, my son, for that body to be revived, return its soul to it, and immediately it lives.

*O Master, I do not understand.*

Son, I say to you more clearly: It is one stone, or rather only one thing: because the body is reduced into its own nature—namely, into its own water—that is, into its <term>first matter</term>. For the first matter of bodies is an unctuous water, and then it is first called "one thing" when the substance of the body and the water of union are indivisibly united through the smallest parts; it is the Philosophical Stone from which infinite branches are multiplied. And this is called the "Stone" known in the books of the Philosophers. Therefore, son, from that stone its own proper water is extracted, and in the spirit by way of separation.

Our **sublimation** is the elevation of the non-fixed parts.

<sig>Mm 4</sig>

...from fixed parts. But the parts that are not fixed are lifted up through smoke and wind. 

But we desire that these two be fixed together at the same time, and that they provide an easy fusion. And in this way you may understand our true and certain <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimationem"; the process of vaporizing a substance and then condensing it back into a solid form to purify it.</note>, and the stone which no one can touch with their tongue. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> says: "Separate the subtle from the gross," etc. Earth is <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcinatur"; reduced to a dry powder through intense heat.</note>, and water is sublimated: the earth remains below, while the water ascends above. The earth is purged by calcination, and the water by sublimation: both are cleansed through <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactionem"; the stage of "death" or decomposition in the vessel, often marked by the color black.</note>. The water defends the earth so that it is not burned, and the earth binds the water so that it does not flee. When both have been sufficiently purged, they become one and are thereafter inseparable, because one cannot exist without the other. One part of this substance, when <term>projected</term> <note>The act of "projection" involves throwing a small amount of the transformative Stone onto a molten base metal to change its nature.</note> upon a hundred parts of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury.</note>, tinges it into true silver. And if such a <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; a concentrated substance capable of transmitting its qualities (like color or purity) to another body.</note> has been made, one part turned into red tinges just as many parts into true gold—gold better than which none is found—and this comes from a hidden nature, acquired through the heat of fire, etc.

**Note:** The Spirit of the Lord was moved over the waters before the creation of heaven and earth, Genesis 1.

It is to be seen, therefore, that all things were created from water. God divided this water when He spoke and commanded a part of the water into dryness, and that He called "earth." The water that was not converted into earth He preserved for irrigating and moistening, because dry earth does not produce much fruit unless it is frequently moistened by its rain-water from above; without water, it produces hardly anything, or nothing at all.

is achieved, namely, that the body to be <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimandū"; in alchemy, sublimation refers to the process of purifying a substance by turning it into vapor and then solidifying it again, symbolizing the transition from a "gross" physical state to a "spiritual" one.</note> has now been made so spiritual that it can be raised. Therefore, that royal Philosopher **Geber** says well: "Because in the work of our <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterij"; the Great Work of alchemy.</note> we need nothing but a single vessel, one furnace, and one disposition," which you should understand applies after the preparation of the first stone.

**Genesis**: From water all things were made, and the spirit of God was carried over the water, and the beginning of the generation of man is from it.

**Hermes**: O strong nature, conquering and overcoming natures, and making the poured-out natures rejoice.

**Geber**: It is expedient not to be ignorant of the principles and primary roots of this art, which belong to the essence of the work.

**Basius** <note>Possibly a variant of Basilius Valentinus or another early alchemical authority.</note>: Our sulfur is stronger than any fire.

**Alanus the Philosopher**: One thing is to be chosen out of all, which is of a leaden <note>original: "liuidi"; can mean bluish, lead-colored, or bruised-looking.</note> color, having a metallic appearance, clear and liquid; it is a hot and moist thing, watery and burning; it is the living oil, and the living tincture, the mineral stone, and the water of life of wondrous efficacy.

**Aristotle**: No tinting poison <note>original: "venenum"; in alchemy, this often refers to a potent, transformative substance or "elixir" rather than a simple toxin.</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow: that is, the wife.

Sublimation is twofold: The first is the removal of superfluity, so that the purest parts remain separated from the elemental dregs, and thus they may possess the power of the <term>quintessence</term> <note>original: "quintæ essentiæ"; the "fifth essence," a pure, incorruptible substance beyond the four earthly elements.</note>. And this sublimation is the reduction of bodies into spirit—namely, when the bodily density passes into the subtlety of the spirit.

The second Sublimation is the extraction of that which is within the substance of the nature of the quintessence, separated from the elemental dregs. Now, I call the quintessence the "tinting soul"; for which washing is necessary, so that through it the oiliness of <term>arsenic</term> <note>original: "arsenici"; here referring to a philosophical principle of volatility or "greasiness" rather than the modern chemical element.</note> may be extracted—that is, an oily nature of the purest greasiness, which is bound with its dregs, which dregs do not permit it to be sublimated.

...to do [certain things], which transmutes the bodies upon which it is cast. This is called by them the **Elixir**, and is said to be the <term>stone that is not a stone</term> <note>original: "lapis non lapis"; a classic alchemical paradox describing a substance that possesses the physical form of a mineral but the transformative properties of a spirit.</note>: a stone because it is ground into powder, and yet not a stone because it melts and flows without evaporating, just like gold; nor is there any other thing to which that property belongs. **Avicenna** <note>A Latinized reference to Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician and philosopher whose works were central to medieval alchemy.</note> says: The Elixir, therefore, is the thing which is cast upon a larger body and changes that thing from its own nature into another. It is made when the "lesser body" is mixed with the spirit, the elements, and the <term>ferment</term> <note>original: "fermentum"; a substance added to the alchemical mix to act like leaven in bread, triggering the transformation of the whole mass.</note>, and from them all, a single concoction is made. And "Elixir" is a Greek word <note>The author attributes this to Greek, though the term actually derives from the Arabic "al-iksīr."</note> which sounds like "great treasure" or "the best of treasures." And indeed, the Elixir which mixes itself with the body is like <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "Tutia"; an impure form of zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces, used in making brass.</note> with copper. But the copper is augmented or grows because of that tutty; the reason for this is that tutty is an earthy thing, whereas the Elixir is spiritual, and the nature of its genus is returned to another genus.

**The Alchemist:** The Elixir is made in two ways. In one way, it comes from mineral spirits and prepared, "clean" bodies. In the other way, it comes from certain things originating from living beings, namely from hair, or an egg, or blood, and so on.

In the first way, it is done thus: certain <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that can "fly" from the fire.</note> are "killed" and are <term>sublimated</term> <note>purified by being turned into vapor and solidified again.</note> until they become clean. After this, one of the bodies generated by nature is burned until it can be ground; then it is <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to a powder (lime) through high heat.</note> until it is made clean in the manner of lime.

At last, the spirits and bodies prepared in this way are ground and soaked with "sharp" <note>acidic or corrosive.</note> distilled waters. Afterward, they are moistened for so long that they are converted into clear water; then they are congealed, and finally, they are placed in the fire for so long that they are made "fixed" <note>original: "fixa"; rendered stable in heat so they no longer evaporate.</note>.

### On the Completion of the Elixir.

**Avicenna in his letter to Hasen:** And so the Elixir colors with its **tincture**, is submerged with its **oil**, and is fixed with its **lime**; and the "white" Elixir is completed by three things, in which there is no fire. But the "citrine" <note>yellow or gold-colored.</note> Elixir is completed by four things in total. **The Gloss:** It is true that the white Elixir requires nothing except three things, namely oil, tincture, and lime. But the red Elixir requires four: namely oil, lime, tincture, and again a tincture which is called "Fire." And for this reason, Avicenna adds: **In which there is no fire.** <note>The "white" elixir (for silver) lacks the final "fire" or red tincture required for the "red" elixir (for gold).</note>

<summary>This page defines the Elixir as a paradoxical "stone that is not a stone" and outlines its preparation from both mineral and organic sources. It explains the components necessary for the "white" (silver) and "red" (gold) stages of the Great Work, emphasizing the role of tinctures and calcination.</summary>

->Concerning the manifold fire.<-

Fire is indeed *manifold*, and its quality is diverse, distinguished by certain degrees. For a certain [fire] in the first degree is hot, and moist in the second, namely the <term>horse’s belly</term> <note>original: "ventris equi"; a common alchemical term for the heat produced by a heap of fermenting horse manure, which provided a steady, gentle, "moist" warmth for long-term digestion of materials.</note>: its property is that it does not destroy the oil, but increases it because of its moisture; for other fires destroy it because of their dryness. Therefore, nothing else in the world is comparable to this except the material fire of a healthy human body. Indeed, the fire of the Sun is hot in the same degree, but it is dry. This [the horse's belly], however, is what masters the matter, and it arises from an animate thing and is nourished by it, just like a child who is given milk in the beginning. For a child is nourished and grows from the hot and the moist; so also the fire of the horse increases the oil with its moisture, yet it fixes the <term>stone</term> <note>The "lapis" or philosopher's stone in its developmental stages.</note> by tempering it with its heat. 

Between these two there is also another, which is hot and dry in the second degree, like the fire of an oven after the bread has been removed; this melts gently and does not burn, because there is no flame in it, nor any great strength of heat. For the heat recedes by gradually declining; but if it were to remain constant, it would fix the spirit within the body, or outside the body. However, the fire of the horse neither melts nor burns, but masters the matter and increases the moisture. 

There is also a fourth fire, the furnace of <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixionis"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates.</note>; this melts and fixes, but does not burn, because it is not flaming; nor does it differ from the preceding one, except that in this one the heat is continuous, while in the other it is not.

The fifth is called flaming, and it is hot and dry in the third degree: this only <term>calcines</term> <note>original: "calcinat"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or to reduce it to a powder.</note> and does not melt—at least, in comparison to gold, silver, and other bodies in the same degree or beyond—and it is the fire in the furnace of calcination.

The sixth is hot and dry in the fourth degree: and this melts and fixes strongly, softening bodies gently, yet it does not dissipate or disperse them. This is the fire of the furnace of <term>fusion</term> <note>original: "fusionis"; the melting of metals or minerals into a liquid state.</note> in the same degree.

There is also the fire of the bellows, which dissipates and disperses bodies as it melts them, and this is the seventh.

The eighth is that which melts and calcines, and it is flaming, because in it only the flame performs the work. The substance of fire is coals and flame, but in this type, it is the flame of wood alone; this is also in the same degree as the preceding ones. In the same degree is also the ninth, namely, that which is the master of all:

<header>PHILOSOPHERS.</header>

[minister]: like the fire of <term>officiation</term> <note>original: "officiationis"; here meaning the "office" or function of testing. This fire acts as a refining agent.</note>, that is, of examination; here it melts and burns, and dissipates and scatters the evil, [while it] saves and rectifies the good, and is like a judge, discerning the just from the unjust.

### The Fire of Junipers.

This is a continuous, artificial fire, lasting at the same degree as you desire for one, two, or three months, until you expose the coals; therefore, you must always keep them covered. You can increase or decrease the heat at your pleasure by adding more or fewer burning coals. First, you should have sufficient ashes, made only from the wood of the juniper. Then, take a large earthenware pot, in the middle of which is another smaller pot or <term>crucible</term> <note>A heat-resistant container used for melting or heating substances.</note>. Placing the ashes in the large pot, let it stand over the heat of a fire until the ash itself becomes hot. Then, all around the smaller pot, place coals—also made only from the aforementioned juniper wood—upon the ashes.

Finally, have even more heated ashes of the same wood, which you shall sprinkle over the aforementioned coals, covering them very well with their own hot ash. Inside that smaller pot or glass vessel, place your material to be <term>digested</term> <note>original: "materiam digerendam"; in alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow, steady heating of a substance to encourage maturation or chemical change.</note>. Place a lid over the larger pot, and put it in the <term>stove room</term> <note>original: "stuba"; a heated chamber or parlor.</note> under a bench or above it, but always upon a stone, so that no damage may occur by chance. By such a practice, you can prepare several fires of this kind. You could also place warm water into the smaller pot, or a moist <term>horse's belly</term> <note>original: "ventrem equi"; a common alchemical term for the moist, gentle heat provided by a heap of fermenting horse manure.</note>, and place the vial of material into that.

You shall make the aforementioned coals in this manner: Cut the juniper wood into small pieces, the thickness of two fingers or larger. Place them in a large pot, well-sealed on all sides and <term>luted</term> <note>original: "perlutatam"; sealed with "lute," a paste of clay and other materials used to make vessels airtight.</note> and filled. Place that pot for an entire day into the strong fire of a <term>blast furnace</term> <note>original: "furni venti"; literally "wind furnace," designed to reach high temperatures using a draft or bellows.</note> or a wood flame. Afterward, let it cool by itself. Open the pot, and you will have what you desire. The ashes, however, you shall burn in the common way. This fire can be a fire of the first or second degree for the <term>fixation of spirits</term> <note>original: "fixionis spirituum"; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note>.

### General Rules.

Every thing is made of that into which it is dissolved: for ice is converted into water by means of heat; it is necessary, therefore, that it was water before it was ice. In this way, all metals were first <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum"; the liquid metal mercury, viewed as the "mother" of all other metals.</note>, which is evident: because when they melt in the fire, they are converted into it. Here note, that the Philosopher calls molten metal also "Mercury" or "quicksilver." Therefore, the reduction of metals into quicksilver in this manner is called "liquation" <note>melting</note>, even though it is done by the violence of fire. Nevertheless, because in that strong melting it holds the appearance of quicksilver, he therefore also names it quicksilver. But this is not the *philosophical* dissolution, but the *lay* <note>meaning common or non-expert</note> one; therefore, it corresponds in some way to the sayings of Philosophy regarding that particular thing known to you.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions following the philosophical allegories of the previous section. ROSARY

->*The Second Rule.*<-

Every nature naturally desires to be perfected, and abhors and flees from being destroyed: therefore, it greedily embraces that which improves itself, and rejects its contrary as much as it can. According to this, art must imitate nature, otherwise it always errs.

->*The Third Rule.*<-

Every inferior <note>original: "peius," literally "worse" or "lower quality."</note> thing working in any art strives, out of its natural malice, to destroy the superior <note>original: "melius," meaning "better."</note>. And every superior thing working in any art tries to perfect the inferior: therefore, you must first know the natures of things, so that you know how to discern what is better or worse for nature, and from what it is perfected, and by what it is hindered: and see that the quantity of the inferior does not exceed the quantity of the superior; otherwise, you will err greatly.

->*The Fourth Rule.*<-

Every dry thing naturally longs to drink its own moisture, so that it may be joined together in its parts. Here, note what the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The "radical moisture" (humidum radicale) was believed to be the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid found in all matter, comparable to the "oil" in a lamp.</note> of all meltable things is. Feed the overly dry thing with such moisture, and it will become tempered. Thus you will have what you desire.

Therefore, by these things consider that the sulfurs of the common people are not those of the Philosophers, since the Sulfur of the Philosophers is a simple living fire, giving life to other dead bodies, and ripening them in such a way that it supplies what is lacking in nature; for it possesses an abundance of maturity, according to how it is perfect in its own nature, and is purified more and more through the art <note>The "art" refers to the alchemical process itself.</note>.
Hence Avicenna says: "Such sulfur is not found upon the earth, except insofar as it exists in those bodies, the Sun <note>original: "Sole," referring to gold</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Luna," referring to silver</note>, and it is indeed in another thing, which is told to no one, unless it be revealed to him by God." In the Sun it is more perfect: because it is more digested and boiled down. For the Philosophers have subtly imagined how they might extract those sulfurs from these more perfect bodies, and cleanse their qualities through the art, so that they might possess through the art, by the mediation of nature, that which did not appear in them before, although they possessed it fully and secretly earlier. And they grant that this can by no means be done without the dissolution of the body and its reduction into the <term>first matter</term> <note>The "prima materia" or primal substance from which all things originate.</note>, which is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum vivum," also known as mercury.</note>, from which they were made from the beginning. And this must be done without any mixing of foreign things, which, being of a foreign nature, do not improve our stone; since nothing is suited to a thing except that which is close to it, as it is a medicine of a simple and potent nature, produced from <term>Mercurial water</term>, in which gold and silver were previously dissolved. For example, if ice is placed into simple water, it is dissolved in it by heat, and returns into its primary watery substance, and thus the water is tinged by that secret power which was in the ice. But if the ice is not resolved into water by heat, it does not join with the water, but lies in the water; nor does it tinge that water with its power, which was previously congealed in it on the part of its species. In the same way, if you do not resolve the body into Mercury with Mercury, you cannot have the hidden power from it—namely, the sulfur digested and boiled down by the work of nature in the mine. For thus the stone is one, a single medicine, which according to the Philosophers is called <term>Rebis</term> <note>From the Latin "res bina," meaning "double thing," representing the union of opposites like male and female or body and spirit.</note>, from a double thing: namely, from the body and the spirit, white or red, in which many fools have wandered <note>original: "errauerunt," meaning they have gone astray or made a mistake.</note>.

### How red sulfur is in the Sun, and white in the Moon.

Since it has been stated that the <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, fiery, and masculine principle of a substance, believed to give metal its color and solidity.</note> of the Philosophers exists as red in the Sun <note>original: "Sole," the alchemical term for gold</note> through a greater <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "digestionem." This refers to the slow application of heat to mature or "ripen" a substance, much like the body digests food.</note>, and as white sulfur in the Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical term for silver</note> through a lesser digestion. Hence the Philosopher says: <term>Yellowing</term> <note>original: "Citrinatio," the stage of the work where the matter turns from white to gold.</note> is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon the moist first generates blackness, and acting upon the dry causes whiteness; because if the fire exceeds this, acting upon it changes it into the purest yellowness. All these things can be observed in many places during <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder.</note>. And the Philosopher says that each of the perfect bodies now actually contains its own good sulfur along with its <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurio," the fluid, feminine principle of metals.</note>—namely, golden gold and silvery silver. Therefore, white sulfur becomes gold by way of the yellow. For this reason, the sulfur within it is red sulfur, the substance of fire, which has digested this white further. Thus, both white and red sulfur exist on either side in the Sun; wherefore fire is its perfection, and it is generated in the fire. Therefore, nature amicably rejoices in its own fiery nature.

Hence, foreign things cannot cause this in bodies, since the art is nothing other—by the mediation of nature—than the boiling and digestion of that nature through simple labor. For example: when I rise in the morning and see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; then I lie down again to sleep, and after sleeping, the urine becomes yellow. This is on account of the greater digestion of the natural heat existing within me. In the same way, follow nature, to similarly boil, digest, ripen, and <term>sublimate</term> <note>original: "sublimare," the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here to mean refining or elevating the matter.</note> through the art, since nature already actually contains within itself the natural fire by which it is ripened. Foreign things do not possess this, and therefore they cannot give it. In the Moon, however, there is only white sulfur, which is simple and not yet digested like the red, nor so purged of its blackness through the action of the heat which it naturally contains within itself. But the species of fire is covered and hidden, with the art acting upon it more than nature does, and vice versa. And therefore it is not impossible for the art, by the mediation of nature—note here the "mediating nature" or "middle nature"—to digest and perfect it further, since it naturally intends to be perfected; but it cannot do so by itself, unless

PHILOSOPHY.

...unless it is moved by art and operation. But these labors, I believe, will not reach a "stiff-necked" man <note>original: "duræ ceruicis," a biblical idiom for someone who is stubborn or refuses to learn</note>, and therefore true gold is not made unless it is so <term>digested</term> and <term>decocted</term> <note>original: "digestum & decoctum." These terms describe the alchemical process of slow, steady heating to "ripen" a substance, similar to how fruit matures or food is cooked.</note> that the better material improves the worse. For the intention of all Philosophers is to reach perfection by using that which is already better; fools understand this in the opposite way. They strive to perfect the better by using the worse, seeking qualities in substances that were never there to begin with—namely, looking for gold and silver in materials that are easily burnt <note>original: "rebus adustibilibus," referring to chemically unstable or "combustible" substances that do not survive the furnace.</note>, as was explained previously.

->*That it is not useful to seek this sulfur in other "sick" bodies, because it is not there.*<-

It may be asked, and not without merit: Can this white and red sulfur, used for <term>tinging</term> <note>original: "tingendū," to dye or transform. In alchemy, "tinging" is the act of the "Tincture" or Philosopher's Stone changing the color and essential nature of a base metal into gold.</note> Mercury, be drawn out from other "sick bodies"? <note>original: "ægris corporibus." This is an alchemical metaphor where base metals (like lead or iron) are seen as "diseased" or "infirm" versions of the perfect metal, gold.</note> I say no. As stated before, there is no substance of greater <term>temperance</term> <note>The perfect balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> than what is found in these two bodies [gold and silver], in which the "tinging rays" reside. Furthermore, as mentioned earlier, sick bodies contain a foul and combustible sulfur, and not one of a "virtual" <note>In the sense of "virtue" or inherent power/potency.</note> nature like that found in gold and silver. Since all art is worthless unless it follows the nature that preceded it, you might be able to purge metals using <term>lesser minerals</term> <note>Substances like salts, vitriols, or alum, which were used for cleaning metal but not for transmutation.</note>; however, once purged, they would still not possess the nature of gold or silver. This is because the "golden digestion" and decoction never occurred in them as it did in the others, nor was their sulfur so mature. Therefore, these immature substances must be assisted by mature ones so that they may be ripened. Thus, they do not tinge others, but are themselves tinged. The <term>tincture</term> of gold and silver shares a proportional nature with these immature or imperfect metals, because they all draw their origin from Mercury. From this, it is clearly evident that lesser minerals cannot tinge. Imperfect metallic bodies, which do not align with gold and silver in terms of "mature Mercury," cannot transform anything, nor can they infuse the nature of gold or silver. Therefore, one must not attempt to tinge except with those substances that possess the power of tinging. Tinge, therefore, with gold and silver: for gold grants a golden color and nature, and silver grants a silvery one. For this reason, you should despise all other things that do not naturally or "virtually" possess the power of tinging; in them, there is no fruit, but only the loss of resources and the gnashing of teeth.

Hermes, in the seventh treatise concerning the Sun, says: "My sons, the bodies <note>original: "corpora." In alchemy, the "seven bodies" refer to the seven metals known to the ancient world, each linked to a planet: Gold (Sun), Silver (Moon), Mercury (Mercury), Copper (Venus), Iron (Mars), Tin (Jupiter), and Lead (Saturn).</note> of the Philosophers are seven, of which the first is their best gold—the King and the head. Neither the earth corrupts it, nor do burning things consume it, nor does water alter it, because its temperament <note>original: "complexio." This refers to the medieval medical and scientific belief that all things are composed of a balance of four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry. Gold was considered the only "perfect" substance because its qualities were in absolute balance.</note> is balanced, and its nature is perfectly proportioned in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. There is nothing superfluous in it, nor is there anything lacking. For this reason, the Philosophers have preferred and exalted it, saying that gold relates to other bodies just as the Sun relates to the stars by its light and splendor. For by that solar power, the plants <note>original: "vegetabilia"</note> sprout in the earth, and every fruit is brought to perfection by the will of God. Similarly, gold among the bodies [perfects] every body...

# PHILOSOPHY.
Nn 4

the body contains and gives life to itself, because the Elixir is the ferment <note>original: "fermentum." In alchemy, fermentation is the process where a small amount of a "perfected" substance (like gold) is added to the "unripe" mixture to act as a catalyst, similar to how yeast makes bread dough rise.</note> without which the work is never completed, just as dough without leaven does not ferment or rise. In this same way, when you whiten, sublime, and cleanse the bodies, and extract the dregs and filth from them: then, wishing to unite, join, and mix them together, apply the ferment to them. Observe how the leaven of dough is nothing other than leaven. Meditate, therefore, and contemplate whether the ferment of a thing can be anything except from its own nature. This is the key of all the Philosophers. And it should be noted that the ferment whitens the mixture, prevents it from burning, and holds the tincture <note>original: "tincturam." A substance capable of changing the color and quality of base metals into gold or silver.</note> so that it does not escape; it softens the bodies and makes them enter into and join one another, which is the goal of the worker. By this knowledge, the bodies are cleansed, and their work is completed with God's favor.

Raymund <note>referring to Raymond Lully (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note> says in the *Apertorium* <note>original: "Apertorio," meaning "The Opener" or "The Discovery."</note>: Now through the second part, the stone will color itself, and it is fixed and fermented. The ferment of the stone for the "white" stage <note>the *albedo* or silver-making stage.</note> is silver, and for the "red" stage <note>the *rubedo* or gold-making stage.</note> is gold, as the Philosophers demonstrate. This is because without the ferment, neither the Sun <note>Gold</note> nor the Moon <note>Silver</note> arrives, nor anything else that is of their nature. Therefore, join the ferment with its sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" represents the active, masculine principle of combustion and soul, rather than just the chemical element.</note> so that it can generate its own color, and also reach its own nature, weight, taste, and even its sound; for like generates like. The ferment, like the Sun, dyes and changes its sulfur into a permanent and penetrating medicine. 

Therefore the Philosopher says: He who knows how to dye sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or Mercury.</note> has reached the greatest secret <note>original: "maximum arcanum."</note>. For this reason, it is necessary that the Sun and Moon be in the tincture, along with the ferment of the spirit itself and of the "permanent water" of quicksilver. By that water, those natures must be fixed <note>original: "fixari." Fixation is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> and nourished with natural heat until they achieve their perfect fixation and fusion. After this comes the rule of joining the stone with its ferment, until the work has reached its completion. This does not happen all at once, for that is not the intention of nature; rather, it happens through coupling—that is, little by little. Also, through coagulation <note>the process of a liquid becoming solid.</note> a true, uniform medicine is made, and for this reason, that coupling is caused by subtle parts that have been transmuted and altered into the proper form.

# THE ROSARY

...and spiritual essence: for it is written that a dense, thick body cannot join with a simple one, nor a simple with a dense one because of their opposition, unless the dense is converted into its own refinement <note>original: "subtilitatem." In alchemy, "subtle" matter is refined, vaporous, or spiritualized compared to "gross" or solid matter.</note> through its own simple <note>In this context, "simple" refers to a pure, unmixed elemental state.</note> spirit. Only then are they able to be mixed together. The Philosophers make this known when declaring it to a certain son of truth, saying that a perfect mixture is the union of altered bodies that can be mixed, joined to one another by their indivisible parts. Open reasoning requires this because mixing or union cannot occur without alteration, which is the refining of the body and its return to a spiritual form.

Regarding this stage, the Philosophers say that the medicine <note>The "medicine" is another term for the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone in its healing and transformative capacity.</note> is now completed, changing from one form into another crystalline form. Then it will appear that this thin layer <note>original: "lamina."</note> is composed of refined natural parts, joined uniformly by natural skill, without any division between those parts, bit by bit. Such a result cannot happen without the refining and homogeneity <note>original: "homogeneitate." The state of the substance becoming entirely uniform in its nature.</note> of the nature. For this reason, it is necessary that the matter becomes so refined that all parts, equal in nature, are mixed with the water. You will be able to see this through your own intellect when one transparent body has been made, joined into a single whole by the union or mixing of many parts—without division, interruption, or ending—into one thickness and a form that is transparent through all its parts.

Now, my son, you possess no small secret: first illuminate the body before you introduce the soul, because otherwise it could never receive or retain the spirit. Thus says Raymond <note>referring to Raymond Lully, the philosopher mentioned on the previous page.</note>.

Calidius the Philosopher <note>likely Kalid ibn Yazid, a legendary figure in early alchemy.</note> says: No one has ever been able, nor will ever be able, to dye <note>original: "tingere." To "tinge" or "color" in alchemy means to permanently transform the nature and appearance of a base metal into a noble one.</note> the foliated earth <note>original: "terram foliatam." This refers to the purified white matter that has reached a flaky or "leaf-like" consistency during the work.</note> except with gold. Therefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> commands, saying: Sow your gold in the white, foliated earth, which has been made fiery, refined, and airy through calcination <note>original: "calcinationem." The process of heating a substance until it is reduced to a fine, dry powder.</note>.

Therefore, we sow gold into that earth when we apply the tincture of gold <note>A concentrated liquid extract or the refined essence of gold used for transformation.</note> to it. But gold can never perfectly dye another body except itself—certainly, this cannot happen unless it is perfected by the Art.

### PHILOSOPHY

Nn 5

Gold is the ferment <term>fermentum: a substance that initiates a transformation, much like yeast in bread or a catalyst in chemistry</term> of the work, without which it is by no means completed. For it is like the leaven of dough, the curdling agent <note>original: "coagulum."</note> of milk in cheese, and like musk in fine perfumes. With gold, the composition of the "Greater Elixir" <note>The Greater Elixir refers to the final, most potent version of the Philosopher's Stone capable of transmuting metals into gold and healing the body.</note> is made, because it illuminates the work and preserves it from "burning" <note>original: "adustione." In alchemy, "burning" refers to the loss of volatile spirits or the corruption of the matter by excessive heat.</note>, which is a sign of perfection.

And you should know that without gold, the work is neither perfected nor improved, because gold is the "bridle" of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum; literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term>. No one can congeal <note>to "congeal" mercury means to turn it from a liquid metal into a solid, stable state.</note> quicksilver except in the body of "magnesia" <note>original: "magnesia." In medieval alchemy, this did not mean the element magnesium, but rather a mystical "first matter" or a specific dark mineral like magnetite or antimony used as a base.</note>, in which one part is burning and the other is fleeing <note>This describes the volatile nature of mercury (fleeing) vs. the fixed nature of the base (burning).</note>. Gold itself is the third among them, receiving the tinctures <note>A "tincture" is a soul-like color or quality that can be transferred to other bodies.</note>; it is the tincture of redness, and quicksilver transforms every body along with it.

Regarding this, a certain author says: "Unless you place gold in gold, you achieve nothing." Arisleus <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often cited as an ancient master.</note> says: "Know most firmly that if too little gold is placed in the composition, the resulting tincture will appear only as white." By the "Ferment of the Sun" <note>original: "fermentum Solis." In alchemical shorthand, the Sun always represents Gold.</note> we understand the "sperm" of the man, and by the "Ferment of the Moon" <note>original: "fermentum Lunae," representing Silver.</note> the "sperm" of the woman. From these, first comes the union <note>original: "coitus."</note>, and afterward follows true and chaste generation. The ferment of gold is gold, just as the ferment of bread is bread. *The Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius." Likely referring to the 'Rosarium Philosophorum,' one of the most famous alchemical texts of the Middle Ages.</note> states: "Just as in the making of bread, a small amount of leaven lifts and ferments a great quantity of dough, so also that small amount of 'earth' which that Stone <term>lapis; the Philosopher's Stone</term> contains is sufficient for the nourishment of the whole Stone."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of mineral classification. It explains why "minor" minerals (salts, vitriols, etc.) cannot be used to create true metals, contrasting them with the "living sulfur" and "mercury" that form the true basis of gold and silver. # ROSARIUM

...it is congealed alone, except by earthly dryness which alters the wateriness, since there is no oily moisture in them: because their congealing <note>original: "congelatio"</note> comes from earthly dryness, they are not easily dissolved except by the action of vehement heat upon them, depending on how strongly they are mixed.

There are, however, "minor" or "middle" minerals, as has been said, which do not take their origin from Mercury. Some of these are salts, which liquefy easily in moisture, such as alum, common salt, sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniacum: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in alchemy</term>, rock salt, and all types of salts. And indeed there are some that do not liquefy easily by moisture alone, such as orpiment <term>auripigmentum: arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment</term>, arsenic, and sulfur, since the wateriness of sulfurous bodies is mixed with viscous earth in a strong mixture through the boiling of heat, until they become potent, and afterwards they are coagulated by cold. 

Vitriols <term>atramenta: literally "blackings," referring to sulfate minerals like copperas or green vitriol</term>, however, are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; and it is believed that within them lies the mineral power of certain liquefiable bodies which are made from them, such as chalcanthum <term>calchantum: blue vitriol or copper sulfate</term> and *olocari* <note>original: "olocari." Likely a corruption or specific term for a type of vitriol or mineral salt.</note>. But metallic bodies cannot be made artificially from these, since they are of a different nature and did not take their origin with metals from the proximate "First Matter" <term>materia prima: the fundamental substance from which all things were thought to be created</term>, namely from Mercury, that is, from quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo."</note>. I do not deny that metals can be purified or dissolved by them, or that a "sophistical" <note>In alchemy, "sophistical" refers to fraudulent or deceptive imitations of gold or silver that look real but lack the true properties of the metal.</note> form can be introduced through them to deceive men, etc.

Sulfur is twofold, namely "living" and "burning." Living sulfur <term>sulphur vivum: native sulfur or the pure alchemical principle of sulfur</term> causes metals to form, although they still differ significantly from one another depending on how much they are tainted by the viscosity of the earth; yet simple living sulfur, which causes gold and silver, is nothing but a hot and dry vapor generated from the purest earthly dryness, in which fire predominates in every way; and this is called an element along with the Mercury of metals, etc. As for sulfur, it is clear above.

### PHILOSOPHY

<meta>catchword: cor-</meta>

...is Mercury, they are not generated <note>original: "generata"</note>, because their generation differs from the generation of Mercury in the first place in form, in nature, and in composition. Therefore, metals cannot be made from them: because for things of a single species, there is one primary matter <term>materia prima: the fundamental, formless substance from which all physical things are thought to originate</term> and one seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> from which they are generated. The first part of the preceding argument is clear: that the minor minerals are not generative from Mercury, which is the cause. This is because Mercury always remains in the primary matter of metals and not in extraneous sulfurous matter. Whence Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Aristotle and the Persian physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina) were the two primary authorities for medieval alchemists.</note> state: therefore, if metals are to be made, it is necessary that they first pass into the primary matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, metals can least of all be made from them; thus the first part of the argument is sufficiently declared. 

Secondly, regarding the same point: the minor minerals cannot be made artificially into the principle <note>or beginning</note> of metals, which is Mercury. Therefore, they also do not reach the middle or the end, which are the metal itself and the tincture <term>tinctura: the transformative agent or "elixir" that dyes a metal into gold or silver</term> which it holds. For nourishment in a human cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into seed, and thus added to its own kind, a new human is generated. But because the minor minerals are of a nature extraneous to metals—although they may well participate in some mineral power—they are of a weaker virtue and are combustible. Therefore, the metallic nature does not take joy in them, but resolves and preserves those things which are of its own nature. 

For example: if water is mixed with earth, they are separated from one another; because earth seeks the bottom, since it is heavy and dry, while water seeks the surface. In no way can they be joined artificially so that these contrary natures stand together in one nature. Water can indeed wash and cleanse the earth, but it should not be believed that the dryness of the earth can be artificially turned into aqueous moisture, even if the earth is soaked with water. In this same way, minor minerals can indeed be joined with metals to purge them and in some way introduce a new form; but nature does not allow them to remain with them, nor to ripen that which is immature. 

Wherefore fools, as they bring forth various businesses and sophisticated tricks <note>original: "sophistica"</note> to deceive men—namely, using disproportionate things which neither provide matter nor receive it—such as: afterbirth <note>original: "secundinas": the placenta</note>, the eyes of animals, eggshells, hair, the blood of a red-haired man <note>Red-haired individuals were often associated with specific alchemical or magical properties in medieval lore.</note>, worms, herbs, roots, dung—
