-># PHILOSOPHY<-

...sal ammoniac, wishing to produce a tincture <term>tincturam: the transformative agent or "elixir" capable of changing the properties and color of a metal</term> from these things; but they cannot do this, as is evident from the definition of a tincture. For to tinge <note>original: "tingere"; in alchemy, this refers to the process of a substance (the tincture) imparting its color and permanent properties to another substance to transform it.</note> is nothing other than transforming the dyed thing into its own nature during the process, and for it to remain with it without any further transformation, teaching nature to battle against the fire; for the nature of the dyer and the dyed must agree. For example: if you tinge lead or tin, or some other such thing, with gold or silver, these agree in their natures because both sides trace their origin from Mercury <term>Mercurio: here referring to the philosophical principle of fluidity and metallic essence</term>; the mature is joined to the immature, so that the immature may be perfected alongside it in such a way. 

But since those four spirits <note>In alchemy, the "four spirits" are usually sulfur, mercury, arsenic, and sal ammoniac; they are called "spirits" because they are volatile and evaporate when heated.</note> are of a different nature than the metals, as has been sufficiently stated before: therefore, if they are to tinge, I ask: must they convert or be converted? If they are converted, then it is not a tincture, as is clear from its definition. If they convert, then by tinging they convert the metal into their own nature, which is earthy <note>original: "terrea"; meaning non-metallic, brittle, or lacking the fusible, "flowing" qualities of true metal.</note> and foreign to the metallic nature. Therefore, they cannot produce metal through tinging. Furthermore, the fact that it converts into its own nature through tinging is proven by the principle that every generating thing generates its own likeness. But because this generating tincture of the four spirits is earthy, it will therefore generate its own likeness, which is also earthy, just like itself.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for creating the Elixir. Following the previous page’s rejection of non-metallic substances, this section explains the necessity of combining Gold (the Sun) and Silver (the Moon) to provide a "soul" or "ferment" to base metals.</meta>

->PHILOSOPHY<-

...so that the Elixir may be made, composed according to the allegory of the wise, etc. But do we not need gold alone, and no other body? Listen to Hermes saying: Its father—that is, of the first composition—is the Sun <note>original: Sol; representing Gold</note>, and its mother is the Moon <note>original: Luna; representing Silver</note>. The Father is hot and dry, generating the tincture; the Mother is cold and moist, nourishing that which is brought forth. Therefore, if there were only one of these in our stone, the medicine would never easily flow, nor would it provide a <term>tincture: a concentrated substance capable of transmuting and coloring base metals</term>. And if it did provide one, it would not tint except for as much as was there, and the rest and the Mercury would fly away in smoke, because there would be no vessel for the tincture within it. But our final secret is to have a medicine that flows before the flight of the Mercury; therefore, the conjunction of the two is necessary in our work.

For **Geber** says in the *Perfect Mastery*: Gold is the most precious of metals. For it is the soul, joining the spirit with the body—namely, the imperfect body. For just as the human body without a soul is dead and immobile, so also the unclean body without the ferment—which is its soul—is earthy and inert. For it is the tincture of redness, transforming every body; it is the ferment, converting the whole mass to its own nature. Just as the Sun and Moon rule over the other planets, so do these two bodies rule over the other bodies of metals, which are conformably converted to the nature of the two aforesaid bodies. And for this reason, it is called a "ferment"; for without it, the sprouts are not improved. And just as a small amount of ferment "corrupts" <note>In the sense of leavening or transforming, like yeast in dough</note> the whole mass—that is, it transmutes and raises it—so it happens also in our stone. 

Wherefore **Hermes** says: "Son, extract from the ray its shadow." Take therefore a fourth part of it; that is, one part of the ferment and three parts of the imperfect body. Dissolve the ferment in its equal amount of the "water of Mercury"; cook it together over a very slow fire, and coagulate that ferment so that it becomes like the imperfect body. Then, with the vessel's opening closed, let it be prepared in all things in the same manner and order as has been described.

**Aristotle:** Choose for yourself as a stone that through which kings are honored in their diadems, and through which physicians are able to cure their sick, because that thing is close to the fire.

# THE ROSARY

...the round: because the round is closer to simplicity <note>In alchemical geometry, "simplicity" refers to a state of unified, elemental purity, often represented by a circle or sphere</note> than the triangle. ->*What the particulars are that are perfected in this art.*<-

Universally, to all observers to whom the present discourses may come, I declare that in the whole sequence of the art there are only two **particulars** <note>"Particulars" refers to specific chemical processes or limited transmutations that do not achieve the full "Universal" Elixir</note>, which are particularly perfected according to the Philosophers and nature: the first particular, in the white <note>for making Silver</note> as well as in the red <note>for making Gold</note>, exists in **Mercury** <note>original: Mercurius; Quicksilver</note> without the administration of a perfect medicine; although the body with which it is perfected well contains within itself its own <term>tincture: a concentrated essence capable of coloring and transmuting metals</term> in a hidden way, just as nature requires. The first thing that is particularly in it from both species of things is this: since Mercury is composed of the first matter of all metals—from a very sulfurous white earth and clear water—and therefore the whiteness of the earth shines through the clarity of the water, and the color in it is the whitest, as experience teaches; and it contains within itself a good, mature, and clean sulfur; then it is possible for the Sun and Moon to be made from it particularly.

**The Philosopher**: Let it be mixed through artifice with other metallic bodies: because it is of their nature, and they themselves are generated from it, and therefore it can be done through artifice, and it imitates "digested" <note>meaning "ripened" or "cooked" by nature's heat</note> nature in that, so that it may be perfected with them. And thus, to whatever metals it is joined, it becomes similar to them without any foreign mixture, since nature simply rejoices in its own nature, and not through anything foreign: but with the Sun it becomes the Sun, with the Moon the Moon, with Venus <note>original: Venere; representing Copper</note> Venus, etc., since each one sends its own power into it; and also because it contains within itself its own good sulfur, but it is immature.

# PHILOSOPHY

**O o**

...[perfected], which is matured by art. For this reason, other metals—coagulated and stained by combustible sulfur <note>original: sulphur adustibile; in alchemy, this refers to the impure, "burning" principle that causes metals to tarnish or be base</note> in a particular way—cannot become the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>Sun (Sol) and Moon (Luna) refer to Gold and Silver</note> as easily as it [Mercury] can.

**First reason:** For if they were transformed into **Mercury**, and mixed with the **Sun** and **Moon**, then their Mercury would contain within itself that aforementioned "evil sulfur."

And if it were purged, it could not then be purged so thoroughly that it would return to Mercury as it was before such simplicity <note>reverting to a state of elemental purity</note>. Nor could a body be dissolved in it by Mercury; and since it could not be dissolved, it could not then send its locked-away power into it.

But with the natures locked on both sides, each would be separated from the other during the trial <note>original: in examine; the assaying or testing of the metal's purity</note>, since it would not have the perfect nature hidden within itself by which they could achieve perfection through their own solution. But instead, it is always necessary for them, by means of art, that other perfect bodies assist them with their own nature, which is naturally perfect.

**Secondly**, if they were joined to perfect bodies while undissolved, less gold and silver could be made, since naturally, through coagulation, their natures are locked on both sides. When there is no medium to open those natures and allow one power to be sent into the other, they cannot be joined by a natural union so as to return to Mercury, from which they took their origin on both sides. Therefore, by the violence of the fire, they would be separated from one another through the combustion of the imperfect nature, as is clearly seen.

But when you wish to join them, you must make **Mercury** through **Mercury**, which dissolves and opens the locked natures, so that one can simply pass into the other, and the perfect can send its power into the imperfect, so that it may be perfected with it. And these are the labors of the **particular way** <note>original: via particularis; a specific chemical process for limited transmutation, as opposed to the Universal Work of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, and thus Gold and Silver can be made in a particular way.

**Note** that crude **Mercury** dissolves bodies and reduces them to their first matter or nature; but the "Mercury of bodies" <note>Mercury that has been extracted or processed from metallic ores</note> cannot do this. This is because of the crudeness of its sulfur, which it had in the first "white earth," and from which it was made from clear water in the beginning. Because that crude element always seeks to corrode that which is closest to its nature: first Gold, then Silver, etc. But the other Mercury, coagulated from bodies, cannot do this.

...is possible: because by coagulation <note>solidification from a liquid or gaseous state</note> that raw sulfur, which was in it before, is altered in its nature. This is because one nature cannot assist the other; however, with raw quicksilver <note>original: argento viuo; Mercury</note> it can do this—namely, unlock and open the natures so that each neighboring thing may be a help to its own nature. 

Thus, if silver is dissolved, it will find a silvery nature; and if gold, a golden; if lead, a leaden nature, and so on. It is by their own sulfur that they are congealed. Regarding this, the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus, common authorities in this text</note> says: "If indeed those bodies which participate in their own nature—as you seek in many foul and unclean things—and therefore it is particularly possible for gold and silver to be made from it on both sides, but not in other bodies, as you have heard."

**Note:** The solution of bodies is twofold: into Mercury through Mercury, and into Mercurial water. The first solution is required for **particular** works; the second for **universal** ones.

The first solution of bodies into Mercury is nothing but **resolution** <term>Resolution: The process of breaking a solid back down into its constituent parts, in this case, returning a metal to its liquid-mercurial state.</term>; that is, through resolution alone, the locked is opened because of the entry of one nature into another. This resolution is used in particular works.

The second solution is into **mercurial water**, and it is done universally. This occurs not through the mere dissolution of immature sulfur into Mercury, but through the **putrefaction** <note>original: putrefactionem; a stage of decomposition in the Great Work, often associated with the color black</note> of the body and spirit in the moist. Since the putrefaction of all natures bound together is their solution and separation, the parts previously bound are separated from one another—each part from the other. This is achieved through the separation and solution of the elements which are connected in the generation of Mercury—namely, water and earth. 

These same parts, while they are being purified <note>original: mundificationem; a "cleansing" or "world-making" refinement</note> in nature, are joined together by conversion; they love each other more after their purification than they did before in nature. This separation cannot occur in bodies except through the spirit. Thus, art transcends nature in one way; for although artificial things are prepared quite suddenly, they were previously, by nature, very slow-forming. Do not believe that these are common elements, such as water from a cloud, or...

->PHILOSOPHY<-

...or similar things: but Earth is cold and dry, Water is cold and moist, Air is moist and hot, and Fire is hot and dry. And such are the elements in their natural states. Yet art can by no means separate the parts joined during generation in such a way that a substance is simply transmuted back into the elements as they originally were, because primary nature has already changed one quality into another. 

In this manner, art can indeed separate qualities—such as the moist from the dry, or the cold from the hot—but nevertheless, one quality from the natural mixture still possesses the nature of the other in some part. Because of this, they can be rejoined by art just as they were divided. If it were not for the fact that one quality participated in the nature of another—namely, Water sharing the nature of Earth through coldness, and Air sharing the nature of Water through moisture, and so on—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed, since the elements would be reduced to their simplest state, just as they were before. 

Before the generation of Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, art would have destroyed nature, beginning from the "head"—namely, from gold and silver—down to the beginning, which is quicksilver <note>original: argentum vivum</note>. But to go beyond these principles to the simple elements as they existed before the generation of Mercury is so remote that it is impossible for art to achieve. 

If it were possible, then it would follow that art could compose elements anew from outside the primary matter <term>prima materia; the fundamental, formless base of all things</term> of metals, and conversely, art would generate Mercury just as it destroyed it, which is impossible to be done artificially. Indeed, art is destroyed <note>or "deconstructed"</note> from the head down to the feet; that is, building up Mercury from the "foot" to the "head" in a more subtle form, as art allows for the substance of nature that existed previously. Thus are the species of things divided when they are transmuted into a form other than what they were before. 

For Aristotle says: "Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of things cannot be transmuted," <note>This is a famous quote from the "Meteorology," though often attributed to the pseudo-Aristotelian "De congelatione." It was frequently cited by skeptics of alchemy, but here the author provides the standard alchemical counter-argument.</note> which is true unless they are reduced or converted into the primary matter—that is, into quicksilver <note>original: argentum vivum</note>. Beyond this, he does not advise, for otherwise it is impossible to be done, etc.

[...it acqui]res some proximity to its own imperfection. When silver and copper are mixed together into silver, it finds nothing but a corrupted substance. In a general mixture, Mercury is more corrupted by copper, since lead is corrupted in both of its parts—namely, in its Mercury and its sulfur.

Thus, lead burns away the copper from the silver—which is separated more slowly without lead—because the more imperfect a thing is, the weaker and more combustible it will be.

Furthermore, the sulfur of the fire is not of a simple and virtuous <note>possessing the "virtue" or essential power of the element</note> nature like Mercury itself, from which gold and silver are produced; in gold and silver, both parts—namely, the Mercury and the sulfur—are sufficiently digested, well-matured, and perfect in every stage of digestion.

If you then mix in certain powders of the "lesser minerals," the result is not impossible if the Mercury acts with superior power. Nevertheless, because it remains imperfect, it is ultimately diminished and consumed by fire, since its sulfur is not of a virtuous nature like the Mercury itself. Instead, the sulfur remains secretly harmful and continues to corrupt the Mercury; even if the Mercury is well-supplied, the substance will eventually return to "dung" <note>waste or dross; original: "stercus"</note> just as it was before. # THE ROSARY

[The substance is] like the Sun, bright as a carbuncle <note>a deep red gemstone, usually a garnet</note>, flowing out like wax, enduring in the fire, penetrating and retaining quicksilver <note>original: argentum viuum; mercury</note>. **Arnoldus:** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> For the color of redness is created by the completion of digestion <note>the process of slow, consistent heating</note>: just as blood is not generated in a human being unless it is first diligently cooked in the liver. Thus, when we see our urine is white in the morning, we know we have slept too little, and we return to bed; however, once sleep is received, the digestion is completed, and our urine becomes yellow <note>original: citrinatur; turns the color of citron</note>. In this same way, by boiling <note>decoction</note> alone, whiteness can arrive at redness, provided the fire is continued in this way. If our white brass <note>original: aes nostrum album; a term for the purified metal at the "white" stage</note> is diligently cooked, it is most excellently turned red; therefore, let it be boiled with a dry fire and dry calcination <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical state</note> until it grows red like cinnabar <note>a bright red mineral, the primary ore of mercury</note>. To this, you must never again add water or any other thing until it is boiled to its red completion.

->*What produces fusion, penetration, and fixation at the same time.*<-

**Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the father of chemistry, though these "Latin Geber" texts often contain medieval European additions</note> in his second book, chapter five, says: We say that the perfection of every solution is brought about with subtle waters, which are especially sharp, acidic, and harsh, having no dregs: such as distilled vinegar, sour grapes, pears of great bitterness, and pomegranates, likewise distilled, and things similar to these. The reason for their invention was the refinement <note>subtiliatio</note> of those things which have neither fusion <note>the ability to melt</note> nor penetration <note>ingressionem; the ability of the elixir to enter into another metal</note>, by which the great utility of the fixed spirits and those things which belong to nature was being lost. For everything that is dissolved must necessarily have the nature of salt or alum, or things similar to them. Now, it is their nature to provide fusion before they undergo vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass, which would "lock" the medicine and make it useless</note>. Therefore, the dissolved spirits will also provide fusion, and likewise a similar effect. Since, therefore, by their nature they are very much in harmony with the bodies [metals] and with each other, once fusion is achieved, it is necessary to penetrate the bodies through it—to penetrate by transforming, and to transform by penetrating. But this cannot be achieved without mastery; that is to say, after its solution and coagulation, it must be treated with one of the purified spirits that is not fixed, and it should be sublimated <note>heated until it turns to vapor and solidifies again</note> by that spirit as many times as necessary, until it remains with it, provides it with a faster fusion, and [protects] it in the fusion from— <meta>catchword: "ne à"; continued on next page as "so that it is not [separated from the fire]"</meta>

### PHILOSOPHY

...lest it preserve it from vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass, which in alchemy represents a "dead" state where the material becomes inert and can no longer be transformed</note>. For it is the nature of spirits <note>volatile substances that can evaporate, such as mercury or sulfur</note> and bodies not to be vitrified, and to save the mixture from vitrification as long as spirits remain within it: therefore, that which better preserves the nature of the spirit more effectively defends against vitrification. However, the spirit is better preserved when it is merely purified, rather than when it has been purified, fixed, calcined <note>reduced to a dry powder through intense heat</note>, and dissolved. Therefore, it is necessary to mix it in, for from these things results a good fusion <note>the ability to melt and flow like wax</note>, and penetration <note>original: ingressio; the ability of the substance to enter and transform the "pores" of a base metal</note>, and a stable fixation <note>a state where the substance remains solid and does not evaporate under high heat</note>.

From the works of nature, therefore, we can prove that only those things which preserve the nature of salts, alums <note>a specific group of mineral salts</note>, and similar things are soluble: for in considering all of nature's works, we do not find anything dissolved except those. Therefore, whatever things are dissolved must necessarily be dissolved through that same nature, by the repetition of calcination and solution. For this reason, we prove that all calcined things approach the nature of salts or alums; therefore, it is necessary that they follow the same properties.

repetition to the proposed goal, with God’s help. Raymond <note>original: Raymundus; referring to the famous medieval scholar and alchemist Raymond Lully</note> says: "Our infant <note>the 'Philosophical Child,' a common metaphor for the evolving Alchemical Stone</note> has two fathers and two mothers: and because he is dearly nourished by the whole substance in the fire, for that reason he never dies." Ceration <term>Ceration</term> <note>from the Latin 'cera,' meaning wax; the process of softening a hard, dry substance until it flows like melted wax</note> is the restoration of moisture upon the earth <note>the solid matter</note> by means of fire, so that the matter—which was deprived of moisture and dried out through calcination—may soften and be reduced to a fluid state, and consequently gain entry <note>the ability to penetrate and transform other metals</note>. This is not achieved through common liquefaction, which the common people perform by melting with fire, but through the Philosophical method, which is done by means of "water" <note>likely referring to a corrosive liquid or a chemical solution rather than literal water</note>.

Fixation <term>Fixation</term> <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or escapes when exposed to heat</note> occurs when the body receives the tinting spirit and takes away its volatility; this is done through frequent repetition, until it becomes ash of perpetual duration, and the whole remains stable in the fire.

->*How metals are generated specifically from Mercury.*<-

The nature of all things that can be melted comes from quicksilver <note>original: argentum vivum</note>, by its very substance. This is because quicksilver is unique, for it is coagulated by the vapor or heat of white or red sulfur that is "non-burning" <note>alchemists distinguished between "vulgar" sulfur, which burns, and "philosophical" sulfur, which acts as a pure formal principle</note>. Whence Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Meteorologica*: "If the sulfur is white and non-burning, it congeals the Mercury into good silver; but if the sulfur is pure with a clear redness, and within it is the power of fieriness that is simply non-burning, it congeals into the purest gold—better even than what the mine produced." This is because every dry thing naturally drinks up its own moisture, so that it may be unified in its parts. Therefore, the vapor of the quicksilver sulfur must be coagulated from a subtle, airy, boiled, and undigested earthy substance, which was joined to it from the first mixture by the action of heat, and afterward elevated, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies. Gold has much of the power of sulfur but little of its physical substance, and much of the substance of Mercury but little of its power; for this reason, due to the Mercury, it is extremely heavy, and due to the sulfurous power, it is very red. Silver, however, behaves in a contrary way in all respects, because it has much of the substance of sulfur but little of its power, and little of the substance of Mercury, and of...

# PHILOSOPHY

by its power <note>original: virtute; referring to the inherent chemical or spiritual potency of the substance</note> is great: therefore it is white, for color follows the abundance of power, but the power itself is located in a vapor. Its matter is closer to the matter of gold than any other metal, and therefore it is easily turned into gold; it requires no other labor except the changing of its color and the adding of weight.

->*The difference between oil and water in the nature of the tincture.*<-

Arnoldus <note>referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>: There is a difference between the tincture <term>Tincture</term> <note>a potent substance or "dye" capable of transforming the nature and color of base metals</note> of water and of oil, because water only washes and cleanses, but oil tints and colors. An example of this is: if a cloth is dipped in water, it is cleaned by it, and when it is dried, the water departs, and the cloth remains in its own state and in the same color it had before, except that it is cleaner. It is the opposite with oil: for if a cloth is dipped in it, it is not separated from it by the heat of fire or air, unless the whole thing is destroyed; nor can the oil be separated from the cloth itself except by washing and drying by fire. 

Water, however, is the spirit <note>original: spiritus</note> which extracts this soul <note>original: anima</note> from the bodies. When the soul is extracted from the bodies themselves, it remains carried in that spirit, just as the dye of the dyers is carried by water onto a cloth. Then the water departs through drying, and the tincture remains fixed in the cloth because of its oiliness. Thus, water is the spirit in which the tincture of the air is carried; when this is brought back upon the "white foliated earth" <term>White Foliated Earth</term> <note>original: terra alba foliata; a specific stage in the alchemical Great Work where the matter has been purified and appears as white, flaky layers</note>, the spiritual water is immediately dried, and the soul—which is the tincture of the air—remains in the body. 

Therefore, the spirit retains the soul, just as the soul retains the body: for the soul does not stay in the body except by the mediation of the spirit. When they are joined, they are never separated: because the spirit retains the soul, just as the soul retains the earth. This is why Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> commands us to honor the souls in the stones: for their dwelling place is within them. They are the means of retaining those things that would otherwise fly away <note>volatile substances</note> with them. Therefore, this is our coagulation <term>Coagulation</term> <note>the process of turning a liquid or vaporous substance into a solid</note>, because they retain that which flies. Sow, therefore, the soul in the white foliated earth, because the earth itself retains it: for when it has ascended from the earth to heaven, and descended again to the earth, it will receive the power of things below and things above. <note>This is a direct reference to the "Emerald Tablet," a foundational alchemical text</note>

# THE ROSARY

### *Concerning inceration, or the method of returning water upon the earth.*

**Arnoldus** <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> : Therefore, pour in water in turns while grinding, and afterward by gently calcining <term>Calcination</term> <note>original: calcinatio; heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine powder or "calx"</note>, until the earth itself has drunk the fiftieth part of its own water. Know that it is necessary for the earth first to be nourished with a little water, and later with more: just as is seen in the upbringing of an infant. Therefore, grind the earth much, gradually soaking it with water every eight days: cook it in dung <note>original: decoque in fimo; using the gentle, steady heat of a fermenting dung heap, a common alchemical "slow cooker"</note>: because through inhumation <term>Inhumation</term> <note>original: inhumatio; the act of burying the vessel in dung or earth to maintain a moist, warm environment</note> the burning is removed, and the matter is reduced to its first material: and afterward calcine it moderately in the fire, and let it not weary you to repeat this many times, since the earth does not bear fruit without frequent irrigation. 

And if the grinding is not good, until the water becomes one with the earth, the body gains nothing. Therefore, do not stay your hand from the labor of grinding, or from grinding and roasting: because it makes the earth white; yet take care that you do not soak the earth except little by little, and little by little, with long grinding—complete this after the drying of the earth. 

Then the weight <note>meaning the specific proportions</note> in this is to be noted everywhere, namely, lest excessive dryness or superfluous moisture corrupt the work during administration; specifically, that you cook as much by roasting as the dissolution added, and you dissolve by soaking as much as was lost by roasting. Therefore, every time after the calcination of the earth, pour over the water temperately, neither too much nor too little: for if it is too much, it will become a sea of calcination; if however it is too little, it is burned into ash. 

Wherefore, gently and not hastily, every eight days you shall irrigate the earth, cook it in dung, and calcine it, until it has drunk the fiftieth part of its water. And note, that after the soaking <note>original: imbibitio; the process of the dry "earth" absorbing the liquid</note>, it must be buried for seven days. Therefore, repeat the work many times, although it may be long: for you will see neither the tincture <term>Tincture</term> <note>the transformative substance that changes base metals into gold</note> nor profitable progress until it is completed. Therefore, study when you are in every part of the work to remember in your mind all the signs that appear in every cooking, and to investigate their causes.

Indeed, there are three colors: black, white, and yellow: when the earth emerges, there is an imperfect blackness and a complete blackness.

PHILOSOPHY

Therefore, in each turn, gradually and bit by bit, intensify the fire during calcination <term>Calcination</term> <note>original: calcinatione; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine powder</note>, until the earth emerges white from the power of the fire. For just as heat acting upon moisture produces blackness, so heat acting upon dryness produces whiteness. Therefore, if the earth is not white, grind it with water and afterward calcine it again: for Azoth <term>Azoth</term> <note>original: Azot; the essential transformative agent or "universal solvent" in alchemy, often identified with Mercury</note> and fire wash the Laton <term>Laton</term> <note>original: latonem; a term for the impure "body" or base metal that must be cleansed to reach a golden state</note> and remove the darkness from it: for its preparation is always performed with water. Therefore, as the water is clear, so the earth becomes clear; and the more the earth has been washed, the whiter it becomes. From the manifold repetition of soaking with strong grinding and frequent roasting, the greater part of the "wateriness" of Mercury is destroyed—that is, its liquid quality—the remainder of which is similarly removed through the repetition of sublimation <term>Sublimation</term> <note>original: sublimationis; the process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condenses back into a solid, used here to purify the matter</note>. These are the words of Arnoldus <note>Arnold of Villanova</note> in his Rosary, word for word.

### *On the method of sublimating and whitening, and a summary of the entire mastery.*

When the earth has absorbed the fiftieth part of its water, quickly sublimate it with the strongest fire you can, until it rises upward in the manner of a very white powder.

When you see the earth like the whitest snow, and like a "dead powder," adhering to the Aludel <term>Aludel</term> <note>original: Aludel; a series of pear-shaped earthenware pots used as condensers in the sublimation process</note>, its joints, and its sides, then repeat the sublimation upon it without the dregs remaining below: for a fixed part of it still clings there, and it would remain fixed with the dregs, and could never be separated from them by any kind of ingenuity.

The powder rising above the dregs is "ash from ash" and earth that has been extracted, sublimated, and honored; but that which remains below is the "ash of ashes," the inferior ash—cursed, condemned, mere dregs and slag. Therefore, make a distinction between its clear and pure parts: because when the whitest matter has risen like snow, it will be complete. Collect it carefully, therefore, lest it fly away as smoke: for it is the "good" that was sought, the white foliated earth <term>White Foliated Earth</term> <note>original: terra alba foliata; a prized stage in the alchemical process where the matter becomes white and flaky, signifying high purity</note>, which congeals what is to be congealed, and purifies arsenic and white sulfur <note>original: arsenicum, & sulphur album</note>. Of this, Aristotle <note>A common attribution in medieval alchemy, though often to "Pseudo-Aristotle"</note> says that it is the best thing that Alchemists can receive, so that they may make silver from it. No one ought to sublimate the earth for the works of the sophists <note>In this context, "sophists" refers to fraudulent alchemists who use "sophisticated" or deceptive tricks rather than true natural philosophy</note>.

but it must sublimate <term>Sublimate</term> <note>original: sublimare; the process of vaporizing a solid and letting it collect again as a purified solid</note> toward our perfect Elixir <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: Elixir; the final medicinal or transformative substance of the alchemical process</note>: and those things which are sublimated are sublimated in two ways, either by themselves—because they are spirits—or with others, because they incorporate themselves with spirits. For Mercury <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: Mercurius; the volatile, fluid principle in alchemy</note>, since it is a spirit, is sublimated by itself; but our earth, since it is a lime <term>Lime</term> <note>original: calx; the powder remaining after intense heating</note>, is not sublimated unless it incorporates itself with Mercury.

We do not perform sublimation except so that bodies may be reduced to a subtle matter—namely, that they may be spirits—and so that the body may be light and easy to govern in all things, whether toward the Sun <term>Sun</term> <note>original: Solem; alchemical code for Gold</note> or the Moon <term>Moon</term> <note>original: Lunam; alchemical code for Silver</note>. Therefore, when the lime is sublimated for the Moon, it must be white, and the Mercury likewise white. When the lime is sublimated for the Sun, it must be red, and the Mercury likewise red, heated by fire; and it should be a waxed powder <note>original: puluis inceratus; a powder that has reached a waxy consistency through the addition of liquids</note>. 

Do not put red Mercury with the white, nor white with the red; but place each species with its own kind, place it over a lit fire, and sublimate the whole. Do not mix that which remains at the bottom with that which ascends to the top; for that which remains at the bottom you shall repeat for sublimation through the incorporation of Mercury until the whole has ascended; otherwise, do not place it into the mastery <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: magisterium; the completed Alchemical Work or the process itself</note>. 

Let the alembic <term>Alembic</term> <note>original: Alembicum; the top part of a still, used for distilling or sublimating</note> in which you sublimate Mercury be made of glass, and the cucurbit <term>Cucurbit</term> <note>original: cucurbita; the lower vessel of the still containing the matter to be heated</note> be of glazed earthenware, with a wide opening at its base so that the Mercury may ascend more freely. The alembic truly must be joined to the cucurbit in such a way that the Mercury cannot escape or evaporate, lest the mastery perish, etc.

And indeed, lest we be bitten by the impious <note>original: mordeamur ab impijs; a common alchemical trope referring to the fear of being mocked or misunderstood by those outside the "art"</note>, we shall tell the entire completion of this mastery <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: magisterij; the "Magistery" or the completed Alchemical work</note> in a brief, complete, and well-known discourse.

->*The cleansing of the sharpest vinegar according to Geber in the book "The Investigation of Mastery."*<-

Vinegar of whatever kind it may be, even if it is very sharp, is refined and purified, and its virtue or effect is improved through distillation. We have treated sufficiently the cleansing and purification of those things with which imperfect bodies <note>metals like lead, tin, or copper, which alchemists sought to "perfect" into gold or silver</note> can be prepared, purified, improved, and refined—always with the mediation of the appropriate fire. For they are prepared and purified by these means toward the intention of the fire in this manner. 

For these imperfect bodies possess superfluous humidities and a combustible sulfurous quality, which generates blackness when they are mixed, thereby corrupting these same bodies. They also possess an unclean, foul-smelling, and combustible earthiness that is far too coarse, which hinders penetration and melting. These and such things are the "superfluities" in these aforementioned bodies, which have been discovered in them through our certain and ingenious experience and investigation. And because these superfluities happen to these bodies accidentally <note>meaning they are external or non-essential qualities</note> and not radically <note>meaning they are not part of the fundamental essence of the metal</note>, the stripping away of these accidental qualities is therefore possible. It is necessary for us, then, to cleanse these aforementioned things with artificial fire and to take away the accidental superfluities.

# ROSARIVM

...everything, only the substance of quicksilver <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: argentum vivum; mercury</note> and radical sulphur <term>Radical Sulphur</term> <note>original: sulphur radicalis; the fundamental, "root" sulphur believed to be the essential soul of metals</note> remaining. And this is the complete preparation of the imperfect bodies, and their perfect purification. The improvement, cleansing, and refinement of these, or of this pure substance that remains, is done in many ways, according to what the preparation of the Elixir requires; therefore, this is the general method of purification. 

First, all the superfluous and corrupt moisture in their essence must be driven off with a proportionate fire, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity; this is done by calcining <term>Calcining</term> <note>original: calcinando; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or "lime"</note>. Then, the entire remaining corrupt substance within their lime—consisting of the burning superfluous moisture and blackness—must be corroded with the aforementioned cleansed corrosives, whether sharp or bitter, until the lime <note>original: calx; the powdery residue left after calcination</note> becomes white or red: or otherwise colored, clean, and pure according to the body’s nature and properties, and free from all the previously mentioned superfluity or corruption. These are cleansed with these corrosives by grinding <note>original: terendo; using a mortar and pestle</note>, soaking, and washing. 

Afterward, the entire unclean earthiness <note>original: terrestreitas; the solid, "earthy" impurities</note> and the coarse, combustible foulness must be removed or set aside. This is done by using the aforementioned materials—those which are cleansed or pure and do not possess metallic fusion—mixed and well-ground with the purified lime. During the fusion or the reduction of the lime, these materials will retain the coarse and unclean earthiness within themselves, leaving the body pure and cleansed of every corrupting superfluity. 

From this, the general method of improving and refining these pure substances is as follows: First, this purged and reduced body must be calcined again with fire and the help of the aforementioned cleansing agents. Then it must be dissolved with those things which are solvents. For this "water" is our stone <term>Our Stone</term> <note>original: lapis noster; the Philosopher's Stone, here described as a liquid or "mercurial water"</note>: it is quicksilver from quicksilver, and sulphur from sulphur, extracted and refined or thinned from the spiritual body. This can be improved by strengthening the elemental virtues within it using other preparations made from things of its own kind, and by increasing its color, fixation <note>the ability of a substance to remain stable and not evaporate when heated</note>, weight, purity, fusion, and everything else pertaining to the perfect Elixir. And this is the method, investigated by us alone, for the preparation, purification, refinement, and improvement of mineral bodies in general.

->Pp 2<-

The multiplication <term>Multiplication</term> <note>original: Multiplicatio; the process of increasing the quantity or the transformative power of the alchemical Elixir</note> of the Elixir is done in two ways: one by the repeated dissolution and coagulation of the stone; the second by the "projection" <note>the act of casting a small amount of the Elixir onto a large mass of base metal to transform it</note> of the first stone of the Elixir upon a body, either white <note>silver</note> or red <note>gold</note>, in such a quantity that this same body is also converted into medicine. Then, these are put together to be dissolved in their own water and "menstruum" <term>Menstruum</term> <note>original: menstruo; a specialized solvent used in alchemy, named for its cyclical or monthly nature</note>. Thus, the first Elixir acts as the ferment for such a tincture, much in the same way that women who are bakers make bread <note>just as a small amount of leaven or sourdough starter transforms a large batch of dough</note>.

### Concerning the waxing of the White Elixir.

From this point, therefore, extract the crystalline plate <note>original: lamina crystallina</note> which you will find shining at the bottom. First, grind it and perform the final waxing <term>Inceration</term> <note>original: inceratione; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a waxy consistency and melts without smoke</note> by adding its aforementioned "white air" <note>likely a volatile vapor or spirit</note> drop by drop into a crucible over a light fire, until it melts like wax without smoke. Then, test it upon a glowing-hot metal plate; if it dissolves very quickly like wax, it is properly "waxed." If it does not, return it to the process and add its "white oil" drop by drop until it melts like wax without smoke. And this is indeed the command of all the Philosophers: that when you have fixed the sublimated parts—the purest part of the earth—you must repeat the sublimation <term>Sublimation</term> <note>original: sublimationem; the process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then collects again as a solid</note> of the remaining unfixed part over the fixed part until that too is similarly "fixed" <term>Fixation</term> <note>original: figatur; making a volatile substance stable under heat so it no longer evaporates</note>. Then, test it over the fire; if it yields a good fusion, you have repeated the sublimation sufficiently. If not, repeat the sublimation of the unfixed part over it time after time, until it melts quickly like wax without smoke. Then, remove it and allow it to cool.

Also, in the said chapter, note carefully the zealous intention of the author in that he repeats the method of waxing so many times; perhaps it would have been enough to repeat it once. But so that he might more strongly and tenaciously impress upon the reader’s intellect the necessity of tireless repetition in waxing, he repeats it so often, because the entire power of the Elixir depends upon it. Also, consider that waxing, fixation, and sublimation are effectively the same thing and are the same act: for by waxing, the spirit is fixed and the body is sublimated. The same Arnold <note>referring to the famous alchemist Arnold of Villanova</note> says in the previous chapter: "As for the water distilled seven times, keep it aside, for it is the solutive Mercury of the Philosophers <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: Mercurius Philofophorum; not common quicksilver, but the essential 'spirit' or 'solvent' of the metals</note>, the one that performs the marriage and the 'water of life' <note>original: aqua vitę</note> that washes the laton <term>Laton</term> <note>original: latonem; an impure metallic alloy, often copper or brass, representing the 'black' stage that needs whitening</note>." And just as you did with the white water, so shall you do with the red.

# THE ROSARY

...since they have one and the same method of washing <term>Ablution</term> <note>original: ablutionis; the process of purifying a substance by washing away its "impurities" or shadows</note> and a similar effect, except that the white water is for whitening and the red water is for reddening. Therefore, do not mix one with the other, because you will err if you do.

The same Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a legendary alchemist and physician</note> says in another chapter: "If, however, the substance melts with more difficulty—which is due to a lack of waxing <term>Inceration</term> <note>original: cerationis; the process of adding a "spirit" or liquid to a dry powder until it reaches the consistency of wax and melts easily</note>—assist it with oil: that is, with 'air' <note>likely referring to a volatile liquid or spirit</note>, adding it drop by drop over a light fire until it melts like wax. For when you perform the waxing, you mix in more of a hot and moist nature than of a cold and dry one; and when you fix it, you mix in more of a cold and dry nature than of a hot and moist one."

Therefore, understand what I say, for the perfection of this work is the **transformation of nature** <note>original: naturae permutatio; the fundamental alchemical goal of changing one substance into another</note>. From the aforementioned things, note that water, air, and oil are the same thing: that is, the spirit of mineral Mercury, and so on.

The same author says in another chapter: The modes of governance <term>Regimen</term> <note>original: Modi regiminis; the set of rules or stages the alchemist must follow</note> that convert into one another are four principal ones: namely, **to dissolve**, **to wash**, **to reduce**, and **to fix**.

*   **To dissolve** is to break down the coarse into the simple and to make it subtle.
*   **To wash** is to clear the dark into the bright.
*   **To reduce** is to turn the moist into the dry.
*   **To fix** is to bind the volatile upon the fixed body.

Furthermore:
*   **To dissolve** is to divide the bodies and to create the "first matter" or nature.
*   **To wash** is to "inhume" <note>original: inhumare; to bury the vessel in a warm medium, such as a bed of horse dung, to provide steady heat</note>, to distill, and to calcine <note>to reduce to a powder through heat</note>.
*   **To reduce** is to enrich, to wax, or to impregnate, and to make subtle.
*   **To fix** is to marry <note>original: desponsare; the symbolic union or "chemical wedding" of the components</note>, to resolve, and to coagulate.

->By the first, nature is changed within:<-
->by the second, without: by the third<-
->above: by the fourth<-
->below.<-

And let it not be burned by those things which do not burn gold and silver, and let it bring about consolidations with a due and perfect ignition.

I say to you, that you should endure patiently: because perhaps it lingers, and haste indeed is on the part of the Devil. Therefore, he who does not have patience, let him suspend his hand from the work: because credulity <note>In this context, a naive belief that results can be rushed without following natural laws</note> hinders him on account of haste.

For every action naturally has its own manner and a determined time, in which it is completed in a greater or lesser space of time.

For this, three things are necessary, namely patience, delay, and the adaptation of instruments: about which we have addressed the artisan in various chapters in the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Perfectionis*, a foundational alchemical text attributed to Geber</note> of our perfect mastery. In these chapters, he can be tested if he has been sufficiently investigated in our sayings, in which we conclude by manifest and open proof that our stone is nothing other than a stinking spirit <note>original: spiritum fœtentem; often referring to sulfur or the pungent vapors of the raw material</note> and living water <note>original: aquam viuam; usually referring to Mercury</note>, which we have also named dry water <note>original: siccam aquam; a substance that acts like a liquid but does not wet the hands</note>, and which is flooded by natural proportion, and united by such a union that they cannot be absent from one another. To these must be added a third thing to shorten the work, that is, the perfect attenuated body <note>original: corpus perfectum attenuatum; likely refined gold or silver acting as a ferment</note>.

From the preceding points, therefore, the things in which the truth is near are evident, as are those things which perfect the work itself.

### On the coagulation and preparation of the first stone, and its sublimation.

Rather, it is necessary for it to be dissolved in the sharpness of waters <note>likely strong acids or "sharp" solvents</note> and calcined <term>Calcination</term> <note>Reducing a substance to a powder by high heat</note> many times, as is held in the sixty-seventh and seventy-third chapters of Geber. The same author says in chapter six that from the multiple reiteration of soaking <term>Imbibition</term> <note>original: imbibitionis; the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</note> along with grinding and gentle roasting <note>original: assatione</note>, the greater part of its wateriness is destroyed. namely into a higher dignity and virtue, and its true purification, etc.

Chapter seven follows: "But I advise that you begin this work with imperfect stones": for this was the principal and hidden understanding of Geber himself. Thus you have it in chapter seventeen: that the nature of **Mercury** <note>the metal mercury, often used as a symbol for the "spirit" of all metals</note> is the same in [metallic] bodies as it is in [common] Mercury—indeed, in the known stones, it is most perfect. Also, in chapter three, it is said that in **Marcasite** <term>marcasite: a metallic mineral (iron sulfide) often used as a source for extracting the alchemical 'spirit'</term> is the nature of a 'mortified' <note>original: mortificati; chemically altered or killed, meaning it has lost its volatile liquid state</term> and moderately prepared Mercury, which is more effective. This Philosopher <note>referring to Geber</note> in his works desires only the nature of Mercury, but the entire nature of **Gold** <note>original: Sol</note> is from Mercury, as is stated in chapter 8.

Likewise, this Philosopher wants this substance of Mercury to be mortified, but naturally its Mercury is in that venerable stone, as is manifest to all: therefore, etc. Also, this Philosopher wants this substance of Mercury to be **fixed** <note>fixa: made stable so that it no longer evaporates when heated</note>, as is clear: for he teaches the methods of fixing with many precautions and clever devices. But who would doubt that the substance of this precious stone is most fixed? Certainly no one who knows it; therefore, etc.

Likewise, the Philosopher wants his stone to be fixed with a careful use of fire, so that its humidity may be preserved—but where is there a more temperate heat than in the bowels of the earth? Therefore, etc. Also, the Philosopher wants his stone to be melted: therefore, etc. It is clear, then, that the Stone is the Master of the Philosophers—as if he were saying that it does naturally by itself what it is bound to do. And thus the Philosopher is not the Master of the stone, but rather its servant.

Therefore, whoever seeks through art to introduce something into a thing by artifice that is not naturally within it, wanders from the path and will weep for his error.

**Gold** <note>original: Sol</note> is the principle for the **red work** <note>the final stage of alchemy, the Rubedo, aiming for the production of gold</note>, and **Silver** <note>original: Luna</note> for the **white work** <note>the Albedo stage, aiming for silver</note>, having been purged of its burning and combustible sulfur.

Moreover, that such a substance is in it, you have in chapter forty-seven. That **Silver** <note>Luna</note> is the stone for the white work is found in the eighteenth [chapter]. Therefore, take this precious stone—having spirit, body, and soul—and **calcine** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine, dry powder</term> it with its own moisture or with Mercury, in such a way that it cannot be felt by touch <note>meaning it is reduced to an impalpable powder</note>.

# ROSARY
### (ROSARIVM)

But the Stone is also administered in the third degree, which consists of the final completion of the preparation: namely, that you make the now **fixed** <note>stable and resistant to heat</note> Stone **volatile** <note>able to be vaporized or "ascend"</note> by methods of **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify and "spiritualize" the material</term>, and sublime it with non-fixed spirits. To sublime the fixed substance is nothing other than to convert the "body" into "spirit," a secret which is extracted from the sayings of the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus," referring to the alchemist Geber</note> as follows.

For in the thirty-seventh chapter it is held that to a body—that is, to a fixed substance, whatever it may be—a spirit is not mixed unless it is first done with the "mastery": that is, the Stone must first be **dissolved** and then **coagulated**. But you ask how the Stone may be dissolved? It should be said: with sharp waters having **ponticity** <term>ponticity: a sharp, astringent, or acidic quality</term> and a sourness that exists without dregs, such as wine vinegar, etc. 

If you then ask why the Stone should be dissolved, it is answered as found in chapter thirty-seven: that everything which is dissolved acquires the nature of salts and alums. This is because only salts melt before they **vitrify** <note>turn into glass through high heat</note>, and similarly, according to their nature, only salts are truly dissolved. If, therefore, our Stone is dissolved, it will acquire the nature of salts; but that which is melted enters into [other bodies], and whatever enters in, transmutes them, etc.

In the fifty-seventh chapter, it is held that bodies are sublimed by the most excellent degree of fire until the fixed is totally joined with the non-fixed, as in chapter twelve: for if the whole has not been sublimed, a quantity of the non-fixed part should be added to it again, until it suffices for a total elevation. By the "strongest fire," understand the fire of putrefaction and of our **Mercury**, by which alone the body is elevated; that is, converted into spirit. 

When, therefore, it has been "lifted," its sublimation should be repeated until the whole is fixed by the administration of repetition. And the "fixed dissolved"—that is, put it into action as above, repeating everything four times, as you have had sufficiently declared above. And the "dissolved volatile"—as if to say, that through dissolution the Stone becomes volatile. And again: you should make the volatile fixed; for thus the Philosopher continues his thoughts in chapter fifty-seven, etc., until it provides fusion or "flows" <note>melts like wax without evaporating</note>.

Chapter ten: Is this work for the **white** or for the **red**? <note>referring to the *albedo* (silver-making) or *rubedo* (gold-making) stages of the Great Work</note> 

**Adamarus** <note>an alchemical authority often cited in the Rosarium</note> responds: To both. For thus it is written in chapter sixty-six, that the **lunar Stone** <note>original: "lapis lunaris," associated with silver</note> and the **solar Stone** <note>original: "solaris," associated with gold</note> are the same in essence: because both are perfected from Mercury alone. There is also one way...

### Raymond Lully writes to Robert, King of France, in a Letter

You ought to know that from the lead of the Philosophers <term>lead of the Philosophers|Not common lead, but a specialized raw material—often mineral or metallic in origin—that serves as the "First Matter" for the Great Work.</term> a certain oil of golden color—or nearly so—is extracted. If you use this to sublimate the mineral, vegetable, or animal stone (or a mixture) after its first fixation, repeating the process three or four times, it will spare you from all the labor of solutions and coagulations.

The reason is this: because this is the hidden thing that makes the medicine <term>medicine|In alchemy, the "medicine" is another name for the Elixir or the Philosopher's Stone, capable of "healing" base metals into gold or the human body into health.</term> penetrable, friendly, and capable of joining with all things; it will increase its effect beyond measure, so that there is nothing more secret in all the world.

Therefore, I tell of wonders that would be incredible to all the ancient Philosophers: namely, that you have known how to separate this oil well from its wateriness, and have labored in the manner...

...by the [man]ner of mixing already mentioned, you will be able to compose the stone in thirty days.

This, however, is not necessary in itself, because the solutions and coagulations of it (as has been said) occur quickly.

Yet, if its sublimation were performed, I believe the <term>tincture <note>A liquid extract or "stain" that was thought to transform the properties of a base metal into gold or silver.</note></term> of the stone would be greatly increased: therefore, choose your intent from these. Galen’s reasoning on how the <term>Iccir <note>original: *Yccir*; a variant of the Arabic *al-iksīr*, from which we get the word "Elixir."</note></term> or **Elixir** is made: he says that various learned doctors propose different medicines. Some say <term>Iccir</term> is from the minerals of mountains; others from herbs; others from beasts and urine, and so forth. It is, however, made from one of those things which is placed in an <term>alembic <note>original: *ymbick*; the top part of a distillation apparatus used for cooling and collecting vapors.</note></term>, and first the water comes out in smoke: that is, the **spirit**; second, the oil in liquid: that is, the **soul**; third, what remains in the vessel is earthy, and is called the **body**. For from these three—spirit, soul, and body—so cooked that they can be mixed and melted together, the <term>Iccir</term> is made. Others say that if someone makes sulfur and <term>quicksilver <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury.</note></term> fusible, the <term>Iccir</term> is made.

Note that no water, nor oil, nor fire, has its own effectiveness for dyeing unless it is first rectified by the repetition of returning it to the dregs and distillations; we add [this process] up to eight or ten times. Therefore, in all things—whether dissolving, fixing, dyeing, or perfecting—the proper method must be held, so that the intention may adorn and complete the matter in the due way; specifically, that the imperfect bodies should be properly <term>calcined <note>original: *calcinentur*; reduced to a powder or ash through intense heat.</note></term>, finely washed, and softened, imbibed, or waxed <note>original: *cerentur*; the alchemical process of "ceration," making a substance soft and pliable like wax.</note>, fecundated, and put to solution in the manner previously described. The spirits, indeed, should be finely washed and purified, and arranged for softening and humbling. Those things which are hot and dry should be dissolved, calcined, or <term>sublimated <note>original: *sublimentur*; the process where a solid substance is heated and turns directly into vapor, then solidifies again on a cooler surface to purify it.</note></term> according as it is seen and better judged according to the sound sense of the operator.

### PHILOSOPHERS

...from state to state, and from color to color. It is therefore the whole Elixir of whiteness and redness <note>In alchemy, "whiteness" (albedo) and "redness" (rubedo) refer to the final stages of the Great Work—the creation of silver and gold.</note>; it is the permanent water, the water of life and death, the virgin’s milk <note>A term for the white, nourishing mercurial solvent used in the early stages of the work.</note>, the herb of washing, and the animal fountain. He who drinks from this fountain does not die. It is receptive of color and of their medicine, and it makes them acquire colors. It is that which kills, dries, and moistens; it heats and cools, and performs opposites according to the measure of its governance. 

When it is "alive" <note>original: *vivum*; referring to mercury in its raw, liquid, or "quick" state.</note>, it has certain operations; when it is "dead," it has others; and when it is sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, used here to purify the spirit.</note>, it has yet other operations. It is the Dragon <note>The Dragon is a powerful symbol of the volatile matter that must be conquered and transformed.</note> who marries himself, impregnates himself, and gives birth in his own day; he kills all living things with his venom. Fire destroys him and consumes him in a short time because of the quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>; for fire cannot master it, nor does it consume it, but it flees from it. 

However, the first wise Philosophers devised clever methods for it, until little by little it was made to withstand the fire; thus it does not cease to advance step by step through the battle of the fire and is fed by it. So, when a certain fixation <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note> is fixed to it, wonders and mutations occur: for when it is changed, it changes other things, and its blackness appears, as well as its sound and its splendor. 

When it is dyed, it is both dyed and it dyes; when it is dissolved, it is both dissolved and it dissolves. It whitens in the sight of the eye and reddens in succession. It is the gathering water, the milk, the strong urine, the softening oil, and the father of all wonders. Therefore, Gold says to him: "Do you prefer yourself to me? I am the Lord of stones, awaiting the fire."

# ROSARY

...philosophical <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "philosophicus" from the previous page.</note> means for truly procreating Alchemy itself is one in the whole world; whoever wanders from this "one" is believed to have fallen into an abyss. Yet, it is not perfect in its own nature until the art itself has guided it to completion. For without the mastery <term>magisterium: the alchemical process or expert "working" of the materials</term>, it is of no value to us, nor is it of any use, nor does it perfectly provide anything. Rather, it corrupts. I say this so that you might use it with mastery, for it is pure phlegm <note>In this context, "phlegm" refers to a cold, moist, and watery mercurial substance, one of the four humors.</note>.

The Philosophers sometimes call it "sulfur" and "yellow melancholy" because of the effect of its wonderful virtue. As some have maintained, God created all nations from it and established their origin there. Some have also called this stone of ours "white bronze" <note>original: *æs album*</note>. Regarding this, Lucas and Eximenus <note>Authorities often cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*, an early alchemical assembly text.</note> say: "Know all you seekers of science, that there is no tincture except from our white bronze." For our bronze is not the bronze of the common people. Common bronze is corrupted and infects everything it is applied to; but the bronze of the Philosophers perfects and whitens whatever it is joined with. Therefore Plato says: "All gold is bronze, but not all bronze is gold." Thus our bronze has a body, a soul, and a spirit, and those three are one; because they are all from one, and of one, and with one, which is its root. The bronze of the Philosophers is therefore their Elixir, completed and perfected from spirit, body, and soul.

Thus, the Philosophers have named the stone by various names so that it would be manifest to the wise and hidden from the foolish. But by whatever name it is called, it is always one and the same, and from the same source.

These, however, are the modes of operation for this stone, by means of which the thing we seek is generated and brought into actual existence:

The first mode is Sublimation, the second is Descent, the third Distillation, the fourth Calcination <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or reduce it to a powder</term>, the fifth Solution, the sixth Congelation, the seventh Fixation, the eighth Iteration, the ninth Ceration <term>ceratio: "waxing," the process of softening a hard substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency</term>; and they say infinite things similar to these. Though these modes are indeed different in their logic, they are nevertheless the same thing in reality. For sometimes the Philosophers, considering their matter—which, when it is in the vessel and feels the heat of the Sun <note>The "Sun" here refers to the heat of the furnace</note>, immediately exhales or evaporates into a form of very subtle smoke and ascends to the top of the vessel—called such an ascent Sublimation. Seeing later that such matter which had ascended then descended to the bottom of the vessel, they called it distillation or descent. Furthermore, seeing this matter thicken and turn black, and give off a foul stench, they called it putrefaction. Seeing it cast off the black or dark color and the foul stench after a long time, and a certain whiteness come forth like the color of ash, they called it Ceration or whitening <note>original: dealbationem</note>. Therefore Morienes <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist and teacher of Prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: "The entire mastery <term>magisterium: the complete alchemical process</term> is nothing other than the extraction of water from the earth, and the returning of the water upon the earth, until the earth itself putrefies; and this earth putrefies with the water, and when it has been cleansed by the help of Him who rules all things, the whole mastery is completed." Furthermore, seeing the earth mixed with the water, and the water gradually diminishing because of the tempered boiling <note>original: decoctionem</note>, and the earth growing: they all said that this was perfect Ceration. Whence the Philosopher says that the earth is waxed with water and imbibed, and by the tempered boiling of the Sun—that is, the heat—it is dried out, and the whole matter is turned into earth.

<summary>This page explains that the many technical terms for alchemical processes—such as sublimation, distillation, and putrefaction—are actually different stages or observations of a single, unified operation. It concludes by citing the authority Morienes on the importance of the cycle of "extracting water" and "returning it to the earth."</summary>

<keywords>Almisadir, orpiment, sublimation, calcination, ceration, Morienes, alchemical stages, putrefaction</keywords>

# ROSARY
->244<-

Wherefore the same says: This force is whole, if it be turned into earth. <note>original: Hæc vis integra, si versa fuerit in terram; a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus, referring to the "grounding" of spiritual force into physical matter.</note>

Finally, seeing that the whole matter came into a certain dissipation, and how it reduced itself back to a solid substance—and because it did not flow, but rather stood firmly—they said that this was the perfect Congelation. Wherefore Plato says: Dissolve our stone, and afterward congeal it with great caution, just as has been demonstrated to you, and you possess almost the whole mastery <term>mastery: magisterium; the complete alchemical process or the successful creation of the Stone</term>. The same says elsewhere: Take our stone, and place it in a vessel and roast it with a gentle fire until it is shattered, and afterward cook it in the heat of the Sun <note>original: calorem Solis; likely referring to the controlled heat of the alchemical furnace or "athanor"</note> until it is congealed, and know that the whole mastery is nothing other than making a true solution and a perfect and natural congelation. Thus far Plato. The same says: Dissolve and congeal, and thus you shall know the whole mastery.

Likewise, seeing the aforementioned matter perfectly congealed and thickened, so that in no way further did it resolve itself into water nor into smoke, they said that it was truly fixed <term>fixation: the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates</term>. Because they saw that same congelation and thickening or fixation, by reason of the greater decoction <term>decoction: prolonged heating or boiling of a substance</term> of heat, come to a perfect drying and whitening <term>whitening: dealbatio; the alchemical stage of Albedo where the matter is purified</term>. And because this whiteness was above all other whitenesses, they said that this was the perfect calcination <term>calcination: reducing a substance to a fine powder through high heat</term>, seeing this matter stand at its own color and change into infinite colors. Because this could not happen except through the resolution of the matter, they therefore called this resolution "solution." For by this very resolution the elements are separated; they act and suffer in turn, and therefore the Philosophers call the said elements "spouses" <note>original: coniuges; the "chemical marriage" where opposing qualities like hot/cold or moist/dry interact</note>.

Wherefore those foolish ones err shamefully who believe that the Philosophical Medicine is created from any other thing, since the Philosophers say: "Son, the alchemists, trusting in all their dissolutions, sublimations, conjunctions, separations, congelations, preparations, grindings, and other deceptions, persist in their errors." Let those who preach another gold than ours, another water than ours—which is also called the "sharpest vinegar" <note>original: acetum acerrimum; a common alchemical code name for the universal solvent or mercury</note>—another dissolution and congelation than ours (which is done with a gentle fire), and another putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the decomposition or "death" of the matter, usually marked by a black color</term> than ours, etc., be silent.

Plato says in summary: Therefore, let your quest be concerning the nature of both lights of the World <note>original: amborum luminum Mundi; referring to the Sun and Moon, representing Gold and Silver or the masculine and feminine principles</note>; for gold surrounds the upper part,

Therefore, because the nature of the **Sun** overcomes the nature of the **Moon**, our **Mercury** is made from the mineral and the vegetable joined together; for joined together they are more effective than if they were separated by themselves. From these things, consider the necessity of both **Mercuries**.

# ARNALD

## BY ARNALD OF VILLANOVA
### THE BOOK OF THE MOST EXCELLENT PHILOSOPHER AND PHYSICIAN
### *called the Treasury of Treasuries, and the Rosary of the Philosophers, and the Greatest Secret of all Secrets, concerning the truest composition of natural Philosophy, by which every imperfect thing is brought back to the state of Gold <note>original: *Solificum*, literally "sun-making." In alchemy, the Sun always represents Gold.</note> and Silver <note>original: *Lunificum*, literally "moon-making." The Moon represents Silver.</note>.*

->P R O L O G V E<-

For this book is called the Rosary <note>original: *Rosarium*. This title was common for medieval compendiums, suggesting a "rose garden" of gathered wisdom or a collection of "flowers" of thought.</note>: because it is abridged from the books of the Philosophers. In this work, with God as my witness, nothing is hidden, nothing is misleading, and nothing is left out; rather, whatever is necessary for the completion of our Work is contained within it. Furthermore, this book is divided into Theory and Practice <term>Theorica & Practica: The two pillars of alchemy—the intellectual understanding of nature and the physical labor of the laboratory.</term>, and also into various chapters. Indeed, it is only right that one who wishes to treat the most sublime effects of things should not be reluctant to study their natural and higher processes. For then the bounty <note>original: *supplicium*. While this often means punishment, in this context of "blessed nature," it refers to the humble petition or the resulting gift of the natural process.</note> of blessed nature proceeds according to one's intention, especially when one looks forward to the reward of the study itself with greater confidence and is prepared to follow the secret sequence of reason within it. 

Let no one neglect to dig out from these published writings the final and chief mother of all Philosophy, which adorns a person with morals and enriches them with benefits; it aids the poor, heals the ailing body, and even preserves health. For he who is lazy in reading books will not be able to be prepared in the practical preparation of things. For book opens book <note>original: *Liber namque librum aperit*. A famous alchemical maxim suggesting that the secrets of one text are explained by the metaphors of another.</note>, and speech explains speech: because what is diminished in one is made complete in another. For a man cannot become well-accustomed to Practice if his mind refuses to toil in Theory; such a person proceeds to Practice like a donkey to a banquet <note>original: *sicut asinus ad cœnam*. A humorous idiom for someone who has no idea how to behave or what to do in a sophisticated situation.</note>, not knowing how or toward what he should stretch his snout and mouth. I have named this book the Rosary because I have abridged it from the books of the Philosophers as best I could, and I have divided it into various chapters.

<summary>This page serves as the formal preface to Arnald of Villanova's "Rosarium Philosophorum," emphasizing the necessity of balancing theoretical study with practical laboratory work. It claims to reveal the "Greatest Secret" for perfecting base metals into gold and silver while offering health and moral virtue to the seeker.</summary>
