### *On the manner of the generation of metals.*
## CHAPTER I.

Whether by nature all liquefiable things <note>Referring to materials that can be melted, specifically metals.</note> are naturally composed of quicksilver <note>original: *argento viuo*, literally "living silver," or Mercury.</note> and the substance of sulfur: this is because it is characteristic of quicksilver to be coagulated <term>Coagulation: The process of thickening or solidifying a liquid, often through heat or chemical reaction.</term> by the heat or vapor of sulfur; for every dry thing naturally displays its own moisture. Therefore, by the vapor of sulfur, the quicksilver is coagulated from its own earthy, subtle, airy, and digested substance, joined to itself in a primary mixing by the action of heat. Afterward, it is raised, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of coagulating mercury. 

Indeed, quicksilver in its "first root" <note>The "root" refers to the primordial state or fundamental essence of a substance before it takes physical form.</note> is composed of a white earth, exceedingly subtle and sulfurous, strongly mixed with clear water until it becomes a single substance that does not rest upon a flat surface. For it is homogeneous in nature: since it either remains entirely fixed in the fire, or the whole of it flies away from the fire as smoke, as it is incombustible and airy. This is a sign of its perfection. 

For this reason, when it later runs through sulfurous earth and is heated, it ascends to the top; for it is in its nature to be sublimated <term>Sublimation: Heating a solid until it becomes a gas, then allowing it to cool back into a solid; used by alchemists to "purify" the spirit of a material.</term> by heat. Nevertheless, through continuous sublimation, it is greatly purified, cooked, and thickened, and is gradually congealed into "white sulfur" and "red sulfur" <note>These colors refer to the two key stages of the alchemical process: the *Albedo* (whiteness) and the *Rubedo* (redness).</note>.

...[is dissolved]. This sulfur indeed is dissolved many times, and afterward is congealed by quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note>, made waxy by the action of that sublimated heat, until through the work of nature it is successively congealed into a perfect metal over the course of barely a thousand years. And indeed, nature itself works these metals by means of mineral vessels <note>Referring to the natural cavities or veins in the earth where minerals form.</note>. Therefore, in these works, it is necessary to imitate nature, if one wishes to complete a more perfect medicine of the imperfect metals.

### ->That Quicksilver is the Medicine of All<-
### ->Metals. CHAPTER II.<-

Therefore, Aristotle says that quicksilver is the element of all liquefiable things <note>Materials that can be melted.</note>: because when all liquefiable things are bound together, they are converted into it, and it is mixed with them because it is of their own substance. However, these metallic bodies differ in their composition from quicksilver in the same way that it was once pure from the impure sulfur that was foreign to it. For quicksilver is made from true, non-burning sulfur. For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was almost always referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval scholarship.</note> said: White, non-burning sulfur congeals <term>Congealing: The alchemical process of turning a liquid substance into a solid or semi-solid state.</term> Mercury into good Moon <note>original: *Lunam*; the alchemical name for silver.</note>. And that is the best thing that those who practice Alchemy can undertake, as they convert it into good silver. 

If, however, the sulfur is pure, clean, and of the highest quality, bright with redness, and if there is in it the power of a sulfurous fieriness that does not burn, it will be the best thing that Alchemists can undertake, so that they may make Sun <note>original: *Solem*; the alchemical name for gold.</note> from it. For if the quicksilver is of good substance, but the sulfur is impure and burning, it converts that quicksilver into bronze <note>original: *æs*</note>. Also, if the quicksilver is stony, impure, and earthy, and the sulfur is not clean, iron will be produced from it. 

Tin <note>original: *Stannum*</note> indeed seems to have good and pure quicksilver, but bad sulfur that is not well mixed. Lead <note>original: *Plumbum*</note> truly consists of coarse, bad, heavy, and yellowish quicksilver; its sulfur is bad, of a foul and stinking taste and weak virtue, which is why it is not well coagulated. These, word for word, are the words of Aristotle in the fourth book of his *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle’s *Meteorology* was the foundational text for medieval mineralogy; Book IV discusses the composition of materials.</note>. One must believe this natural philosopher in all things, rather than fables or lying works that are entirely foreign to the workings of nature. And so you must profess to follow: for he who believes in lies loses the secret of the Philosophers.

<summary>Arnaldus explains the Mercury-Sulfur theory, asserting that all metals are composed of quicksilver and sulfur in various states of purity. He cites Aristotle to argue that gold and silver result from pure components, while base metals like lead and iron result from impure ones.</summary>

### *That foreign sulfur, or the sulfur of the common people, is the cause of the imperfection of all metals.*
### CHAPTER III.

Note therefore these words, and mark these mysteries: for the whole truth of this science is to be gathered from the previously mentioned words of the Philosophers, so that vanity might be left behind. This truth exists through a double superfluity <note>An excess or waste material.</note> within the body: one is indeed hidden deep within the quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note>, having been added at the very beginning of its mixing; the other is outside its true nature and is corruptible. Of these two, the latter is removed with great effort, but the former can be removed by no skill of the craftsman. For this reason, combustible sulfur is removed by the calcination <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state, often to reduce it to a powder.</term> of fire, or is otherwise deleted from the metallic bodies. And this is why: because quicksilver holds onto and defends from burning that which is of its own nature; the other sulfur it rejects, exposing it to the fire, which infects it. Thus, quicksilver is friendly and peaceable toward its own nature.

Quicksilver adheres more strongly to quicksilver, and is even more "befriended" by it; after that, it favors gold; and after that, silver. From this, it follows that these two metals participate more in its nature. Other bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" almost always refers to the seven known metals.</note> do not have such a conformity to it because they contain within themselves a foreign, earthy, impure, and foul-smelling sulfur. Therefore, we can truly say that they participate less in the nature of perfection because they are foul, combustible bodies. This is because no matter how sulfur is prepared by human art, it always burns and is burned, and it creates a blackness in every work. For this reason <term>Avicenna</term> <note>original: *Auicenna*; the Latinized name of the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a primary authority in medieval alchemy.</note> says: "It does not enter into our mastery <note>original: *magisterio*, referring to the 'Great Work' or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> because it is not from quicksilver, nor from the substance of quicksilver, nor part of its perfection, since it always infects, blackens, and corrupts it."

It remains, therefore, that quicksilver is the most perfect of the bodies and the savior from burning <note>original: *adustionis*; the destructive process of being consumed or scorched by fire.</note>, because those other bodies are entirely burned away unless they participate in and possess its nature. From this it is clear that a high quality of quicksilver is the cause of perfection in metallic bodies, while a high sulfur content is the cause of corruption—that is, some metals are burned more and some less according to the test of the fire, just as those which have more sulfurous—

Through the other nature, however, it has neither fusion <term>Fusion: The process of melting or flowing together.</term> nor ingression <term>Ingression: The ability of an alchemical substance to penetrate and transform the interior of another body.</term>; for if it were fixed, it would prevent fusion, and yet it is never fixed itself. ->*That only quicksilver is the perfection of all metals.*<-
### CHAPTER IV.

However, this happens least of all in quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury.</note>: because it is fixed without being turned into earth; and similarly, it is fixed by its conversion into earth. For through haste toward its fixation, which is done by precipitation <term>Precipitation: A process where a solid is made to settle out of a liquid solution.</term>, it is fixed and turned into earth; but through a gradual and repeated sublimation <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a substance so it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid, used here to purify the mercury.</term>, it is likewise fixed, and does not turn into earth; rather, it provides a metallic fusion. 

And this is so because it has a viscous and dense substance: the sign of which is its grinding with imbibition <term>Imbibition: The soaking of a solid in a liquid to saturate it.</term> and its stronger mixing with things of its own kind. Therefore, its manifest viscosity is established by its great adherence. That it has a dense substance is clearly seen by even a one-eyed man <note>original: *videt monoculus*. A Latin idiom meaning something is so obvious that even someone with severely limited vision could not miss it.</note>, on account of the heaviness of its immense weight: for it outweighs gold while it remains in its own nature. 

Moreover, it is of the strongest composition and uniform nature: because it is not separated into parts, such that it allows itself to be divided in no way. For it either remains standing in the fire with its entire substance, or it withdraws from the fire with its entire substance. From these things, therefore, it is concluded that quicksilver can be fixed without the consumption of its radical moisture <term>Radical moisture: The fundamental, life-giving fluid thought to exist in all matter, which alchemists sought to preserve while removing "superfluous" moisture.</term>, and without its conversion into earth. And therefore, the true cause of perfection is noted in it: because it alone suffices for the perfection of fusion in every degree, namely with ignition <term>Ignition: The act of heating a substance until it glows or catches fire.</term> and without ignition. For on account of the good adherence of its parts and the strength of its mixture, if in any way its parts are thickened by fire, it no longer permits itself to be cor- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "corrupted" is the likely completion.</note>

Nevertheless, it mixes easily with Gold <note>original: *Sole*, literally "the Sun."</note> and Silver <note>original: *Luna*, literally "the Moon."</note> because they share more of its nature; yet nothing is submerged within it except Gold.

From this you may draw a great secret: that Mercury receives into itself what is of its own nature and rejects what is alien, because its nature rejoices more in its own kind than in foreign things. From this it is clearly shown that bodies of greater perfection are those that contain more Mercury, and those that contain less are of lesser perfection.

### That Quicksilver Contains Its Own Sulfur Within Itself. CHAPTER V.

It is therefore clear that quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> contains within itself its own good, fixed sulfur, by which it is coagulated into gold and silver according to the different method of preparation. For according to the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, whose theories on the generation of metals from sulfur and mercury formed the basis of medieval alchemy.</note>, even if quicksilver is pure, the power of white, non-burning sulfur will coagulate it into silver. And this is the best material for alchemists to use their skill to create the Elixir for silver. If, however, the sulfur is excellent and clear with redness, and there is in it the power of fieriness that is simply non-burning, it will be the best thing for making the Elixir for gold. The Philosopher rightly taught first the white sulfur for silver, and afterwards the red for gold; because gold cannot be made unless it was first silver, since there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through the middle.

Therefore, the transition from black to perfect lemon-yellow <term>Citrination: The yellowing stage of the alchemical process, following whiteness and preceding the final red color of the Philosopher's Stone.</term> cannot occur unless it was first white; for the lemon-yellow is composed of much white and a very small amount of red. Nor can a transition be made from lemon-yellow back to white unless it was first black; for gold cannot become silver unless it is first destroyed, corrupted, and blackened, because that which is better cannot become worse except through its own corruption. For the generation of one is the corruption of another <note>This is a foundational Aristotelian principle: *generatio unius est corruptio alterius*.</note>. Thus, he who knows how to convert gold into silver also knows how to convert silver into gold; for white, non-burning sulfur used for silver can, through greater digestion <term>Digestion: The application of gentle, consistent heat over a long period to mature or "ripen" a substance.</term>, become red sulfur for gold. This is because yellowing is nothing other than complete digestion, just as whiteness is nothing other than the removal of blackness. For heat acting upon moisture first produces blackness; acting upon dryness it works whiteness; and in the white it produces yellowing. This can indeed be observed in the calcination <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash, often used to "purify" metals.</term> of lead, which is converted into black ash, then into white, and finally into an intense yellow or red. Thus, white or red sulfur is obtained from a single metallic matter to the ful...

It establishes the alchemical principle that metals must pass through intermediate stages and that "corruption" (breaking down) is necessary for a new, better form to be generated.</summary>

...fully purified, yet digested and cooked down in a different manner. Therefore the Philosopher <note>Likely Aristotle, who was the primary authority for the sulfur-mercury theory of metals.</note> says that in every silver there is white sulfur, just as in every gold there is red sulfur. Gold, therefore, since it is precious, is a tincture <note>A concentrated essence or "dye" capable of transforming the quality of a substance.</note> of redness for all metals, dyeing and transforming every body. ->*That there is one Stone of the Philosophers.*<-
### CHAPTER VI.

It is necessary, therefore, that the seeker of this science be of a constant will in the work. Let no one presume to approach it in this way [with distraction]: since our art is not perfected in a multitude of things: for it is one. For there is one stone, one medicine, to which nothing foreign is added, nor is anything taken away, except that the superfluous things are removed. For all sulfur that is external <note>original: *linternum*; likely a corruption of *externum* (external) or *vulgare* (common).</note>—that is, common sulfur, or the "butter" of quicksilver—is foreign, because it is destructive or corruptive of itself. On the contrary, however, that which is able to be converted through our mastery into gold and silver is not foreign. Therefore, nothing suits a thing except what is closer to it by its own nature. For nothing is generated from a man except a man, nor from other animals except those similar to themselves. Since whatever is generated follows its own likeness. Let us, therefore, use true nature: since it is not improved except within its own nature, to which nothing alien is joined. Do not, therefore, introduce, nor...

...powder, nor water, nor any other thing: for things of a different nature do not improve our Stone, nor do they enter into it, because the Stone did not originate from them. For if any foreign substances are added to it, the Stone is immediately corrupted, and that which we seek to create does not come to pass. Therefore, it is necessary to gather the medicine from those corporeal <note>Physical or bodily things.</note> things that are most compatible in their nature. 

Hence, it is necessary that the medicine itself agrees with the metals in nature, and adheres to them in their deepest depths: so that it may fulfill the completion of what is lacking, and also so that the Mercury may be mixed through the smallest parts <note>original: *per minima*; a term meaning mixing at the atomic or most basic level.</note> before it can escape <note>Referring to the "flight" or evaporation/volatilization of mercury when heated.</note>. However, no body remaining in its own raw nature can coagulate Mercury or adhere firmly to it; nor does Mercury itself, on its own, heal "diseased" <note>In alchemy, base metals were often described as "infirm" or "sick" versions of the "healthy" or perfect gold.</note> bodies, because during the trial of the fire it is separated from them. For coarse things do not combine well with simple ones, nor simple things with coarse ones. Therefore, it is necessary for that medicine to be of a more subtle substance and a more liquid fusion than the bodies themselves, and also of a greater fixation <term>Fixation: The process of making a volatile substance (like mercury) stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</term> and retention than quicksilver is in its own nature.

->*From what materials the Physical Stone is extracted.*<-
### CHAPTER VII.

It may therefore be asked, and not without reason: from where can this medicine of ours most especially be drawn? Responding to this, we say that it is drawn from the very things in which it resides. It exists both in the metallic bodies and also in quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*</note> according to nature, since they are found to share a single nature. However, it is extracted from the bodies with greater difficulty, while in the Mercury itself it is more immediate, though not more perfect. 

And this is the reason: because no body is worthier than the Sun <note>Gold</note>, or purer than it or its "shadow," which is the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Without these, no dyeing quicksilver is generated. Truly, he who strives to "dye" <note>To transform a metal's color and nature.</note> without this quicksilver proceeds blindly to the practice, "like a donkey to a banquet" <note>A common Latin proverb (*asinus ad coenam*) meaning someone is totally unprepared or out of their depth.</note>; for gold provides a golden color, and silver provides a silver color. He, therefore, who knows how to dye quicksilver with the Sun and Moon has reached the secret called "white sulfur," which is best for making silver; when this is made red, it becomes "red sulfur," which is best for making gold. From those bodies, therefore, is extracted sulfur that is exceedingly white and red, since the purest substance of sulfur resides within them.

substance, which is most highly refined by the ingenuity of nature. It follows, then, that our medicine is a most pure and subtle substance, which takes its origin from the matter of quicksilver and was created from it. Yet, it is not the matter of quicksilver in its raw nature, nor in its whole substance, but was a part of it. However, it is not what it is now; when our Stone is made, it is simply quicksilver, even though it was once a part of it: for it illuminates it, and defends and preserves it from burning <note>original: *adustione*; the chemical process of oxidation or "scorching" by fire which base metals cannot withstand.</note>, which is the cause of perfection. Therefore, the substance of the precious Stone is sought out for whatever cause the medicine is generated, both in the metallic bodies and in the substance of the quicksilver itself. Nevertheless, I advise that you do not work except with Mercury and the Sun for Gold, and with Mercury and the Moon for Silver: because the entire benefit of this art consists in these alone.

### CHAPTER X.

Here, therefore, is our famous stone: because there is no transition from one extreme to another except through a <term>medium<note>original: *medium*; a middle state or intervening substance.</note></term>. Now, the extremes of our stone are, on the first side, <term>quicksilver<note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver."</note></term>, and on the second side, the complete Elixir. For some of the substances in the middle of these are more purified, boiled, and <term>digested<note>original: *digesta*; a process of slow heating similar to metabolic digestion.</note></term> than others; and those are better and closer to the work, which I believe you, dearest reader, are not ignorant of, but know well.

Do not err because of this: for "whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap." For a seed corresponds to its own kind, and every shrub brings forth its own fruit according to its species. Nature is indeed wise, always desiring to be perfected, for she always contains her own increase within herself. Therefore <term>Avicenna<note>original: *Auicenna*; Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval science.</note></term> says: "Unless I saw gold and silver, I would say for certain that Alchemy is not a true art." Therefore, although our stone here contains the <term>tincture<note>The soul or color-giving property of the stone that transforms other metals.</note></term> materially within itself, just as it is created as a subtle thing within the body, it would not have movement of itself toward being a complete Elixir unless it were moved by art and operation.

And so, diverse arts have been invented by diverse Philosophers so that what is left incomplete by nature may be completed by artifice; for nature is prone toward her own perfection. Work, therefore, prudently and not by chance; know the natures of the stone and its strengths, and which stone is a friend or enemy to another stone. See that you recognize what the stone itself has done. And before you can know the coarse, make it fine; lighten the heavy, smooth the rough, soften the hard, sweeten the bitter, and you will possess the entire <term>mastery<note>original: *magisterium*; the complete skill or the finished "Great Work" of alchemy.</note></term>. ### On the perfect investigation of the Physical Stone.
### CHAPTER I.

It is manifest, therefore, that through the operation of the medicine, there is the operation of nature, and that the medicine itself is that same nature: for the medicine itself is composed solely of nature. It is certainly true that every thing is made of that into which it is dissolved; for frost is converted into water by means of heat. It is clear, therefore, that the water itself existed before the frost. Thus all our <term>Stone<note>The "Physical Stone" or Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work.</note></term> is dissolved into <term>quicksilver<note>original: *argentum viuum*; literally "living silver." In alchemy, this refers to the primordial metallic moisture rather than just common mercury.</note></term> through our mastery: therefore it was previously quicksilver. 

Moreover, the way of converting this quicksilver is the conversion of natures into their first root: for to convert nature is to "rotate the elements in a circle." For the elements are, by their own aptitude, convertible into one another, and thus they are generated, corrupted, and altered by each other. Therefore, convert the elements and you will find what you seek: because our operation is nothing but the change of natures, and the friendly mixing of those elements—the cold with the hot, the moist with the dry. 

Nevertheless, the dry is not converted into the moist unless it has first been cold, that is, water; nor is the cold converted into the hot unless it has first been moist; for a transition does not happen from <term>extremes<note>The "extremes" are the opposing pairs of elements: Fire (Hot/Dry) vs. Water (Cold/Moist), and Air (Hot/Moist) vs. Earth (Cold/Dry).</note></term> except through a middle state. Earth is not converted into air unless it is first turned into water. Indeed, air and water are the middle elements; fire and earth are the extreme elements. 

Air is truly next to fire, just as earth is next to water; and this is because water is the contrary of fire, and earth the contrary of air: for water is cold and moist, and fire is hot and dry, whereas earth is cold and dry, and air is hot and moist. And so water and air agree in moisture, and fire and earth in dryness; and therefore one is converted into the other. And similarly toward each other, they are thus immediately converted and more slowly separated from one another. On the contrary, air and earth, or fire and water, are not converted into each other unless fire is first converted into air and earth into water.

If, therefore, the dry is converted into the cold, and the cold into the moist, and the moist into the hot, and the hot into the dry: then you will possess the entire <term>mastery<note>original: *magisterium*; the complete alchemical process or Great Work.</note></term>. There are four principal modes of the regime which convert into one another: namely, to **dissolve**, to **wash**, to **reduce**, and to **fix**. To **dissolve** the coarse into the simple and to refine it; to **wash** the dark into the bright; to **reduce** the moist into the dry; to **fix** the volatile upon a fixed body. To dissolve is to divide bodies and matter, or to create the first nature. To wash is to <term>inhume<note>original: *inhumare*; to bury in a warm, moist environment (like a water bath or dung) to facilitate slow digestion.</note></term>, to distill, and to <term>calcine<note>To reduce a substance to a powder through heat.</note></term>. To reduce is to <term>wax<note>original: *incerare*; to bring a substance to a waxy, meltable state.</note></term>, to fatten or to impregnate, and to refine; to fix is to "marry," to resolve, and to coagulate. Through the first, the nature is changed internally; through the second, externally; through the third, above; and through the fourth, below.

### On the first regime of the stone.
### CHAPTER II.

Dissolve the dry, coarse stone into <term>quicksilver<note>original: *argentum viuum*; literally "living silver." In alchemy, this refers to the primordial metallic moisture rather than just common mercury.</note></term>, so that it may be returned to its "first matter." And this happens only when it becomes quicksilver, because that alone has the <term>Sun and Moon<note>original: *Solem & Lunam*; Gold and Silver.</note></term> within it to return it to its matter, or its primary matter. But because quicksilver contains within itself an earthy and combustible dross—though without actual flame—and a watery substance, it is necessary to take away the superfluous and to fill or supply what is absent if we wish to make or extract the full medicine. Indeed, it is necessary to entirely remove the earthy dross through <term>sublimation<note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collecting the purified solid that forms when it cools.</note></term>, lest the moisture create heat and wateriness during the <term>projection<note>The final stage of the Great Work where the Stone is cast upon base metals to transform them into gold or silver.</note></term>. In the same way, one must save the "fugitive" substance of that medicine, for it is its property to cleanse, to defend against burning, and even to fix and make fixed. Therefore, it happens that from the diversity of the medicine itself—according to its various states of corruption—there is sometimes created **Saturn** from it, sometimes **Jupiter**, sometimes **Venus**, and sometimes **Mars**; this necessarily happens or occurs because of impurity.

But those things which are not dissolved do not have refined parts, unless you soften them. This form is indeed black in color, foul in odor, and subtle and fragmented to the touch: and this is the sign of the perfect dissolution of the bodies. For heat acting upon moisture first generates blackness, which blackness is the <term>raven’s head<note>original: *caput corvi*; a classic alchemical symbol for the *nigredo* or "blackness" stage, representing the death of the old substance and the beginning of the transformation.</note></term>. But it is the beginning of our work, which is to dissolve our stone into Mercury, or into mercurial water. Now you have the first regime of the work.

### *Concerning the recapitulation of the first regime.*

Now I shall briefly state the whole method of dissolution. And this is done so that we may have <term>sulfur<note>original: *sulphur*; in alchemy, sulfur represents the active, masculine, and combustible principle.</note></term> and Mercury from that matter out of which <term>gold<note>original: *aurum*</note></term> and <term>silver<note>original: *argentum*</note></term> were created beneath the earth: because if there were true sulfur and quicksilver, we could easily make gold and silver from them. 

This <term>Mastery<note>original: *magisterium*; the supreme secret or goal of the alchemical art.</note></term> is only for the wealthy and for the high-ranking of the world. And he who possesses it has an everlasting treasure. In it, therefore, three things must be sought: namely, the subtle genius of the craftsman, the work of the hands, and judgment. This indeed requires wealth, wisdom, and books.

### Concerning the second regimen, which is to wash.
### CHAPTER VI.

The second <term>regimen<note>original: *regimen*; a specific stage or systematic procedure in the alchemical process.</note></term> of the stone is to wash what is black, corrupt, and foul, so that it may become exceedingly bright, clear, and free from impurities. This can in no way be accomplished without the division of the elements, the distillation of the waters, and the <term>dissolution<note>original: *dissolutione*; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note></term> of the stone. For of the elements, two are "stony" and two are "aquatic." The stony ones are fire and earth, because they are dry; the aquatic ones are air and water, because they are moist. 

Therefore, fire consumes that which exists on the outside: for it eats away, wastes, and devastates the filth of the waters through distillation, and it makes them subtle through the lightening effect of the air. It also crushes the thickness of the stone through <term>calcination<note>original: *calcinationem*; heating a substance to high temperatures in a crucible to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note></term>, and devours the saltiness of their <term>sulfureity<note>original: *sulphureitatis*; the quality of containing sulfur, which in alchemy often represented the active, combustible, or "staining" principle.</note></term>. For this reason, our stone is divided into the four elements, so that it may be more refined, more thoroughly cleansed of filth, and afterward more firmly joined together. For nothing was ever born or grew, nor was it ever animated, except after <term>putrefaction<note>original: *putrefactionem*; the chemical and symbolic "rotting" or breakdown of the matter, seen as essential for its rebirth into a higher form.</note></term>. Thus they are putrefied so that, once digested, they may be better separated. Indeed, if it has not been putrefied, it cannot be melted, nor will it be dissolved; and if it is not dissolved, it will be reduced to nothing.

Therefore, the separation by water is more subtle, since it does not endure the <term>ignition<note>original: *ignitionem*; the process of being set on fire or subjected to intense, direct heat.</note></term> which is drawn out through the ashes. In this way, therefore, you shall divide the four...

### *Concerning the washing of the air.* CHAPTER IX.

From this point, divide the air from the fire through distillation: because that which is distilled is the purest air; that which remains in the bottom is the dry fire. Air is therefore distilled with fire: because air is itself "tinted water," and its tincture is fire: since the body is the air of the spirit carrying the fire. If therefore you mix the stone with fire, it will immediately be red, and they will always love each other. Whatever you wish to redden, redden with the fire of the stone, and it will be red forever.

### *What is the difference between water and oil.*
### *CHAPTER XI.*

There is a difference between the tincture of water and of oil: because water only washes and cleanses, while oil truly tints and colors. An example of this is seen when a cloth is dipped in water; it is cleaned by it, and when the cloth is dried, the water departs and the cloth remains in the same state and color it was in before, except that it is cleaner. It is the opposite with oil; if a cloth is dipped in it, it is not separated from it by the heat of fire or air unless the cloth is totally destroyed. Nor can the oil be separated from the cloth itself except by washing and the drying heat of fire. 

Now, <term>water<note>In alchemy, "water" often represents the "spirit" (*spiritus*), the volatile medium that moves between substances.</note></term> is the spirit extracting this soul from the <term>bodies<note>original: *corporibus*; the solid metallic or mineral starting materials.</note></term>; when the soul is extracted from the bodies themselves, it remains in that spirit, because the spirit is its dwelling place. Therefore, the soul is a tincture dissolved and carried in the spirit, just as the dye of dyers is carried by water onto a cloth. Then the water departs through drying, and the tincture remains fixed in the cloth because of its oiliness. Therefore, if the spirit is made of water, it is the vessel in which the "tincture of air" is carried. When this is brought back onto the <term>white foliated earth<note>original: *terram albam foliatam*; a purified, flaky white solid achieved after several stages of the Great Work.</note></term>, the spiritual water is immediately dried, and the soul—which is the tincture of air—remains in the body. Thus the spirit retains the soul, just as the soul retains the body: since the soul does not stay in the body except by the mediation of the spirit. But when they are joined, they are never separated: because the spirit retains the soul, just as the soul retains the earth.

### *On the washing of fire and earth. CHAPTER XII.*

As for the dregs <note>original: *fæces*; the solid sediment or residue left after distillation.</note> of the oil that are made, collect them every time and put them back with the fire: for they are of the fire and hold the blackness—that is, the redness—which must be ground with the "first water" and burned gently until it becomes a powder entirely free from the humidity of the air. For in this way it is necessary to join the dregs, and even the water, with the earth, and to <term>calcine<note>To reduce a substance to powder by means of intense heat.</note></term> them strongly with a lit fire until it is off-white and void of humidity. Therefore, calcine fire with fire, and earth until it becomes clean and deprived of blackness. That which ascends from the fire is the red oil; but that which ascends from the earth is the precious white [oil]. Indeed, the oil that is separated more slowly from the bodies is considered more precious. Therefore, complete all things in their proper time, part by part, and preserve each one of them.

The sign of this will be when nothing evaporates from the body if a small piece of it is placed upon an glowing-hot plate; then it will surely be "appropriated" <note>original: *appropriatum*; rendered fit or specifically suited for the next stage of the work.</note>. By the name of "spirit," we mean that which is subtle, pure, and appropriated; by the name of "body," we mean that which is off-white and dry. Indeed, in none of our operations is water necessary, except...

### CHAPTER XIV.

The third regimen of the stone is to <term>reduce<note>original: *reducere*; here meaning to bring back or restore a substance to its previous state, specifically by adding liquid back to a dried solid.</note></term> the moist water upon the dry earth, so that it may recover its lost moisture. But since the earth consists of two bodies, and two elements are dry, hard, and stony—namely fire and earth, which agree in dryness—they are to be prepared together, since they share a single preparation. Therefore, join the thickness of the fire with the earth after the withdrawal of the air, and prepare them together for the sake of shortening the time, and also so that their mixture may be good, and the preparation not be confused, and that one may dye the other well, and lest they be burned by the "fight of the fire." Whence to prepare them together is safer and more direct. Their preparation, moreover, is so that they might receive their greater moisture. For the <term>calcined<note>Reduced to a dry powder through intense heat.</note></term> body is disconnected, because it is entirely deprived of water. Whence since it is naked, empty, and very thirsty, it drinks up its own aqueous moisture.

Grind the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: *Mercurius*; here referring to the purified substance or "spirit" of the work.</note> strongly until it becomes one: we do not perform <term>sublimation</term> <note>A process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then condenses back into a solid; it was used to purify materials and "spiritualize" them.</note> except so that bodies may be reduced to a subtle matter—namely, so that they may be spirits, and so the body may be light enough to be directed into all things, whether into the Sun <note>Gold</note> or into the Moon <note>Silver</note>. We have therefore performed this sublimation for three reasons. The first is: so that the body might become a spirit of subtle matter and nature; the second is, so that the Mercury may incorporate itself well with the <term>lime</term> <note>original: *calce*; the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly roasted or calcined.</note>; the third is, so that the whole may take on a white and red color. For this reason, when the lime is sublimated for the Moon, it must be white, and the Mercury likewise white; and when the lime is sublimated for the Sun, it must be red, and the Mercury likewise red, heated by fire, and it must be a "waxed" powder <note>A powder that has reached a consistency that melts like wax without smoking.</note>: because one cannot work well for the Sun or the Moon except in such a way.

And with the Mercury which you sublimate for the Moon, do not mix any other thing: because the heat of the Sun does not enter into the Moon, nor that of the Moon into the Sun. Therefore, do not send red Mercury to the white, nor white to the red; but place each species with its own kind, and place it over a lit fire, and sublimate the whole. Do not mix that which remains below with that which rises upward <note>original: *descendit sursum*; literally "descends upward," a common linguistic paradox used by alchemists to describe the rising of vapors toward the top of a vessel.</note>, but put each part aside: since that which remains in the bottom you shall repeat for sublimation through the mercurial incorporation, until the whole has risen; otherwise, do not place it in the <term>Mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterium*; the final, perfected state of the alchemical work.</note>.

Let the <term>alembic</term> <note>The upper, cooling part of a still.</note> in which you sublimate the Mercury be made of glass, and the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower, gourd-shaped vessel that holds the material to be heated.</note> be of glazed earthenware, whose opening at the base is wide so that the Mercury may rise more freely. The alembic, indeed, must be joined with the cucurbit in such a way that the Mercury cannot escape: because Mercury is not sublimated except through the smokiness of the air. Therefore, if it found an open place, it would fly off into smoke, and the Mastery would be ruined. See then what we have said, see: for all these words are necessary and worthy of praise. Let these things therefore suffice for the completion of the white and red sulfur.

### *Concerning the fourth regimen, which is to fix, and how a ferment that is otherwise fixed is necessary for the process of fixing.*
### CHAPTER XIX.

The fourth regimen of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> is truly to <term>fix</term> <note>original: *figere*; to make a substance "fixed" or non-volatile so that it no longer evaporates or escapes when heated in a furnace.</note> the white sulfur and the red sulfur upon a fixed body—namely, so that the white sulfur is fixed upon silver, and the red sulfur is fixed upon gold. This is because, according to Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher was often cited as a legendary authority in alchemical texts, representing the "wisdom of the ancients."</note>, whoever does not <term>coagulate</term> <note>To turn a liquid or vapor into a solid mass.</note> the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum viuum*; mercury.</note> extracted from the bodies into a white sulfur that can endure the fire, finds no path to the white work; and whoever does not coagulate the said quicksilver into a red sulfur that can endure the fire, finds no path to the red work. Therefore, do not weary your body so much in these high matters which you cannot reach if you are ignorant of how to perform these things, for you will wander far off the path.

Work prudently, then, and not by chance. For without a <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermentum*; a small amount of a noble metal (gold or silver) added to the mixture to "leaven" the whole mass and transform it into its own nature, much like yeast transforms dough.</note>, neither the Sun <note>Gold</note> nor the Moon <note>Silver</note> will emerge, but rather something else that does not remain stable in its essence in nature's care, unless you have hidden it in the body which you prepared from the beginning—namely, the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, join the sulfur with that body, so that it may generate its own likeness, and let that which you compose become the Elixir.

When it has been joined with its proper body, it does not stop acting upon the rest until it converts the whole. For this reason, when you wish to ferment, mix the sulfur with the body so that the whole becomes a ferment; for the ferment will bring our sulfur back to its own nature, color, and flavor in every way. Wherefore, the ferment for the white work shall be white, and the ferment for the red work shall be red. This is evident because if you were to place a ferment of silver with the sulfur of gold, it would bring it back to its nature, but not to its color. Similarly, if you were to place a ferment of gold with the sulfur of silver, it would convert it not to its nature, but to its color, and vice versa. Therefore, do not mix the ferment of one sulfur with the sulfur of the other, because the ferment of gold is gold, and the ferment of silver is silver. And note well that there are no other ferments upon the earth, because that which was never fixed, and is not fixed, can never fix anything else.

<summary>This page describes the "fixing" stage of the Great Work, explaining that the volatile alchemical sulfur must be stabilized by joining it with a "ferment" of gold or silver to create the final Elixir. Arnald emphasizes that gold must be used for the red work and silver for the white work, as the ferment dictates the final nature of the Stone.</summary>

### That the weight of the ferment must exceed the weight of the sulfur, or be equal to it.
### CHAPTER XX.

Therefore, in every <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermento*; in alchemy, a small amount of precious metal—gold or silver—added to the mixture to "leaven" or transform the base material into more of itself.</note>, the weight of both parts must be noted, so that the total amount of volatile <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: *sulphuris*; here referring to the active, combustible, and volatile principle of the metal, rather than common brimstone.</note> does not exceed the total amount of its body. Otherwise, the bond of the marriage would be turned into the flight of a spirit that is not <term>fixed</term> <note>original: *fixi*; made stable so it no longer evaporates under heat.</note>. Hence Plato says: "If pure sulfur is cast upon a multitude of the body, such that it has power over it, it quickly converts it into a powder, the color of which will be like the body upon which the spirit is cast—namely, gold or silver." I will speak later of the weights of all things; but because the sulfurs cannot enter the bodies except by the mediation of water <note>original: *aqua*; often referring to a chemical solvent or "mercurial water" rather than common water.</note>, which acts as a middle ground between the sulfur and the ferment in every arrangement:

First, as Avicenna says, you shall place the **earth**, for it is closest to the ferment. Second, you shall place the **water**. Third, you shall place the **air**, for it is closest to the water. Fourth, you shall place the **fire**, for it is closest to the air. Nevertheless, do not place fire in the **White Elixir** <note>original: *Elixir ad album*; the stage of the work that produces silver.</note>, for the White Elixir is completed by three elements in which there is no fire; the **Red Elixir**, however, uses all four wheels <note>original: *quatuor vtitur rotis*; a metaphor for the four elements or the complete cycle of the Great Work.</note>.

Open, therefore, and close; dissolve and bind by these things, and dry them out; for water is the medium for joining their <term>tinctures</term> <note>original: *tincturas*; the coloring principles or transformative powers of the metals.</note>—namely, those of the oil, the air, and the fire. I speak now a word of Philosophy: If you first put in the oil, then mortify it in the earth, for the water would enter it. If, however, you have placed it: afterward the oil will stand upon the water; but if you have placed the water and afterward the earth, the water will be heavier than the earth. Therefore, tinge the water with the earth so that it may cling to it. If you have killed one of the four, all are dead. If one has more of the **soul** than the other, it is worth nothing. Therefore, prepare the ferment, which is the soul, before the fermentation, so that it becomes a powder that is <term>calcined</term> <note>original: *calcinatus*; reduced to a fine powder through high heat.</note>, dissolved, and hardened; for if you do not prepare the ferment well, your <term>magistery</term> <note>original: *magisterium*; the "Mastery" or the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note> is worth nothing.

Therefore, by as much as [you refine] your body, by so much you will have a better result, so that you can project one weight upon a hundred; and a hundred upon a thousand; and a thousand upon ten thousand; and ten thousand upon a hundred thousand, and a million upon ten numbers, and so on unto infinity.

...from the air, and the air from the aid of water, and the water from the aid of earth. Therefore, fix the water in the earth so that the air may be fixed in the water; for if you have killed [the process] with water, all the elements are dead. <note>In alchemy, "killing" or "drowning" the work refers to adding too much liquid solvent, which prevents the substance from ever reaching a stable, solid state.</note> Nevertheless, water is not fixed without earth because:

> *No fruit ever rises without a seed,*
> *In which, while the seed dies, it is said to bear fruit;* <note>original: "Consurgit nullus vnquam sine semine fructus, / In quo dum moritur semen fructum dare fertur." This refers to the concept of "mortification," where the initial matter must "die" or decompose to be reborn as the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

Since earth is fixed in itself, it retains and fixes the other elements with it. Water, however, being moist and cold, surrounds the earth, and constricts and holds it; for cold and moisture are the constrictors of dryness. Nevertheless, [moisture] receives an impression quickly and loses it quickly. Dryness, on the other hand, receives an impression with difficulty and loses it with difficulty. Therefore, when the moist and the dry have tempered one another, the dry gains from the moist a construction of parts—or a continuity and an ease of impression—and the moist gains from the dry the ability to hold an impression firmly and to endure all fire. Thus, by this means, the moist prevents the dry from separating, and for this same reason, the dry prevents the moist from its fluidity. 

Air, for its part, surrounds the water and clarifies it, or rarefies the earth, and <term>tinges</term> <note>To "tinge" is to permanently change the color and nature of a substance, a key goal of the Elixir.</note> or fixes it so that it is fit for extension and fusion. Fire, however, matures the whole compound, refines it, turns it red, mixes the air, and consolidates it; it also constricts the coldness of the earth and water so that they return to a healthy balance of <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionis"; the specific ratio of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determines a substance's nature.</note>. Therefore, the heavy elements like earth and water are more helpful for <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio"; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to evaporation by heat.</note> and for the tincture. Do not eat, then, that which you do not drink, but eat one after the other according to reason; for excessive heat makes the body [ripen] faster than is proper. Do not be a spendthrift, nor a miser, but maintain moderate weights according to an equal and unequal complexion. Understand what I have said, for I have omitted nothing that is true.

For fixed sulfur, since it is a "coagulator of things already coagulated," naturally congeals its Mercury through frequent sublimation upon it.

This is because every dry thing naturally desires its own moisture, seeking continuity within its parts. 

Whence it is necessary for the practitioner of this science to fully know the powers of nature and to adhere firmly to them; for nature is sufficient for you and for herself, just as she is sufficient in everything she requires for her own perfection. ->*How we ought to understand solution, sublimation, and coagulation.*<-

### CAP. XXX.

However, do not think that I teach solution here so that the **Elixir** <note>The perfected alchemical substance.</note> is reduced to mere water; rather, it is so that you may refine <note>original: "subtilies"; to make a substance thinner, purer, or more volatile.</note> it as much as you can, and divide its parts that were joined in fixation <term>fixio</term> <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>, and convert its dryness, moisture, and coarseness into a simple form. For the work of solution was invented for the sake of sublimation, and for nothing else. Thus the union of bodies with spirits <term>spiritus</term> <note>The volatile or gaseous components of a substance, as opposed to the solid 'body'.</note> occurs through dissolution, and not through sublimation; for bodies require nothing but sublimation so that they may be better joined with spirits. Indeed, their sublimation is a dissolution into water; for distillation <term>destillatio</term> <note>The process of purifying a liquid by boiling and condensation.</note> draws the stone <term>lapis</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note> from potential into actuality, because it makes it entirely refined. Wherefore, when the body is totally refined, the spirit is joined with it universally, and they cannot be separated from each other by any kind of ingenious method. For the firming of spirits with bodies happens when the bodies become refined, so that they are able to retain the spirits. Therefore, he who can separate the bodies with the first sublimation achieves the best end; for the entire intention of the worker must be in the union of spirits with bodies. And the union of these spirits occurs when the bodies are refined, so that both spirits and bodies become subtle through dissolution, grinding, and roasting <note>original: "assationem"; the process of heating a substance in its own moisture or in a dry vessel.</note> them with the spirits. Understand, therefore, what I have said, for it is all useful, and nothing in my words is superfluous. If indeed you do not...

# ARNALD. CHAPTER 1.

Understand therefore the saying of the Philosopher: *The actions of active agents are according to the disposition of the receiver* <note>original: "actus activorum in patientis sunt dispositione"; an Aristotelian principle meaning that for a change to occur, the material being acted upon must be in the right state to receive that change</note>: by which it is understood that the <term>Elixir</term> <note>a preparation capable of changing base metals into gold or silver</note> cannot be made except from matter that possesses this perfect disposition. I testify to you, moreover, that such a readiness exists in the matter from which—by my own hands and witnessed by my own eyes, though through another's teaching as I said before—the Elixir was made, converting <term>Saturn</term> <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note> into the <term>Sun</term> <note>the alchemical name for Gold</note>. 

Indeed, I have already named this matter for you: it is the **Magnesia of the Philosophers**, from which the Philosophers extracted the gold hidden within its body. From this they found <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note> from quicksilver and sulfur from sulfur, which is a stone in appearance and action, but in its nature it does not imitate the qualities of a common stone. Therefore it is called the **Stone that is not a stone**, and it is mixed to dissolve—our aforementioned quicksilver, not quicksilver in its own [common] nature, nor yet in the nature to which it is brought by the mine. Rather, it is our quicksilver in the nature to which our craftsmanship leads it. 

This is our <term>copper</term> <note>original: "æs"; also translated as bronze or brass, here referring to a specific alchemical stage or material</note>, from which the true <term>tincture</term> <note>the coloring agent or elixir</note> is made; from this is made the marriage of **Gabricus and Beya** <note>original: "Chabrici & Veyæ"; legendary alchemical figures representing the union of the active sulfur and the passive mercury</note>, in which the King is with his wife. And all these things that refine them are in the air itself, so that it may be made more clearly evident through the record of the operation. 

This is the spirit by which we dye, and it is the body of which it is said in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Quicksilver is not obtained from bodies melted by common melting, but from that which lasts as long as the spouses are united in true marriage, namely until the **whiteness** <note>original: "albedinem"; the *albedo* stage, signifying the purification of the matter</note>." 

This is the stone found on the summit of mountains. It is rightly called "mineral," yet it is also said to be "animal" because it possesses a soul <note>original: "animam"</note>. Wherefore it is said in the *Assembly*: "Copper, like a man, has a body and a soul." Likewise, everything that has a spirit also has blood. Likewise, it is called "spirit," that is, sulfur through the body; and "copper," that is, of magnesia or of the earth—which, having been made spiritual, is called the **gold** that was hidden in the body of magnesia. Wherefore it is said: "Son, extract from the ray its shadow." It is also clear that the soul can be applied in this way, since it shows certain virtues of the mind. For it moves and is moved; it acts and it suffers <note>is acted upon</note>. Wherefore in the *Assembly*: "O nature, how all..."

...it dominates <note>The Latin text begins with a fragment, "nib. imminet," likely "omnibus imminet" (dominates all) or "ignibus imminet" (stands over the fires), describing the substance’s power</note> and surpasses all things. It is the **sharpest vinegar** <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; a common alchemical term for a powerful acid or solvent used to dissolve metals</note>, which makes gold become pure spirit; and when it is mixed with a body, it becomes one with it and turns it into spirit. Since it is called "animal" <note>in alchemy, substances were often classified as animal, vegetable, or mineral based on their perceived vitality or growth potential</note>, it is therefore also rightly called a **vegetable** substance. For in the operation, it will be "vegetated" <note>meaning to grow or develop vitality</note> from strength to strength, refining and purifying itself and improving its own colors until it assumes the desired redness, in which lies perfection, and gains the power of penetrating and dyeing. Many wanderers do not recognize this animal, **Berbel** <note>possibly a code-word or a reference to a specific mountain plant or substance used in the process</note>, this saffron or saffron-colored thing, this vegetable stone nurtured in the mountains. Yet it is sold openly at a very low price.

### *The purification of the stone follows, before it is placed in the cooking. CHAPTER II.* <note>original: "decoctio"; the process of heating a substance in a liquid or its own moisture</note>

This work which I have shown to your understanding—pure, clean, pleasant, sincere, and upright—reveals itself when fashioned into thin plates. Through the process of melting in fire, it is purged of its mineral coarseness; through the methods of **elevations** <note>original: "elevationum"; refers to sublimation, where a solid is heated into a gas and then recollected as a solid higher up in the vessel</note>, it becomes subtle, leaving behind certain residues of burning and earthiness mixed in the union of the thin and the strong, while certain corrupting moistures are exhaled. 

There are two signs of this refinement: one is that the substance being elevated is a **lemon-yellow spirit** <note>original: "spiritus citrinus"</note>, which has become a less-hard stone with a degree of transparency. The other is that which remained in the bottom of the vessel: a thin, **black earth** <note>original: "terra nigra"; often representing the "nigredo" stage or the impurities left behind after the spirit has risen</note>. Note this: in this elevation, if done correctly, something permanent is found, which must by force be brought over the abundant **volatile** <note>original: "volatilis"; a substance that easily evaporates</note>, elevated, and that which was elevated must be returned to the part that remains, until the whole becomes "fleeing" <note>meaning the entire mass becomes capable of sublimation</note>. 

And then the aforementioned black earth remains from both, and the stone is converted into that hard, very yellow stone. Do not be content with the aforementioned volatility until the entire mass of this stone, elevated by fire and returned to its vessel, continually ascends through it; so that nothing—neither clean nor filthy—remains at the bottom. When it is thus most perfectly elevated, it will be fulfilled in the perfection of the **Philosophical Work**, which the scripture commands, saying: *Gently with* <note>the text breaks off; this is likely a reference to the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus: "Separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity."</note>

### CHAPTER III.

Therefore, let that "spiritual roundness" <note>likely referring to the refined, spherical essence of the matter</note> which has been made, which turns copper into the four elements, enter a temperate bath. This bath should be such that the body becomes gentle and contains a light fire, which is meant to consume the corrupting moistures. A furnace of such a design must therefore be made so that a slow fire may be administered within it—one that cannot be increased. The glass vessel holding the matter must be covered with a cap <note>original: "ferto"; a circlet or lid</note> made from a vessel of the same shape cut through the middle. This vessel must be one cubit <note>roughly 18 to 22 inches</note> long and narrow at the top; the narrowness should permit nothing of the spirit to exhale. Its length should cause any fumes that happen to rise to fall back down, and it should consume the corrupting moistures within itself. 

Regarding this furnace and vessel, for those seeking them, it is a "vision of the lily" <note>original: "lilij visio"; a poetic expression suggesting that the arrangement requires practical insight or divine inspiration rather than just following a written recipe</note>, not merely a piece of writing. The heat must circulate around the vessel from all sides, so that the heat is equal everywhere; otherwise, it could not truly be called a "bath." At the top of the furnace, there should be a hole through which a long, round piece of glass should exit, closing the mouth of the said vessel. By touching this glass piece, one can know if the matter is being cooked with the proper heat. And if by chance any smoke is seen to rise within the vessel, the weight <note>original: "dosis"; here likely referring to the seal or the specific arrangement of the apparatus</note> does not allow it to exhale, even if the vessel were held open. ### On the degree of fire when blackness arrives.
### CHAPTER IV.

When indeed the whole is black, let the fire of the same degree be continued until the whiteness, which is hidden in its belly, appears: for in this way the "fixed" <term>fixum: a substance that has become stable and can withstand the heat of the fire without vaporizing</term> draws near. It should be noted, however, that many colors appear within that blackness, of which the Philosophers make mention. For sometimes the whole becomes green, sometimes leaden, sometimes a violet color; sometimes it is green on one side of the vessel and black on the other, or leaden inside and green outside; yet all these colors are understood to be included under "black." And since no essential perfection exists in them, the Philosophers principally name only three colors among the rest, which are called the "virtues of the soul": namely black, white, and red. Therefore in the *Turba*: "Venerate the King and his wife; and do not burn them, lest you drive them away with excessive fire: for you do not know when you will need those who improve the King and his wife. ### CHAPTER VIII.

This ash, however, lacks the ability to melt <term>fusione: the state of being liquid or molten</term>. As for how it might enter to perform its staining <term>tingat: the alchemical action of "dyeing" or transforming a base metal's nature</term>, surely liquefaction—or a "sweat"—is returned to it through the method handed down by the Philosophers. What then is that method? Is it by dissolving into water? Certainly not, for the Philosophers do not care for waters that stick to the touch and moisten it. For it is said in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the most famous early Latin alchemical texts, written as a debate between ancient sages</note>: "Beginners, hearing of 'water,' thought it was the water of the common people; but if they had read our books, they would surely know that our water is permanent." What then is the true water, which does not stick to the touch, but flows over the surface moistening nothing, like quicksilver <term>argentum viuum: literally "living silver," or mercury</term>? Who then shall make such water? Truly I say, he who knows how to make glass. For this matter is nothing other than what wants to be joined to itself, for it contains within itself everything it requires. And if what I have said before is well considered, you will know how to obtain from this ash a red stone <term>lapis rubeus: the final Philosopher's Stone, representing the pinnacle of the work</term> of intense color, possessing little transparency, breakable with a slight blow, yet fusible, penetrating, entering, and staining with a perpetual yellowing <term>citrinatione: the shift toward a golden color</term>. One weight of this converts a hundred thousand parts and more of Saturn <term>Saturni: the metal lead, associated with the slow, heavy planet Saturn</term> into the Sun <term>Solem: the metal gold, associated with the brilliance of the Sun</term>. Yet there is a subtlety in the method of projection <term>proiectio: the final act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto a molten base metal to transform it</term>; if this is ignored, the one holding the Elixir gains nothing from it.

<unclear>the matter would carry out</unclear> its work, but they strive for the impossible in their materials: as if they believed they could generate a human from a dog. Is it any wonder, then, if they turn out to be liars in their works? For even with the Stone, and from what is known in the Practice of the work, many very subtle doubts remain; but you should truly believe that the Philosophers set down the truth in their books. But after the death of any writer, their writings are misunderstood by some—whereas if the author himself were present and could explain them theoretically according to the word, he would verify the works through their effects <note>Arnald is arguing that alchemical texts are not intentionally deceptive, but that the "experimental" or "practical" knowledge is lost when the author is no longer there to guide the student.</note>. I, however, have explained the entire work to your wisdom in all things; and I have confirmed certain points through the sayings of the Philosophers, though I have bothered to cite few of them. I omitted these for a specific reason: because I assume that you have enclosed all the writings of the Philosophers within the casket of your own heart. And so I do not doubt that you have applied all those things to my words by yourself—just as I, through the experience I have seen, understand the writings of the wise; otherwise, I would not know them. And if I have been brief in this short account, it is for this reason: for I assume you know the foundation so well that the intention of this matter will not be hidden from you. And it is enough for me that my understanding is open to you alone, and that this kind of truth might not depart from this light <note>original: "ab hac luce," meaning from this world or life</note> with me. Out of reverence for your fatherly person, I have produced this *New Light* upon these matters, since I have chosen you among all others in the world as the one most worthy of this matter in my judgment. May the Most High lead you to the desired end.

->*Here ends the New Light.*<-

### Here begins the Perfect Mastery and the Joy of Master Arnald of Villanova, sent by him to the illustrious King of Aragon <note>Likely King James II of Aragon (reigned 1291–1327), who was a patron of Arnald.</note>; which is indeed the Flower of Flowers, an incomparable Treasure of all things, and a Pearl. In this is found the composition of the true Elixir <term>Elixir: the "medicine" or catalyst used to transform base metals into gold or silver</term>, both for the white and for the making of the red—namely, for the Sun and the Moon <term>Solem & Lunam: alchemical code for Gold and Silver</term>—declared in a summary.

### THE FLOWER OF FLOWERS
<note>original title: FLOS FLORVM</note>

...of the science of the elements, they have handed down this science: but not understanding it, they work with blood, hair, eggs, and urine, and many other things. From these, they first extracted the <term>four elements</term> <note>The classic building blocks of matter: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> so that they might complete the work with them. First, they separate by <term>distillation</term> <note>A process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then condensing it back into a liquid to purify it.</note> a clear water from the materials mentioned above; then, a lemon-colored oil on the surface, which they say contains fire and air, while the black earth remains at the bottom. Afterward, they wash the earth with water and whiten it by soaking it, boiling that water repeatedly until the earth is whitened.

Then they return that oil to a prepared fire by distilling it until the said earth "drinks" everything—namely, the water, the oil, and the <term>tincture</term> <note>The "color-giving" essence or the soul of the material.</note>. And they cast this earth (or ash) upon a molten body—specifically upon copper or another metal—and they find nothing. And yet, they act and work according to what the Philosophers say in their books; thus they have fallen into error by failing to find the entrance. Their error is this: it is certain that from a human, only a human is generated, and from a horse, only a horse. Similarly, other animals produce only those like themselves. Since, therefore, these biological substances are utterly foreign to the nature of metals, it is impossible for a "generation" of metals to arise from them. This is because metals are not generated except from their own <term>seed</term> <note>original: "spermate proprio". Alchemists believed metals grew in the earth like plants or embryos from a specific "sperm."</note>.

Now, <term>quick-silver</term> <note>mercury; original: "Argentum vivum"</note> is the seed of metals and their origin, as all the Philosophers say, and as both practice and reason teach, which I shall declare further below. However, the things mentioned before—namely blood, hair, eggs, and other vegetable matters—are not quick-silver. Therefore, the generation or <term>transmutation</term> <note>The changing of one metal into another, specifically base metals into gold.</note> of metals from them is impossible. Consequently, the aforementioned things are not our "Stone," even though they are sometimes used as examples in books.

There are others who take the <term>four spirits</term>—namely, arsenic, sulfur, quick-silver, and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux in soldering and in various alchemical recipes.</note>. These are called "Spirits" because they flee from the fire and fly away into smoke. They take these in place of the four elements, seeing that the Philosophers say in their books that the science lies in the spirits. They treat these as being of an "airy" nature, or work to make them airy. Afterward, they "fix" them by <term>calcining</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note> them so that they become "earthy" in nature; they dissolve them so they become "watery" in nature; and they distill them so they become "fiery" in nature.

# ARNALD'S [WORK]

->Vu 3<-

And they put these things together according to books, believing they possess the science of the elements; they combine these mixtures in ways that are beyond understanding, and yet they find nothing, falling into error just as the first ones did. The causes of their errors are many, but two are sufficient for the present discussion. 

One cause is that, as previously stated, metals are not generated except from their own **seed** <note>original: *spermate*. In alchemical theory, metals were thought to grow in the earth from a specific "seed" or "sperm," much like plants or animals.</note>. These other substances, however, are not the seed of perfect metals—with the exception of **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argento vivo*. We know this today as the element mercury.</note>. Therefore, it is impossible for generation or **transmutation** <note>The process of changing one metal into another, specifically base metals into gold or silver.</note> in metals to occur from them. 

The second cause is that **sulfur** and **arsenic** are quickly burned in the fire, and by the fire's heat, they are turned into charcoal. How, then, can anything good be expected from such a substance? Since it is so quickly consumed and reduced to coal, it cannot even withstand the "water." Thus, it is clear to anyone looking closely that neither these things by themselves, nor joined with metallic bodies, nor mixed with oils extracted from eggs, blood, hair, urine, or other vegetable matter, nor mixed with each other, constitute our **stone** <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> or our **medicine**. This is for the reasons stated above: just as in the generation of a human, a land animal, or a plant, no foreign mixture is used, but only their own specific seeds or sperm. Therefore, our **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*. This refers to the highest goal or process of the alchemical art.</note> requires no foreign mixture.

Some believe they can find this science in salts or alums; they dissolve, **calcine** <term>calcine</term> <note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to reduce it to a powder or change its properties.</note>, melt, and prepare them. Some cast these alone upon **imperfect bodies** <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper, which alchemists hoped to "perfect" into silver or gold.</note>. Others mix them with **spirits** <note>Volatile substances that "fly" from the fire, such as sulfur, arsenic, or ammonia.</note>, as has been mentioned. They prepare them with "prepared bodies," and find nothing. The cause of their errors is similar to the ones before.

And some believe they can draw the medicine from metallic bodies alone; they prepare them by calcining, dissolving, and congealing, and they cast the result upon a metal body, yet they are deceived. Their error lies in the fact that they did not take the seed of those metals from the beginning, but rather the "body" as it exists in its final nature. From the reasons given, it appears that our science will not be found or possessed in blood, nor in eggs, nor in hair or vegetables, nor in the aforementioned "spirits" by themselves, nor in salts, **vitriols** <term>vitriols</term> <note>original: *atramentis*. Historically referring to metallic sulfates or "inky" substances used in chemical processes.</note>, or any other such things.

But some, looking more deeply, have considered **quicksilver** to be the beginning of metals, and it—

...the origin [of metals] is found in the sulfur of heat. They have cooked and sublimated **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: *argentum vivum*. The cause of their error is this: just as the seed of a man is of no use and brings forth no fruit unless it is cast into the woman’s **womb** <note>original: *matricem*. Alchemists frequently used reproductive metaphors; the "womb" here refers to a vessel or a metallic base that can receive the "seed."</note>; so also **Mercury**, which is the seed, is of no use unless it is cast into the **womb of bodies** <note>original: *matricem corporum*. Some have mixed it by amalgamating it with a "body" and washed it with fresh water for so long that it appeared to them that the body had been rendered clean. They then cooked it until the end, believing that the quicksilver would be mixed into such a body, but they found nothing. They found the body remained unclean and the quicksilver simply vanished; though the body was indeed cleaner than it had been before. The cause of their errors is this: the seed is not joined with the body except by the mediation of the **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*. In alchemical coding, the Moon represents the metal Silver.</note>, because the **soul** <note>original: *anima*.</note> is the medium between the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritum*. Volatile substances like mercury were called spirits.</note> and the body, joining them to one another. Now, the soul is the **leaven** <term>leaven</term> <note>original: *fermentum*. Much like yeast in bread, alchemical leaven was thought to "infect" and transform the whole mass into a higher state.</note>; for just as the soul gives life to the human body, so the leaven gives life to the "dead" body that has been completely altered from its nature. Hence the soul holds the leadership, exercising its powers; therefore, what the leaven is shall be explained below.

Some mix **imperfect bodies** <note>Base metals like lead, tin, or copper.</note> with **perfect bodies** <note>Noble metals, specifically gold and silver.</note> and put them to the test, believing that the good and pure parts of the imperfect bodies will remain with the perfect ones, while the rest vanishes. But, failing to see the truth, they were deceived, and a wicked thought took hold of them. The cause of their error is this: the corrupting nature of the imperfect bodies prevents them from being perfected. And note that here one must have a double power: one which separates the burning sulfurous earth from the mixture, and another which converts that which is already separated back to its own nature. A body in its coarse state cannot possess this power. All common workers have tried these things, just as I myself have already tried them, and they were led into a state of shock, as if despairing of the science, abandoning the **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*. The completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note> because of the weakness of their intellect.

But now I want you to know that the matter of all metals, and their seed, is Mercury—cooked and thickened in the belly of the earth by a cooking, sulfurous heat, and—

...and according to the variety of the **sulfur** <note>Sulfur was viewed by alchemists not just as the chemical element, but as the active, masculine principle of heat and combustion in metals.</note>, and its quantity in the earth, different metals are generated.
