With this being assumed—that metal can be resolved into quicksilver—the opinion of those is refuted who say: "Spirits and other substances cannot be transmuted into the elements and nature of metals." This is not true, as they assert, unless the metals are first reduced to their **primary matter** <note>original: *primam materiam*. The fundamental, formless substance from which all physical things are created.</note>. The reduction of a metal to its primary matter is both easy and possible. 

Likewise, I show you that **multiplication** <term>multiplication</term> <note>The process of increasing the quantity or the potency of the alchemical substance.</note> in metals is possible. For everything that grows and is born is multiplied, as is evident in plants and trees: for from one grain, a thousand grains are procreated; from one tree, infinite branches proceed, from which different and infinite trees are made. And thus they increase and multiply their number. Since metals are born and grow in the earth, then augmentation and multiplication in them is possible, even unto infinity.

I have shown you, dearest son of wisdom—if you have understood what has been said—the errors of all those commonly working [in this art] along with their causes, and I have affirmed this to be true with an open and clear demonstration. I tell you, dearest one, that it is necessary first to reduce the **bodies** <note>Solid metals.</note> to their primary matter, so that generation or multiplication may occur in those same matters. Once this is done, take all of that and place it in a glass vessel, cooking it over a slow fire until you see a **blackness** appearing on the surface. Remove this as delicately as you can, and continue the cooking, repeatedly skimming the blackness from the surface until no more blackness appears and the water remains clear. Now you possess the **water** and the **earth**, which is to say, the two principal elements.

Next, take that earth and the blackness <note>In alchemy, this black stage is called the *nigredo*, signifying the death or decomposition of the material before its rebirth.</note> which you collected and place them in a glass vessel. Pour the aforementioned water over it until the water floats above the earth, and cook it over a slow fire for four days. Then set the water aside and cook again, and so on, until the earth is **whitened** and clear. And this is what the **Philosophers** <note>The ancient alchemical authorities.</note> meant when they said: "This earth putrefies and is purified with water"; for once it has been purified, the whole <term>mastery</term> <note>original: *magisterium*. The completed alchemical process or the production of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> will be directed by the help of God. When it has been cleaned and clarified, or whitened, as has been said, by means of the water—which, together with the said earth and the mediation of heat, is both coagulated and thickened—you must cook the earth itself (which has been thickened and coagulated with its own water) without any other water. Do this over a strong fire in a glass **cucurbit** <note>The bottom part of a still, shaped like a gourd.</note> with a glass **alembic** <note>The "helmet" or lid of the still that collects vapors.</note> placed on top, until whatever water remains ascends into the alembic and the earth remains **calcined** <note>Reduced to a dry powder by high heat.</note>. The third word is: Which is the **purification of the earth**. Concerning which purification Morienus the Philosopher says: *This earth putrefies and is purified with water; which, when it has been purified, the whole mastery will be guided by the help of the deity.* Concerning which Pheyret also said in the *Book of the Assembly* <note>original: *libro Turbæ*, referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts appearing as a transcript of a debate among Greek philosophers.</note>: *Join the dry with the moist, namely, the earth to the water.* Behold, you now have the water by itself, and the earth whitened with the water.

Therefore, this calcined earth is that of which Miseris the Philosopher says: *Do not despise the ash in the lower place, for it stands as witness. For in it is the crown of the heart, which remains.*

The ash is afterward mixed with the aforementioned earth. The **Ferment** is added, which the Philosophers call the **soul**. And this is because, just as the human body is worth nothing without its ferment, or its soul, so it is in this work. For the <term>ferment</term> <note>original: *fermentum*. A substance (usually gold or silver) added to the alchemical base to "leaven" it and transform the whole into a precious metal.</note> is a body, as has been said, and it converts other things to its own nature. And know that there is no ferment except the **Sun** and the **Moon** <note>original: *Sol & Luna*</note>, that is, gold and silver assigned to these planets. This is because, just as the Sun and Moon rule over the other planets, so these two bodies rule over others and convert them to their own nature; and therefore they are called "Ferment" by many.

It is necessary, therefore, for the ferment to be introduced into the bodies, because it is their soul. This is what Morienus said: *Unless you have cleansed the unclean body, and returned it whitened, and put the soul into it, you have directed nothing in this <term>mastery</term>.* <note>original: *magisterio*. The "Great Work" or the achievement of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> Therefore, let there be a conjunction of the ferment with the cleansed body; and then the spirit, when it is joined, rejoices and is glad

### THE FLOWER OF FLOWERS
<note>original: *Flos Florum*, a common title for alchemical treatises attributed to Arnaldus de Villa Nova.</note>

...more subtle, it is just like that which is above; and the whole shall be turned into earth.

It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that **our stone** <note>original: *lapis noster*, the goal of the Great Work</note> consists of the four elements, and is composed of soul, body, and spirit. And our stone, as certain Philosophers say, is made from one thing with one [thing]: and certainly they speak the truth. For certainly our whole **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*, the complete chemical process of transformation</note> is performed with **our water**, and from it, and through it. For this water dissolves the bodies (as was said above) not by that solution which the ignorant believe—where a substance is merely converted into "cloud-water" <note>likely referring to simple evaporation or condensation</note>—but by the true Philosophical solution: namely, that the substance is converted into the **first water** <note>original: *aquam primam*, the primordial matter from which metals were thought to originate</note> from which they were formed from the beginning. 

For this very water **calcinates** <note>original: *calcinat*, to reduce a metal to a powder, or "calx," through heat or chemical action</note> the bodies and reduces them to earth. This same water transforms the bodies into ash, and incinerates, whitens, and cleanses them, according to the word of **Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist often quoted in medieval texts</note> who says: "That **azoch** and fire wash the **laton**, and cleanse it, and utterly snatch away its darkness from it." 

Now, **laton** <note>original: *lato*, an impure alloy of base metals representing the "black" stage of the work</note> is an unclean body, and **azoch** is **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*, mercury</note>. And the water joins diverse bodies prepared in the aforesaid manner with such a union that the power of fire cannot separate them, nor can any other tempering or testing; it defends them from being consumed by fire and merges one into the other. 

Furthermore, the water **sublimates** the bodies, but not by the "common sublimation" which fools intend—thinking that to sublimate is simply to cause a substance to ascend upwards through the force of fire. Because of this error, they take calcinated bodies and mix them with "sublimated spirits"—namely with mercury (☿), arsenic, and salt—and by means of a strong and sudden fire they cause the bodies to rise with the spirits, and they claim that the bodies are then "sublimated." In this, such people are mistaken and deluded, because they find those bodies afterwards to be even more unclean than they were before.

Know, most dear one, that our sublimation is not "to ascend upwards"; rather, the **sublimation of the Philosophers** is to make something high and great out of a low and corrupt thing—that is, to make it pure. Just as we say: "That man is sublimated," meaning he is placed in a position of dignity; so too we say the bodies are sublimated—that is, converted into subtlety and into another nature. Nevertheless, among the Philosophers, to sublimate is the same as to refine and to separate, all of which our **blessed water** <note>original: *aqua nostra benedicta*</note> achieves. Thus, therefore, understand our sublima-

And this is what the Philosophers mean when they say that our mastery is nothing other than the male and the female and their joining. When the earth is whitened, then it is called "pregnancy": because now the earth has been impregnated. Next, the **ferment** <note>original: *fermentum*, an agent used to "ripen" or stabilize the chemical transformation</note> is joined with the prepared imperfect body, as has been said, until they become one in color and appearance, and then it is called the **Birth**. For then our **stone** <note>original: *lapis noster*, the goal of the alchemical work</note> is born: which, having been born, is called the **King** by the Philosophers. Whence the Philosopher says in the book *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *liber Turbæ* (Turba Philosophorum), one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "Honor your king coming from the fire, crowned with a diadem, and nourish him until he reaches a perfect age." Whose father is the **Sun**, and whose mother is the **Moon**. However, they take the Moon for the imperfect body: and the Sun for the perfect body. Truly, at last follows the nourishment, until it is increased by a great augmentation. Moreover, let the nourishment—its own milk and the seed from which it was from the beginning—be soaked in **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury (argentum vivum), considered a primary fluid in alchemical theory</term> often and again, until it has what suffices: that is, until perfection, which is the end of our whole work.

Dearest friend, through those things which have been said, you can easily understand all the obscure words of the Philosophers, and you will know that they all agree on the same thing. And the **mastery** <note>original: *magisterium*, the secret process of the Great Work</note> is nothing other than what I have told you before. Now you have, dearest friend, the solution of the body and its reduction to the **prime matter**. Then you have its conversion into earth. After the whitening, you have its refinement into air; because then, by distilling the moisture that is found, it becomes airy. That which descends, and the earth remains **calcined** <note>original: *calcinata*, reduced to a white powder by heat</note>: and then it is of a fiery nature. And you also have the joining of these to one another: and you have the mixing of soul and body: and also the joining of soul, body, and spirit together, and their conversion into one another: and finally, you have the augmentation. The utility of which is greater than can be perceived.

# ARNALD OF VILLA-
## NOVA’S EPISTLE CONCERNING
### *Alchemy to the King of Nap-*
->les.<-

Know, O King, that the wise ones have placed many things and many modes of working into this labor—namely to dissolve and to coagulate—as well as many vessels and weights. This they did to blind the ignorant and to explain the aforementioned work to those who understand. And note, O King, that the wise have declared the work in brief words: although they set down and added many other words so that it would not be understood except by the wise. Indeed, the wise have said that there is one **stone** <note>original: *lapis*</note> which is composed of four natures: which natures are, in fact, fire, air, water, and earth. This stone is a stone in appearance and to the touch, but not in its inner nature; it is called a "stone," or a certain "composite." This composite, when it is guided along the correct path, is that which is sought, in which there is nothing superfluous nor anything lacking. On the contrary, all things that are in the stone are necessary to it, and it needs nothing else. This stated composite, or stone, is of one nature and is one thing; this thing, in the **cooking** <note>original: *decoctione*, the process of heating a substance in a fluid</note> of the fire, displays diverse colors before it becomes the perfect **white stone**.

And note, O King: that the longer the said stone remains in the fire, the more its goodness increases. This is not so in other things, because all other things are burned up in fire and lose their **radical moisture** <term>radical moisture: *humiditas radicalis*, the fundamental life-giving fluid thought to exist in all matter, which keeps it from being brittle or combustible</term>. Truly, this stone alone is always improved in the fire and its goodness grows; the fire is the very nourishment of that stone. And this is one of the clear signs for recognizing the stone itself: understand this well. This composite or stone is divided before the operation in two ways: the first is **physical** <note>original: *corporalis*</note>, the other is **spiritual**. One comes out of the other, they are united, they are governed one with the other, and one improves the other. And the Philosophers named one **Masculine** and the other **Feminine**.

And note, O King, that when the Philosophers named **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: *argentum vivum* (mercury)</term> and **magnesia** <note>original: *magnesia*, in alchemy this refers to a primary "mother" substance or mineral, not the modern chemical magnesium</note>, saying:

It congeals **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver," known today as mercury</note> in the body of **magnesia** <term>magnesia: in alchemy, this is not the modern magnesium, but a term for the "raw" or "primordial" material that contains the potential for the philosopher's stone</term>: which the wise ones did not understand as the common quicksilver that is seen; rather, they understood that quicksilver is the **moisture** <note>original: *humiditas*</note> of the said stone. For magnesia is not that which is commonly seen; instead, they called the entire composite "magnesia," in which is contained the whole of the said moisture, which is quicksilver. This moisture is not like other moistures, for this moisture runs through the fire, and in that same fire, it dissolves, congeals, blackens, whitens, and finally reddens and perfects the entire composite.

And note, O King, that in the work no additional things are placed: but one thing only, nor is it necessary to perform any grinding by hand, nor should anything be added to the said stone. And note, O King, that the **white earth** is called the **perfect white stone**, and the **red earth** is called the **perfect red stone**: and indeed this white earth, through the governance of the said work and without the help of any other thing, is converted into redness.

The water, or quicksilver, is called the moisture that is in the said stone. And note that while the water or moisture exits from the composition or stone, the whole composite is turned black at the bottom of the vessel: and thus by continuing the fire, this blackness in which the moisture resides is turned into diverse colors, and finally into whiteness. This moisture is also called **air**, and this air or moisture is mixed with its earth and with the other elements existing in the stone itself, until it becomes a certain white thing.

And note, O King, that the said airy moisture, which is quicksilver, is one and the same thing with its aforementioned earth and the other elements persisting in the stone itself. This moisture, although it be little, is sufficient to nourish and to perfect the entire stone from which the moisture itself originated. And it must be known that in the said composition, or stone, there are **Sun** <note>original: *Sol*, representing Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>original: *Luna*, representing Silver</note> in virtue and power, as well as the elements in their nature. For if these were not in the composite itself, they would not be produced; neither Sun nor Moon would be made from it. And yet this is not the same Sun as the common sun, nor the same Moon as the common moon: because the Sun and Moon existing in this composition are better than common nature, because the Sun and Moon of the said composite are alive, while the others, the common ones, are... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "sunt" suggests the next page begins with "sunt mortui," meaning "are dead."</note>

# THE LITTLE BOOK OF BROTHER ROGER
## BACON, AN ENGLISHMAN, ON THE
### Marvelous Power of Art and
### Nature.

I respond to your request: For although nature is powerful and wonderful, nevertheless **art** <term>art: *ars*; in this context, it refers to human technology, skill, or scientific application rather than fine art</term>, using nature as an instrument, is more powerful than natural force, as we see in many things. Whatever, however, is outside the operation of nature or art is either not human, or is fake and filled with frauds. 

For there are those who—by swift movement, the appearance of limbs, the variety of voices, the subtlety of instruments, by darkness, or by conspiracy—offer many wonders to mortals which do not have the truth of existence. The world is full of these, as is manifest. For **jugglers** <note>original: *ioculatores*; these were medieval entertainers who performed sleight-of-hand and acrobatics.</note> lie with great speed of hands, and **pythonesses** <term>pythonesses: *pythonissæ*; female soothsayers or ventriloquists, named after the Pythian priestesses, who were believed to be possessed by spirits</term> form human voices in the belly and throat by fictions and with the mouth, from far or near, as they wish, as if a spirit were then speaking in human fashion; they even feign the sounds of animals. 

Truly, the causes hidden under the grass and buried in the sides of the earth <note>Bacon is likely referring to hidden acoustic tubes or mechanical devices used by fraudsters to simulate "spirits" speaking from the ground.</note> show that it is a human force, and not a spirit, which they feign with a great lie. When, truly, in the shadows of twilight or at night, inanimate things are moved swiftly, it is not truth, but fraud and deceit. Conspiracy, moreover, feigns all things that men desire, according as they are arranged among themselves. 

In all these things, neither physical reason considers them, nor art, nor does the power of nature hold sway. For this reason, it is a most wicked occupation when a person despises the laws of **Philosophy** <note>In Bacon’s time, "Philosophy" encompassed all of what we now call science and logic.</note> and, against all reason, invokes nefarious spirits so that through them he may fulfill his will. And in this lies the error: that they believe spirits are subject to them, and that spirits are compelled by human will. For this is impossible, because human power is far inferior to that of spirits. Or because they wander further in this error, that through some natural things which they use, they believe that evil spirits are either summoned or given form, and...

<summary>Roger Bacon begins his treatise by arguing that human technology (art) can surpass nature, while simultaneously debunking "magic" and spiritualism as mere trickery, sleight-of-hand, or ventriloquism.</summary>

Regarding what should be held concerning charms <note>original: *carminibus*; refers to spoken incantations or ritual songs.</note> and characters <term>characters: *characteres*; magical signs, sigils, or symbols inscribed on talismans.</term>, and things of this sort, I consider them in this way. If someone, wishing to perform this work before the people, were to make characters and utter charms so that the force of attraction might be completed, this whole work would be an error. In this same way, very many things are hidden in the books of Philosophers in many modes; in these, a wise man ought to have the prudence to neglect the charms and characters and test the work of nature and art. Thus, he will see both animate and inanimate things concur with nature because of a natural conformity, and not because of the power of a charm or character. And so, many secrets of nature and art are thought to be magical by the unlearned, and magicians foolishly trust in charms and characters, believing they provide power; for the sake of attaining these, they leave behind the work of nature or art because of the error of charms and characters. Thus, both types of these men are deprived of the utility of wisdom, forced by their own folly. 

There are, however, certain prayers instituted in ancient times by men of truth, or rather ordained by God and angels, and things of this sort can retain their original power. Just as in many regions, certain prayers are still made over glowing iron, and over the water of a river, and similarly other things in which the innocent are proven and the guilty are condemned, and by the authority [they] believ- <note>original: *credun-*; the catchword for the following page's first word, *credunt* (they believe).</note>

Indeed, some sensible powers are produced by things. # OF MARVELLOUS POWER
## ON THE POWER OF WORDS AND SPIRITS

as was said) and similarly in good things. When a man possesses these qualities—a good **temperament** <term>complexion: *complexio*; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) that determines a person's health and personality</term>, bodily health, youth, beauty, elegance of limbs, a soul clean of sins, strong thought, and a vehement desire for some work—then whatever can be achieved through the **species** <term>species: invisible emanations or "likenesses" that objects and living things project into the air to interact with the world</term> and virtue of a human, and through the **spirits** <term>spiritus: in medieval medicine, these are subtle, refined vapors produced by the heart that carry life, heat, and thought through the body</term> and **natural heat** <term>calor naturalis: the biological warmth essential to life and digestion</term>, it must necessarily happen more strongly and more vehemently through such spirits, vapors, and influences than if any of those qualities were lacking. This is especially true if a strong desire and a valid intention are present.

And for this reason, some great things can be performed through the words and works of a man, provided that all the aforementioned causes concur. For words originate from within, through the thoughts of the soul and the desire moved by the spirits, heat, and the **vocal artery** <note>original: *vocalem arteriam*; refers to the trachea or larynx, which medieval thinkers believed was a direct conduit for the heart's heat and spirit.</note>. The generation of these words has open paths through which there is a great exit of spirits, heat, evaporation, virtue, and the **species** which are produced by the soul and the heart.

Therefore (all other things being equal), alterations in spiritual matters are produced through words, according to what is owed to them by the power of nature. For we see that through these arteries from the heart, in our interior parts, breath, yawning, and many releases of spirits and heat occur. These sometimes cause harm when they proceed from a body that is sick and of a bad temperament; conversely, they are beneficial and strengthening when they are produced from a body that is clean, healthy, and of a good temperament.

In the same way, certain natural operations can occur during the generation and speaking of words, when they are accompanied by the intention and desire of the speaker. Hence it is not without merit that it is said that the **living voice** <note>original: *vox viua*</note> has great virtue—not because it possesses that imaginary power which magicians pretend it has, nor merely to "make and alter" things in the way they imagine, but according to what nature has ordained.

Therefore, one must apply oneself to these matters with great caution, for a man can easily err. Many do err on both sides: some deny every such operation, while others go too far and decline into **magic**. There are many books in the world filled with **charms** <term>carmina: incantations or songs meant to produce a physical effect</term>, **characters** <term>characteres: magical signs, symbols, or sigils</term>, prayers, conjurations, sacrifices, and such things, which are purely magical. By **Notory Art** <term>notoria arte: a medieval system of magic that sought to gain knowledge or memory through the use of complex diagrams and prayers</term>: and an infinite number of such things, which possess the power of neither art nor nature, but are the fictions of magicians. **It must be considered, however:** that many books are regarded as magical which are not so, but contain the dignity of wisdom. For if one finds a work of nature or art in any of them, let him accept it; if not, let him leave it as suspect and unworthy of a wise man. It belongs to the magician to treat things that are superfluous and unnecessary; for as **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli the Elder (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher</note> perceived in his *Book on Fevers*: the rational soul is not hindered in its operations unless it is held back by ignorance. And **Aristotle** <note>The following refers to the *Secretum Secretorum*, a text Bacon believed was written by Aristotle to Alexander the Great</note> maintains in the *Book of Secrets* that in such matters, a healthy and good man can do all things that are necessary for a human, provided there is an influence of divine power. And in the third book of the *Meteorology*, he says that there is no power except through God; and at the end of the *Ethics*, he says that there is no virtue, neither moral nor natural, without celestial and divine influence. Thus, when we speak of the power of particular agents, we do not exclude the governance of the **Universal Agent** <term>agentis universalis: God or the primary moving force of the universe</term> and the **First Cause** <term>primæ causæ: the philosophical concept of the ultimate origin of all motion and existence</term>; for every first cause has more influence upon the effect than the second cause, as the first proposition of the *Book of Causes* <note>original: *de causis*; refers to the *Liber de Causis*, a widely read Neoplatonic philosophical work</note> proposes.

I will now relate, therefore, wonderful works of art and nature, so that I may afterwards assign the causes and methods of things, in which there is nothing magical; thus it may be said that all magical power is inferior to these works and unworthy of them. And first, through the configuration of art itself: for **instruments of navigation** can be made without men to row them, so that the largest ships, even sea-going ones, may be borne along with a single man steering them, and with greater velocity than if they were full of men rowing. These things are wonders, if anyone knew how to use them fully in the proper quantity and material. 

But regarding another kind, I propose many wonders which, although they may not have much utility, nevertheless provide an unspeakable spectacle of wisdom, and can be used to prove all hidden things which the inexperienced common folk contradict. These are similar to the attraction of iron by a **magnet** <term>adamantem: here referring to a lodestone or magnet</term>: for who would believe an attraction of this kind unless he saw it? And many miracles of nature exist in this attraction of iron which are not known by the common folk, as experience teaches the diligent seeker. 

There are even more and greater things than these. For similarly, by a "stone of gold and silver," there is an attraction of all metals. Likewise, a stone "runs" toward vinegar <note>likely a reference to the movement caused by the chemical reaction of calcium carbonate—like a piece of coral or shell—in acid</note>: and plants [move] toward each other, and parts of animals divided by location run back together by natural motion. After I have perceived things of this kind, nothing is difficult for me to believe, when I consider it well, whether in divine or human matters. 

But there are things greater than these: for the whole power of mathematics only produces a surface instrument, according to the artifice of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> in the 8th book of the **Almagest** <note>The definitive astronomical manual of the Middle Ages</note>, in which all things that are in the heaven would be truly described by their longitudes and latitudes. That they might be moved naturally by the **daily motion** <term>motu diurno: the apparent daily rotation of the heavens around the Earth</term>, however, is not in the power of the mathematician. 

Yet a faithful and magnificent **experimentalist** <term>experimentator: Bacon’s term for a practitioner of experimental science</term> strives that a model might be made from such material and with such artifice. That it might naturally be moved by the daily motion of the heavens seems possible to him, since many things are carried along by the motion of the celestial bodies—such as comets, the tides of the sea, and other things in their entirety or in their parts. For then all the instruments of **astrology** <note>original: "Astrologiæ"; in Bacon's time, astrology and astronomy were often used interchangeably as the study of the stars</note> would cease to be necessary, both the learned ones and the common ones, and the treasure of a single king could scarcely be compared to its value. And although not regarding a miracle, yet regarding public and private utility, greater things can be done: namely, that an abundance of gold and silver may be brought forth as much as a man pleases, and yet not according to the possibility of nature <note>Bacon is hinting at alchemical transmutation, suggesting that science can surpass natural limits</note>...

[mo]tility <note>This completes the word "motilitatem" from the previous page, referring to the natural movement of substances toward one another</note>, but according to the perfection of art; for there are seventeen modes of gold, specifically eight from the mixing of silver with gold. Yet, what follows is even greater: though the **rational soul** cannot be coerced, it can nevertheless be effectively disposed, induced, and stirred up so that it might freely choose to change its character, affections, and will according to the judgment of another. However, the highest degree to which the perfection of art can reach, combined with all the power of nature, is the **prolongation of life** for a vast amount of time. Many experiments have shown that this is indeed possible. For **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of *Natural History*</note> recounts that a soldier, strenuous in body and mind, lasted in his integrity beyond the usual age of man. When **Octavian Augustus** asked him what he had done to live so long, he replied in a riddle: that he "placed oil on the outside and mead <note>original: "mulsum," a drink made of wine and honey</note> on the inside." 

But many things happened afterward. For a peasant digging in the fields with a plow found a golden vessel containing a noble liquor; thinking it was "dew from heaven," he washed his face and drank it, and he was renewed in spirit, body, and the excellence of wisdom. From a mere cattle-driver, he became a porter for the **King of Sicily**, which happened in the time of King Ostis. It has also been proven by the testimony of papal letters that a **German** <note>original: "Almanicus"</note> captured among the Saracens received a medicine by which he prolonged his life for up to five hundred years. Neither Hippocrates nor Galen reached a prolongation of life of this kind. I respond to you that they did not even reach many modest virtues which were later known by other diligent scholars; and therefore they could very well have been ignorant of these greater things, even though they labored toward them. But they occupied themselves too much with other matters, and were led more quickly to old age, consuming their lives in lesser and common affairs, although they did perceive many secrets.

But we know in these days that this truth is known, and therefore Aristotle could have been far more ignorant of the deeper secrets of nature. Even now, the wise are ignorant of many things which the common crowd of students will know in future times. Hence, this objection is entirely vain.

Having enumerated certain things concerning the power of nature and art—so that from a few things we may gather many, from the parts the whole, and from particulars the universal—let us see that it is not necessary for us to aspire to magic, since nature and art suffice. I wish now to pursue these specific things in order, and to give the causes and the method in detail. 

But I consider that the secrets of nature are not handed down on the skins of goats and sheep <note>referring to parchment</note> so that they may be understood by just anyone, as Socrates and Aristotle intended. For Aristotle himself says in the *Book of Secrets* <note>original: "libro Secretorum," likely the *Secretum Secretorum*, a popular medieval text attributed to Aristotle</note> that he would be a "breaker of the celestial seal" who would communicate the secrets of nature and art, adding that many evils follow the person who reveals secrets.

And in the *Book of Stones* it is written that he diminishes the majesty of things who divulges mysteries; nor do secrets remain secret when the crowd is conscious of them. Indeed, by a probable division of the common crowd, one might say the opposite against the wise: for what seems true to everyone is true; and similarly what seems true to the wise, and especially the famous. Therefore, what seems true to the many—that is, to the common crowd <note>original: "vulgo"</note>—must necessarily be false. I speak here of the "common crowd" as it is distinguished from the wise in this discussion. For in the common conceptions of the mind, the crowd agrees with the wise—

...of this intention. But know truly that when you have finished, you must begin again. <note>This suggests the cyclical nature of alchemical "rotations" where the process is repeated to increase potency.</note>

I wish to hide another secret from you. Prepare **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> by **killing it** <note>original: "mortificando"; the process of changing mercury's liquid, metallic state into a powder or chemical compound</note> with the vapor of tin for the sake of pearls, and with the vapor of lead for the **Iberian stone** <note>original: "Ibero lapide"; likely a reference to a specific mineral or a stage in the transmutation process associated with Spain/Iberia</note>. Then let it be ground with drying agents and **vitriols** <note>original: "atramentis"; literally "inks," referring to metallic sulfates like green or blue vitriol</note> and such things (as has been said), and let it be roasted: then let it be **sublimated** <note>original: "sublimetur"; heated until it rises as vapor and solidifies at the top of the vessel</note>. If it is for the sake of union, do this 10 times; if for redness, 21 times, until the humidity in it is destroyed. It is not possible for its humidity to be separated by vapor alone, like the oil mentioned before, because it is so strongly mixed with its dry parts and has no fixed boundary; as was said regarding the metals mentioned earlier. In this chapter, you will be deceived unless you understand the hidden meanings of the words.

It is time for the third chapter to be unfolded so that you may understand the **key to the work** which you seek. The **calcined body** <note>a substance reduced to a dry powder by high heat</note> is sometimes applied, and this is so the moisture in it may be broken down by salt, **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "sal armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, used as a powerful solvent and flux</note>, and vinegar; and sometimes it is "fed" with quicksilver, and sublimated from these things until it remains as a powder. Therefore, the "keys" of the art are **congealing, dissolving, waxing, and projection** <note>original: "congelatio, resolutio, inceratio, proiectio"; these are the fundamental operations of the Great Work</note>, and this is both the end and the beginning. But **purification, distillation, separation, sublimation, calcination, and investigation** work together, and then you may rest.

Six hundred and two years of the Arabs having passed <note>This dates the request to approximately 1205 or 1206 AD</note>, you asked me about certain secrets. Take, therefore, the **Stone**, and calcine it with a light roasting and a strong grinding—but without sharp <note>corrosive or acidic</note> substances. But at the end, mix in a little fresh water, and compose a **releasing medicine** <note>original: "medicinam laxatiuam"; in this context, a solvent that "loosens" the bonds of the material</note> from seven things, if you wish, or from six, or from five, or however many you wish: but my mind rests upon two, the better of which will be in a proportion of six, or thereabouts, as experience can teach you. Nevertheless, **dissolve the gold** at the fire, and strain it better. But if you believe me, you should take one thing: this is the **secret of secrets of nature** <note>original: "secretum secretorum"; a term for the highest hidden knowledge</note>, powerful in wonders. Therefore, with the mixture of two, or more, or the **phoenix** <note>original: "phœnice"; a symbol for the highly refined Red Sulfur or the final stage of the work</note> (which is a unique animal) at the fire, incorporate them by strong motion: if a hot liquor is applied to this four or five times, you will have your ultimate goal. But afterwards, the celestial nature is weakened if you pour in hot water three times, or...

->### OF ART AND NATURE<-
->#### Yy 3<-

...or four times. Therefore, divide the weak from the strong in different vessels, if you believe me: then pour out what is good. Likewise, apply the **powder**, and carefully squeeze out the water that remained; for certainly it will draw out the parts of the powder that have not been incorporated, and therefore collect that water by itself: because the powder dried from it has the power of the **medicine** in a laxative body.

Do therefore as before, until you distinguish the strong from the weak, and apply the powder three, four, five times, or more, and always do it in the same way. And if you cannot work with **hot water**, you shall apply force. If, however, it breaks because of the sharpness and softness of the medicine, with the powder applied, cautiously add more **gold** and soft substance. If, truly, it is because of an abundance of powder, add more of the medicine. If, indeed, it is because of the strength of the water, moisten it with a pestle, and gather the material as best you can, and separate the water bit by bit, and it will return to its state; you shall dry this water, for it contains the powder and the water of the medicine, which are to be incorporated just like the powder.

Do not sleep here: because a very useful and great secret is contained within. If indeed you knew how to properly arrange parts of a burnt branch, or willow, and many other things, they will naturally preserve the **union** <note>original: "vnionem"; a term for a large, high-quality pearl, often used symbolically for the alchemical goal</note>, and do not forget this, because it is worth much. 

Truly, you shall mix the **Trinity** <note>likely referring to the three alchemical principles: sulfur, mercury, and salt</note> with the liquefied union, and there will arise (as I believe) something similar to the **Iberian stone**, and without a doubt it has been **killed** <note>original: "mortificatum"; a process of chemical transformation where a metal's external characteristics are destroyed to reveal its inner nature</note> by the **vapor of lead**. You will find the lead if you squeeze it from the **corpse** <note>original: "mortuo"; the "caput mortuum" or solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation</note>, and you shall bury the corpse in the furnace with twigs. Keep this secret: for it is of no use <note>A common warning suggesting the knowledge is useless to the uninitiated or if performed without exactitude</note>, and do the same with the vapor of the **Pearl**, or the **stone of the Tagus** <note>original: "lapide Tagi"; the Tagus river in Spain and Portugal was famous in antiquity for its gold-bearing sands</note>, and bury the corpse nonetheless, as I said.

With the years of the Arabs having passed <note>A chronological marker, likely referring to the transmission of alchemical knowledge from Arabic sources to the Latin West</note>, I respond to your petition in this manner: You must have a medicine which dissolves in the melt, and is rubbed into it, and penetrates into its second limit, and is mixed with it, and let it not be a **fugitive slave** <note>original: "seruus fugitiuus"; a classic alchemical name for Mercury (quicksilver), because it evaporates and "escapes" the fire</note>, and let it transmute it: let it be mixed with the root of the spirit, and let it be fixed by the **calx** <note>original: "calcem"; the powder produced by heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures</note> of the metal. 

It is estimated, moreover, that **fixation** <note>original: "fixio"; the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note> prepares [the matter], when the body and spirit are placed in their proper location and are **sublimated**: and let it be done so many times that the body becomes spirit, and the spirit becomes body. Take, therefore, from the **bones of Adam** <note>original: "ossibus Adę"; a symbolic term for the "earth" or primary matter used in the work, sometimes identified as salt or a specific clay</note>, and from the calx under the same...

<meta>This page concludes the "Epistle on the Secret Works of Art and Nature, and on the Vanity of Magic" by Roger Bacon. # ON THE MARVELOUS POWER OF ART AND NATURE
#### Yy 3

...by weight, and there are six parts for the stone of stone <note>original: "lapidem petralem"; likely referring to the mineral stage of the alchemical work</note>, and five for the stone of union <note>original: "lapidem vnionis"; a pearl, symbolizing the perfected substance</note>, and let them be carried together with the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; here referring to concentrated alcohol or a powerful solvent</note>, whose property it is to dissolve all other things, so that it may be dissolved and roasted within it. The sign of inceration <note>the process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency</note> is that the medicine melts upon a red-hot iron. Then, let it be placed in that same water in a humid place, or suspended in the vapor of very hot and liquid waters; then let it be congealed in the Sun. Finally, you shall take salt of stone <note>saltpeter</note>, and you shall convert quicksilver <note>mercury</note> into lead, and again you shall wash and purify the lead with it, so that it may be very near to silver; and then work as before. Likewise, you shall drink the whole thing thus. But however, of salt of stone <term>LVRV VO PO VIR CAN vtriet</term> <note>This famous anagram is traditionally decoded as "pulvere carbonum" (charcoal powder). Combined with the mentioned saltpeter and sulfur, this constitutes the recipe for gunpowder.</note> and of sulfur, and thus you shall make thunder and lightning; thus you shall perform the artifice. See, however, whether I speak in a riddle or according to the truth. 

And some have thought otherwise; for it was told to me that you ought to resolve everything to the primary matter, concerning which you will find information from Aristotle in common and famous passages, for which reason I remain silent. And when you have those things, then you will have many simple and equal things, and this you shall do through three contrary and various operations, which I previously called the "Keys of the Art." Aristotle says that the equality of powers concludes the action and passion of bodies. Averroes <note>a 12th-century Andalusian philosopher</note> also says this, in his disagreement with Galen <note>an influential Greek physician</note>. And this is considered the simplest medicine that can be found, and the purest, which is effective against fevers and passions of the soul and bodies, and yet it is cheaper than anything else. He who rewrites these things shall have the key which opens and no one closes, and when he has closed, no one opens <note>A reference to Revelation 3:7, suggesting the divine or absolute nature of this secret knowledge.</note>.
